refuted.problem: The two planes are typeset at incompatible measures inside one column, and only one of them is governed. Measured at 1440: the desk paper is 1262px wide carrying an 812px text column, leaving a 403px void of white to the right of every line the person wrote, while the .topFoot right-aligns "Put it back" against the far 1262 edge — so nothing on the desk shares a right edge with anything else. One plane down, index rows run the full 1262px and carry 155 characters on a single 14.5px line. At 1920 the desk void is 883px and the index line is 1520px; at 2560 the void is 1523px and the line is 2160px. The read column is the one thing that never grows. The result is that the desk stops reading as the primary plane and starts reading as a wide empty box above a very long list, which is the opposite of the locked architecture: the index is denser, darker and edge-to-edge, so it wins the eye.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The finding's central mechanism is measured wrong, and its fix would damage the widths that matter.

1. The load-bearing claim is false. "Index rows run the full 1262px and carry 155 characters on a single 14.5px line… at 1920 the index line is 1520px; at 2560 the line is 2160px." I measured the ink, not the grid cell, with a Range over .idxText at 1280/1440/1920/2560. The row's grid cell does stretch (1040 / 1520 / 2160), but the line of text does not: ink width is 1018px / 927px / 1052px for the first three rows and is IDENTICAL at 1440, 1920 and 2560. notebook.js word-safe-trims the preview to a cap (~155 chars) and the cap binds from 1440 up, so the "line" the finding says reaches 2160px is 1052px of text followed by an empty cell. The index does not become "denser, darker and edge-to-edge" as the window grows; it becomes sparser. The stated failure — a very long dense list winning the eye over the desk — is the opposite of what the file does.

2. The desk numbers are also derived rather than measured, and they are off. At 1440 .readBody is 766px, not 812 (68ch of Geist at 18px), inside a 1214px content box, so the void is 448px, not 403. At 2560 it is 1568px, not 1523. Small, but it confirms the measurements were reasoned from ch values rather than read off the page.

3. What remains is taste stated as defect. A held prose measure with the paper's own chrome (.readSrc, .topFoot) spanning the full card is the standard and correct answer, not a fault: iA Writer, Bear, Notion and Linear's issue body all hold the text column and span the action row. The finding's own complaint that "nothing on the desk shares a right edge" argues for making the toolbar obey the prose measure, which is worse ergonomics — the primary action would float mid-paper. Everything on the desk already shares a left edge at the gutter, which is the edge that governs reading.

4. The fix would make it worse where people actually are. A 76ch (~840px) column centred inside a sheet that is 1322px at 1440 strands ~240px of dead white inside the sheet on each side, and shrinks the desk's paper so it no longer fills the desk — which weakens the locked "paper lifted off a sheet" depth reading rather than strengthening it. It also deletes preview text from every index row at exactly the width the pressure state (36 notes) needs it. The fix then contradicts itself: "above ~1500px hold the column and let the ink floor take the extra width" describes capping the SHEET, which is a different change from the one specified, and the only one of the two with any merit.

5. Scope. The interaction check's no-sideways-scroll sweep runs 1920/1440/1280/1024/768/390; 2560 is outside the tested envelope, and 2560 is the only width where the finding's grievance has any visual force.

The one salvageable grain, which this finding does not state: above roughly 1600px .idxTag and .idxWhen drift ~1100px away from the text they annotate, so a tag stops reading as belonging to its row. That is a sheet-level cap or a right-hung metadata rail, not a 76ch measure imposed on both planes, and it is a different finding from the one filed.

refuted.problem: The loudest object on the resting sheet is a filled black pill counting undone work, sitting third in the header reading order, and the second loudest is the indigo-washed index row below it. The desk — the surface that carries the product's entire promise of the three seconds between a thought and it being safe — is white paper on a white sheet, a 1px 9% ring and a 4-6% shadow, with an ink-3 placeholder: the quietest object on the page. The eye lands on the count, then the index, then the place to write. It gets worse after use: capturing a note increments the pill 8 to decide → 9 to decide (measured), so the visual reward for capturing a thought is watching the blackest object on screen count up. At 390 the pill is the single largest element on the phone and the workspace name "The Orchard, events" is dropped entirely, so on the capture device you can see how far behind you are but not which venue you are writing into.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Drove ?state=notebook at 1440 and 390 in chromium, measured geometry and computed styles, read master.css and notebook.js, and read the 1440 and 390 locked-notebook frames.

The load-bearing salience claim is false where the finding stakes it hardest. "At 390 the pill is the single largest element on the phone" — measured at 390x844 the chip is 85x26 = 2,222 px². The elements above it: .sheet 281,604, .index 247,380, .dock 23,800, .head 23,064, .rail 22,320, and every single .idxRow 13,265. The chip is one sixth of one index row and one eleventh of the dock. It is not the largest element by any reading; it is not close.

"The desk is the quietest object on the page" is taste asserted as measurement, and the frame contradicts it. .top is 1262x154 white paper carrying the largest type in the product (18px topField vs 14.5px index), sitting under a 62px header with nothing competing, lifted by --ring plus a three-layer --paper shadow off two visible .behind sheets at translateY 11/22px and opacity .92/.66. In locked-notebook--1440x960.png the desk owns the top third of the sheet unambiguously. Quieter objects than the desk on that same frame: the .behind sheets at 40% opacity, .verb ("Dictate", "Read a photo") at --ink-3, .topMeta "Nobody else can read this" at --ink-3, and every .idxWhen timestamp. The genuine largest ink mass on the resting sheet is the index's column of twelve 600-weight titles at full --ink-1, not the 85px pill.

The core prescription is already implemented. head() reads `state === "review" ? "" : ...` — verified: at ?state=review the chip count is 0, and the only filled-ink object in the hand is .act[data-ink] "Turn into a task". The file already suppresses the counter the moment you enter the hand and transfers filled ink to the decision verb. "Reserve the filled-ink fill for the review hand, where deciding is the job" describes the artifact's existing state discipline.

The fix would make the work worse, in three of its four parts.
1. `.chip[data-off]` is `background:none; color:--ink-2; inset ring 1px --line; font-weight 400` — pixel-for-pixel the grammar of `.idxTag` ("To decide" / "In Tasks"), which is passive decoration. The chip is a button (data-act="review") and on the phone it is the only route into the hand in the entire header. Outlining it collapses the one call to action into the same grammar as a status label. That is the checklist's own "facts stated in two grammars" defect, introduced rather than removed. (Note: `.chip[data-off]` is dead CSS — never emitted by notebook.js.)
2. `--ring-strong` on .top breaks the direction's stated surface ladder, written in master.css at the token: "Nothing on white goes above 9%: a heavier rule reads as a box, and this product does not draw boxes around a person's own writing." --ring-strong is 16%.
3. `--paper-lift` on .top at rest is not a new idea — it is `[data-paper="deep"] .top { box-shadow: var(--ring), var(--paper-lift); }`, an authored decision axis the "press" room already ships. The founder's locked room chose "stacked". Worse, --paper-lift is the token that makes `.top[data-live]` distinct; spending it at rest reduces the rest→live transition to the indigo ring alone, deleting a designed state delta.
4. Placeholder --ink-3 (0.62, 5.3:1) → --ink-2 (0.72) narrows the gap to typed text at --ink-1 (1.0) to a tenth of an alpha step, so an empty field and a full one stop reading apart at a glance. --ink-3 already passes AA, so this is not an accessibility fix; it degrades the empty/full signal that Things, Bear and iA Writer all preserve by sitting placeholders well below body ink.

The one grain with substance — .headName is `display:none` at ≤720px while the chip survives, verified — dies on its own fix. Restoring the name at 390 was measured live: the header is 372px carrying wordmark 51 + chip 85 + headActions 163 plus four 13px gaps, and .headName gets 50px, so `min-width:5ch` plus text-overflow renders "The O…". The fix does not deliver "which venue you are writing into"; it delivers a truncated stub, and does not name what else would leave the header to make room.

Finally, the "it gets worse after use" argument is unresponsive to its own fix. 8 to decide → 9 to decide is verified (typed a note, Ctrl+Enter, chip reads "9 to decide"), and it is honest: the new note is created `pending: true`, and the announcement says "Kept. 15 notes, 9 waiting on a decision." Demoting the chip's fill does not stop the number going up. The actual reward for capture is the named settle animation, the live-region confirmation and the undo strip — none of which the finding weighs.

refuted.problem: Both of the product's promises are typeset as fine print. The voice disclosure — the legally required sentence saying the words leave the device — is 12px, the smallest size in the entire product, at a 92-character measure, wrapped to three lines in the bottom-left corner, while 'LISTENING 0:07' above it gets 12px at weight 600 in uppercase with a pulsing dot. The seam is the same shape: 'Your note is still here, still private, still yours to edit.' is 12px in --ink-3, the faintest permitted ink, sitting below a 12.5px explanation and beneath a 16.5px/600 field. So on the screen whose entire purpose is 'the note never leaves', the sentence stating that is the smallest and faintest object present, and the derived fragment that does leave is the boldest. Hierarchy is carrying the opposite of the argument.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The seam half of the finding is factually false about the artifact, and every clause of the proposed fix is a no-op, invalid CSS, or a regression.

1. "Sitting below a 12.5px explanation and beneath a 16.5px/600 field" is wrong. Measured live at 1440x960 (?state=seam): `.stays` top=203, `.peelField` top=290, `.peelWhy` top=399. `.stays` is inside `.top` on the note sheet itself (notebook.js:627), 87px ABOVE the peel field and 196px above `.peelWhy`, and the peel is a separate sheet that starts below it. The locked-seam frame shows it plainly: the lock glyph and "Your note is still here, still private, still yours to edit." close the note, directly under the person's own writing, before the peel exists. The promise is already attached to the object it is about and already read first.

2. The fix "move `.stays` above `.peelWhy`" is therefore a no-op on markup that is already in that order — which is evidence the finding was written from the CSS file's line order (496 vs 495), not from the rendered page.

3. "12px, the smallest size in the entire product" is wrong. master.css carries 10px (x3), 10.5px (x3) and 11px (x7), and the seam screen alone renders 10px, 10.5px and 11px live. `.peelLabel`, `.indexHead`, `.idxDay`, `.specName` and `.saidWas b` are all 11px.

4. The disclosure's ink concern is already handled and documented as handled. `.darkNote` is `--on-ink-2` = 7.7:1 on the ink floor, not the faintest ink on that screen — `.darkSaid .tail` uses `--on-ink-3`. master.css:405-407 records the exact decision: "The one thing on this screen that must be readable is the sentence saying the words are leaving the device. At --on-ink-3 it measured 4.1:1 and failed AA, which for a disclosure is not a nicety." The finding restates a concern the artifact already resolved, and the AA pass is inside the measured baseline.

5. `var(--measure)` does not exist. grep for `--measure:` in master.css returns 0. The proposed `max-width: var(--measure)` is an invalid value, the declaration is dropped, and the disclosure — currently capped at 62ch / 493px — would flex to the full width of `.darkFoot` minus the two buttons, roughly 900px, near 160 characters a line. The fix makes the measure it complains about about twice as bad.

6. `color: var(--on-ink-1)` would set the legal boilerplate to pure white, the same ink as the 34px live transcript and heavier than the Cancel button. On the screen whose subject is the person's own words landing, promoting third-party retention boilerplate to maximum ink inverts the hierarchy in the other direction.

7. Dropping `.peelField` to 400 is a regression. It is 16.5px/600 against `.readBody` at 17px/400 — 0.5px apart, so weight is the only thing separating the editable task wording from the note text it was cut from. At 400 the one editable field in the panel stops announcing itself and reads as more note prose.

The single residue: the disclosure's real rendered measure is ~89 characters a line (62ch of a wide figure glyph), above a comfortable 45-75. That is a narrow, unargued sub-observation inside a finding whose central claim is false and whose fix widens that very measure. Not a defect at the 9.5 bar as filed.

refuted.problem: The chrome speaks the designer's metaphor, not the operator's. "The pile" is the word for being behind, and the reward for capturing a thought is a button that says "Put it on the pile" — the product tells you your thought joined a backlog. "Still in the hand" asks a venue manager to decode a card-game figure that is never explained on screen. The same plane is then named six different ways across states (The pile / Still in the hand / What has crossed into Tasks / Everything you have written / Found / Every other empty in this product). The header's "Private to you" is presented in data.js as verbatim from notes-copy.ts and is not in that file at all — the shipped strings are "Private until you send it on" and "Yours until you send something on", both of which carry the one-way edge that "Private to you" drops. The same promise is then restated six ways in one product (header, desk foot, empty body, seam line, peel footnote, empty ledger), which reads as anxiety rather than confidence. And ?state=nothing and ?state=not-yet put design-review prose inside product chrome — "A dead end is a defect.", "one first move each", "nothing here is an apology" — the studio talking to the panel on a surface Orla is meant to read. Separately, the wedding register in notes-copy.ts ("Only the two of you can see this", "Make this something to do", "Add to our list") never appears anywhere in the master, so half the stated audience is invisible.
refuted.why: Refuted on measurement. (1) "Private to you" IS the shipped header string — src/modules/notes/app/workspace/NotesWorkspace.tsx:909, same lock glyph, same slot, with an explanatory popover; it is absent from notes-copy.ts, so data.js's provenance comment is imprecise, but the finding's proposed swap to privacyLong would make the lab DIVERGE from the shipped header. (2) The privacy promise is not "restated six ways in one product": driving all ten states, the maximum co-visible is TWO (header badge + "Nobody else can read this" in the desk foot), and that second line is replaced by the character count the moment you type; the seam's second statement is the load-bearing boundary the finding itself says should stay. The finding counted across states that are never co-visible. (3) .specWhy count in ?state=not-yet is ZERO — the finding names a state that carries none, and attributes "nothing here is an apology" to rendered prose when it is the catalogue head's count slot. The four .specWhy lines exist only in ?state=nothing, inside a plane whose own head reads "EVERY OTHER EMPTY IN THIS PRODUCT · one first move each" above four uppercase specName eyebrows: a declared catalogue, not a screen Orla navigates to. (4) The announcement is ALREADY "Kept." — Ctrl+Enter fires "Kept. 15 notes, 9 waiting on a decision.", matching the "Kept" row chips. (5) The six index heads name their CONTENTS, which differ in every case (all notes / remaining cards of the hand / the crossed ledger / search results / two catalogues); labelling a list by what is in it is correct, not inconsistent. (6) The central premise is contradicted by the artifact's own model: the pile head sits above rows stamped "In Tasks" and "Kept" — a settled archive — while the backlog is carried separately by the "8 to decide" chip and the hand, so "the pile is the word for being behind" is taste asserted against the design's actual semantics. "Still in the hand" is not load-bearing either: the card says "1 of 8", the seam line says "8 still to decide", the head says "7 left", above seven visible rows. (7) Two fixes make the work worse: "Keep it" on the capture button collides with the shipped "Keep it" (cancel-delete, NotesWorkspace.tsx:1403) and the lab's own "Just keep it" (don't make a task), giving one phrase three meanings.

refuted.problem: The review queue prints the seven undecided notes in full underneath the card you are deciding, at the same typographic weight as the index everywhere else. The entire emotional payload of a triage queue is one thing at a time and the rest out of sight; that is why Things hides the backlog during Today review. Here you decide card one while reading cards two through eight, so the relief of finishing one never arrives and the queue reads as a to-do list with a card stuck on top rather than a hand you are playing down. Compounding it, the progress pips top-right are eight 2px dashes at 1440 and carry no weight against the black "Turn into a task" button, so the one element that would give a sense of getting somewhere is invisible.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on measurement and on behaviour.

1. The pip claim is factually wrong. Measured in the live DOM at 1440 (`.pips i`, master.css:463-466): each pip is 15px x 3px, not "2px dashes", and the strip is 148px wide sitting on the title's own baseline. They are not uniform grey: the current pip is Indigo #4f46e5 (rgb(79,70,229)) — the only indigo anywhere on that screen apart from the wordmark dot — decided pips fill to solid Ink rgb(17,17,17), and remaining sit at ink 16%. The finding's own proposed fix ("ink-filled for decided and ink at 12% for remaining") is what is already shipped, minus the indigo you-are-here marker, so adopting it would strictly remove information.

2. "The one element that would give a sense of getting somewhere is invisible" is false. Progress is stated five ways in this state, four of them in words: `.handOf` prints "1 of 8" beside the 20px/600 title; `.deckNote` prints "8 still to decide"; the index head prints "STILL IN THE HAND · 7 left"; the pips carry `role="img"` with a live `aria-label` that I watched go "0 of 8 decided" → "1 of 8 decided" → "2 of 8 decided"; and `.handCard` stack depth (notebook.js:520, `Math.min(3, left-1)`) physically thins as the hand goes down. The pips are the redundant fifth channel, not the only one.

3. The core taste claim — "the relief of finishing one never arrives" — is contradicted by what the file does. Pressing T then K, I logged the index rows going 7 → 6 → 5 in real time, `.deckNote` going "8 still to decide. Nothing is decided until you say so" → "7 still to decide. 1 decided just now, and every one of them can be put back" → "6 still to decide. 2 decided just now…", the counter head going "7 left" → "6 left" → "5 left", and the pip filling to solid ink. Scroll and focus survive every repaint. The visible list shortening under your hands IS the relief; it is the most legible proof in the state that the hand is going down.

4. The fix would therefore make the work worse in three ways. It deletes that shortening list — you would decide eight notes and watch a static sentence, which is the actual "queue that never resolves". It duplicates copy that already exists: "Seven more after this one" restates `.deckNote`'s "8 still to decide" in a second, off-by-one grammar, which is precisely the "facts stated in two grammars" defect on the standing checklist. And moving the pips out from the far right and under "Worth doing something about?" puts them on top of the `.readSrc` source line ("Spoken · 3 hours ago"), collapsing the card's header rhythm of question-left / progress-right.

5. It also brushes the locked architecture. "An index below it carrying everything older, one line each" is a founder-locked plane present in every state; hiding it behind a disclosure in exactly one state removes the second plane where the product's whole spatial idea is two planes with depth.

The Things comparison does not carry the argument either: Things' Today has no card-over-list review mode, and the tool that does review-one-at-a-time (OmniFocus) keeps the remaining list in view beside the item. Eight items is a hand you can hold, not a backlog; the pressure state is where a long list would be the question, and that state is not what was filed.

rounds.headline: Six seats up, one down, and the same three seats independently named the same missing thing. Interaction, UX and Taste all arrived at picking: the sealed one-way edge, the promise this product is sold on, worked only because four notes in the fixture carried hand-authored picked words. A person could not highlight anything. Measured evidence dropped 0.4 to 5.7 and was right to — it found that a note you had just written could not be opened at all, and that the review hand incremented a counter while the notebook behind it went untouched.
rounds.body: Twenty-two findings confirmed, thirteen refuted. Two of the confirmed were mine, introduced by the previous round's own fixes, which is the argument for grading by driving rather than by reading. Picking is now real: highlighting words in a note raises one control beside them, seeds the task from exactly that range, and marks it in place. And the subject view stopped being an option filed in a drawer — the product opens on what the venue is facing, ordered by stake rather than by whichever date is nearest, so a college reading due today no longer outranks a wedding in two days.

wins.biggestWin: Cap the desk paper to the measure plus its margins (`max-width: calc(var(--measure) + 300px)` on `.top`, `.behind`, `.handTop`, `.handCard`) and stop right-packing that paper's metadata to the far edge. Right now the primary plane is a 1262px card holding a 527px column, so the architecture's central claim — two planes with depth, a piece of paper on a desk — fails at the level of shape: the desk is a big empty rectangle and the index is the only surface that looks lived in. Narrowing the paper to its own content makes the desk read as a desk, makes the index's full-width authority deliberate rather than accidental, closes the 515px gulf between the words and the facts about them, and fixes it in seven of the ten states at once. Nothing else in this file returns as much per line changed.

Build the type system that this file never built. Everything else in it is tokenised with real discipline — a tracking curve declared by size, a radii ladder that argues about its own seventh step, one duration, one measure — and then the type itself runs 18 ad-hoc font sizes across the ten states, eleven of them crammed into the 10–15px band on half-pixel increments, with leading left to the browser on 49 of the 76 text-bearing elements in the resting state. Declare an eight-step ramp and a three-step leading ladder in :root, collapse every half-pixel size onto it, set an explicit line-height on every rule that currently omits one, and add a gate assertion that fails on any rendered size outside the ramp or any text-bearing element computing `line-height: normal`. That one change closes the gap to Geist and Linear, and it fixes the 1px baseline shiver between a note's words and its timestamp on all 36 index rows as a side effect, because that drift is `align-items: center` resolving boxes whose leading was never declared. Second, and cheap: the phone capture field's typography is dead — one `font: inherit` at the foot of the file overrides the 15.5px/1.5 the media query declares, so the field the whole product exists for runs at browser leading and 19 characters per line. Both of those are the difference between a file that passes its own audit and a file that reads as typeset.

Build the picking. Bind selectionchange on the note body so a highlighted phrase raises one ink pill — "Make this the task" — that seeds the peel from the person's own range and marks that range in place. Everything else on this list is a state that needs mending; this is the state that was never built. The seam room reads as finished only because four notes in the fixture carry a hand-authored `pick` field, and every note that does not falls back to sending its whole first sentence with nothing marked. Until a person can pick, the sealed one-way edge is a rendering of a decision the fixture made, and Notes is a very good capture field bolted to a Send button. On the structural charge: the "what it is about" grouping is a real answer, not a gesture — "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July · in 2 days" ordered soonest-first is a sentence no standup tool would ever write, and it is the first thing in this file that could not be swapped for engineering words. But it ships as a 102x24 tertiary segment that is off by default, so the product still opens on Today/Yesterday/Monday. The answer exists and is filed in a drawer; make it the posture, not the option.

Make the picked words real. Right now the sealed one-way edge — the only thing that makes this Signal Notes rather than an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words — is prose. A live text selection in the note body is ignored; the peel seeds itself with the note's first sentence, or with the entire note when there is no sentence break, and then prints "The rest of what you wrote stays private here" over a note that has no rest; the three copy strings that would explain the boundary (handoffBoundary, handoffHeading, nothingSelected) are dead in notes-copy.ts; and the review hand's T key sends a note to Tasks with no peel at all. Wire selection in .readBody to startPeel, refuse to seed anything the person did not pick, print the picked words verbatim above the wording field labelled with copy.sourceLabel while the same words stay marked in the note, open the peel with copy.handoffBoundary, and route the hand's T through the same peel. That single change turns the product's central promise from a claim a stranger must take on faith into a mechanism they can watch work, and it is the only change that also answers the "well-made notes app with wedding words" charge on its own terms.

Make the interface's own nouns come from the venue's world and from notes-copy.ts, instead of from the architecture document and the designer's head. Right now the wedding lives almost entirely in the fixture data — Mara and Finn, the marquee sides, the orchard heating — while every word the interface itself owns is a generic notes taxonomy the operator never says: THE PILE, STILL IN THE HAND, To decide, Kept, Nobody else can read this, an extension of the fixture, Not part of this exploration. On the structural charge I was asked to re-test: the "What it is about" grouping half-answers it and no more. The axis is right and it is a real improvement — a venue's notes genuinely do sort by which couple, the house, the studio. But the group names are still furniture ("The house", "The studio", "The course" — three definite-article nouns, one proper name, one plural business noun, four grammars in one column), the metadata slot means a deadline on dated groups and a bare count on undated ones, and the soonest-first rule is blind to consequence: the pile opens on "The course · today", a college reading, above the wedding that is in two days. Swap those five nouns for the words an operator says out loud, give every group the same slot meaning (next date, or "no date"), rank by what the business is facing rather than by whichever row is nearest in time, and bind every promise, count and state string to notes-copy.ts so the product speaks in one voice. Do that and the charge is answered rather than gestured at. Leave it and this is a very well-made notes app with a wedding fixture loaded into it.

Ship the subject view as the resting state and let the subject reach the row — not just the heading. Plainly: this is no longer an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words, but only because of the seam. The seam is a real product idea, specific to this promise, and executed at the bar — the peel under the note, the editable wording, the receipt carrying the edited words, "Tasks receives these words and nothing else from this note". Everything around it is still generic. The pile is where an operator spends ninety-five percent of their time, and by default it is dated buckets of undifferentiated rows chipped "To decide", headed by an inbox count. Default `group` to "about", carry days-to-the-date into the row's own metadata slot and into `.idxMark`'s ink density, sort subjects by the soonest commitment inside their notes rather than by the subject's date, and lead the header with what the venue is facing rather than how many items are unread. That is one afternoon's work inside the locked architecture and the three-colour lock, and it is the difference between a beautiful capture tool and the only tool a venue owner would pay for — because it would be the only one that opens on Thursday morning already knowing that the marquee sides were promised by Thursday.

Make one list the only truth and re-derive every surface from it. Right now three parallel worlds exist: work() (the pile), N.pending (the hand), and N.crossed (the ledger) — and keepDraft() manufactures a fourth kind of object that is missing the fields the first world requires. That single split produces the crash, the eight false announcements in the review hand, the ledger that ignores the task it just watched cross, and the grouping toggle that cannot run. Give keepDraft() a complete note, source the hand from work().filter(n => n.pending), have decide() and sendPeel() mutate that note, and let the header chip, the pile tag, the queue count and the ledger all read from counts(). One change closes the two most expensive findings and every count on screen becomes provably the same fact.

Beyond the defects, the honest verdict on the structural charge: the subject grouping is a real answer, not a gesture. "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July · in 2 days" above the three notes that name them is a thing an engineering standup tool cannot say, and the dated-soonest-first sort is the right instinct. But it ships switched off. The default resting frame, the one every shot in shots/ captures and every reviewer sees, is TODAY / YESTERDAY / MONDAY — the exact grouping the taste seat said could be swapped for standups. The product's own best argument is one click away and never made. Make "What it is about" the default and let "When" be the alternate, and the charge is answered instead of available.

confirmed.element: .idxRow grid, .idxText, .topField and .index padding-bottom at 390×844
confirmed.problem: At 390 the note title gets 118–140px of a 355px row (33–39%) while the state pill and the timestamp take the rest, so every row reads "Saturday weddi…", "Mara & Finn's men…", "Idea for the studi…" — twelve to fifteen characters of the only content that matters, with the machine's metadata given twice the space. The capture textarea is measured at 140px wide with the count and four glyphs occupying the rest of the field, so a person typing a thought on a phone writes at about twenty characters a line. Scrolled to the end, the last row's bottom sits at 618 and the field's top at 621: three pixels, against a 39px row rhythm. The size at which a venue operator actually captures is the size at which the note is the smallest thing on screen.
confirmed.fix: Keep one line per note; reclaim the width from the metadata instead of adding rows. Under @media (max-width: 720px): (1) hide .idxWhen. The pile is already grouped by day with TODAY / YESTERDAY / MONDAY headings, so "35 minutes ago" spends 84px of a 340px row restating the heading it sits under; the full phrasing already lives in the row's accessible name, so nothing is lost to a reader. That returns 53-84px. (2) Drop .idxRow column-gap from 13px to 8px, returning 10px. Together .idxText goes from 118-131px to roughly 215-230px, which clears the measured four-word overflow on every row except the longest lede. (3) Remove the trim's hard four-word floor: when scrollWidth still exceeds clientWidth at four words, keep popping and let the trim's own ellipsis end the string, so the painted row never ends mid-word - the CSS ellipsis fallback is the thing producing "weddi..." today. For the dock: while a draft is live, give the field the full row. Put .phoneField on its own line at 100% width and drop the count plus the glyph cluster to a second flex row beneath it (the dock is still the dock, capture is still in the dock, nothing in the locked architecture moves). At rest the single-line composer can stay as it is. Finally, replace the fixed .index padding-bottom with a ResizeObserver on .dock that writes its measured height plus one row's rhythm (39px) into a custom property the index pads by, so a growing draft never paints over the oldest note - a static padding cannot do this against a content-sized field.
confirmed.done: Same fix.

confirmed.element: .idxRow { width: 100%; margin: 0 -10px; } and .idxRow + .idxRow::before, master.css:371–376
confirmed.problem: `width: 100%` resolves against the containing block, which cancels the right half of the intended `margin: 0 -10px`. Measured, every row box runs 120→1382 while the column it belongs to — the day headers, the desk paper, the head, the head actions — runs 130→1392. So the hover fill, the `[data-open]` fill and the indigo `[data-cursor]` fill all overhang the column's left edge by 10px and stop 10px short of its right, a 20px asymmetry that is visible in the shipped resting frame as the selected row bleeding past the "THE PILE" label. The hairlines inherit it too: `::before` at left:10/right:10 inside that shifted box spans 130→1372, flush to the left edge and 20px short of the right. The one element in the file whose whole job is to say "the keyboard is here" is the one element not on the grid.
confirmed.fix: Use only the calc form, not width:auto. In master.css:371–374 change `width: 100%` to `width: calc(100% + 20px)` and keep `margin: 0 -10px`. Do NOT use `width: auto` — .idxRow is a <button>, and form controls resolve width:auto to fit-content even at display:grid, which makes every row's fill a different, ragged width. Verified with calc at 1440/1280/1024/768/600/390 across ?state=notebook, pressure and search: every row lands 120→1402 centred on the 130→1392 column, the `.idxRow + .idxRow::before` hairlines resolve 130→1392 flush with the .indexHead::after rule, the timestamp column lands flush at 1392 with the head actions and the desk paper, and document.scrollWidth === clientWidth and .index scrollWidth === clientWidth at all six widths, so the existing no-sideways-scroll assertion stays green.
confirmed.done: The row's fill is calc(100% + 20px), not 100%. A percentage resolves against the containing block and cancelled the right half of the negative margin, so every row's highlight ran past the column every other object on the sheet resolves to.

confirmed.element: .phoneField — the un-media-queried rule at master.css:769, ?state=notebook at 390x844
confirmed.problem: The phone capture field is the one surface the whole product exists for, and its declared typography never applies. The @media (max-width:720px) block sets it to 15.5px / line-height 1.5 / letter-spacing var(--tr-16); the later un-media-queried `.phoneField { font: inherit; }` at the foot of the file has equal specificity and wins, and `font:` shorthand resets font-size and line-height. Driven at 390: computed font-size 16px, computed line-height `normal` (~1.2, not the 1.5 declared). Letter-spacing survives only because it is not part of the shorthand — so the field runs the intended tracking at an unintended size and leading, which is the worst of both. Compounding it, the field is a 140px flex child sharing the dock with three 36px glyphs and a floating count: typing one venue sentence gave four wrapped lines at 19 characters each. iA Writer on the same 390px gives ~36. The three-seconds-to-safe promise is delivered at a measure no one would accept in a comment box.
confirmed.fix: Three parts, in order. (1) Kill the shorthand: replace master.css:770 with `.phoneField { border:0; outline:0; resize:none; background:none; color: var(--ink-1); font-family: inherit; font-weight: 400; }`. Dropping `font: inherit` lets the media block's 15.5px/1.5/--tr-16 survive; naming family and weight keeps the UA textarea's 13.33px Arial out. Keep `line-height: 1.5` explicit in the @media block as the belt. (2) Give it the dock's full width rather than a 140px column: inside @media (max-width:720px) set `.dock { flex-wrap: wrap; row-gap: 4px; }` and `.phoneField { flex: 1 0 100%; order: -1; padding: 10px 4px; }`, letting the count, commit and glyph row sit on the line beneath. That puts the field near 300px, which at 15.5px is ~43 characters per line by the gate's own formula — inside the neighbourhood of the 45-78 band instead of at 19. Verify the commit control and the mic still clear 44px in the wrapped row. (3) Close the hole that let this drift: extend the measure assertion in notes-interaction-check.mjs to run at 390 against `.phoneField`, both with and without a live draft, and assert computed line-height is not `normal` — the current assertion only ever sees .topField at desktop width, which is why a dead rule on the product's primary surface passed 171 checks.
confirmed.done: `font: inherit` is a shorthand and it was resetting the size, the leading and the tracking the media block had already declared for the one field the product exists for. The parts are named instead.

confirmed.element: .idxText / .idxRow grid — ?state=notebook and ?state=pressure, 1440 and 390
confirmed.problem: The file's own comment claims one --measure token governs every surface carrying a person's own writing, and the behaviour gate checks exactly two elements for it: .readBody and .topField. The index is neither, and the index is where a person spends their time. Measured at 1440: .idxText is 1040–1067px at 14.5px, which is 159 characters of line box; a note kept during the drive rendered all 109 of its characters on one 1067px line. At 390 the same element is 118px — 18 characters, always truncated — while the tag (59px) plus timestamp (84px) take 143px. On the device where capture lives, the machine's labels get more width than the person's words in every row. The right-hand metadata is also unaligned: pill left edges down the list read 1216.3, 1236.7, 1229.1, 1229.1, 1229.1, 1267.0, 1239.9 — 51px of jitter, so the return sweep has no vertical to land on.
confirmed.fix: Two changes, neither of which caps the desktop text. (1) Lock the right-hand verticals without the dead gutter — keep the row full width and give the metadata fixed columns, the Linear pattern: `.idxRow { grid-template-columns: 20px minmax(0, 1fr) 74px 92px; }` with `.idxTag { justify-self: start; }` and `.idxWhen { justify-self: start; }` so tag lefts and time lefts each land on one vertical (74px clears the widest tag, "To decide" at 66.2px; 92px clears the widest time, "35 minutes ago" at 84.0px). Truncate or re-word any longer relative time rather than widening the column. (2) On a phone, stack instead of squeeze — inside `@media (max-width: 720px)`: `.idxRow { grid-template-columns: 20px minmax(0, 1fr); row-gap: 3px; align-items: start; } .idxTag, .idxWhen { grid-column: 2; justify-self: start; } .idxTag { font-size: 10.5px; padding: 2px 7px; } .idxWhen { font-size: 11px; }` and let the text wrap to two lines rather than clipping at one: `.idxText { white-space: normal; display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 2; -webkit-box-orient: vertical; }`. That hands the words the full ~300px across two lines — roughly 70 characters, enough to tell "Ask the venue whether the ballroom can be accessed from 8am" from any other venue note — and drops the tag and the time to a quiet second line where they still read. Two consequences to handle in the same change: `trimRows()` in notebook.js measures a one-line box and must skip or re-target its trim when the row is clamped, otherwise it will cut the text before the clamp ever sees two lines; and the phone row grows to about 62px, so `.index { padding-bottom }` and the `pointer: coarse` row padding want re-checking against the dock clearance the gate already asserts.
confirmed.done: The index's metadata has fixed columns, so the right-hand verticals hold the whole list down instead of stepping in and out with the length of each timestamp.

Highlighting words in a note raises one control beside them carrying the product's own words, seeds the task from exactly that range, and marks it in place while the wording is edited. confirmed.element: `.idxRow` / `.idxText` at 390 wide, every room
confirmed.problem: Measured at 390: the row is 340px, the person's own words get 145px (43%), a "To decide" chip takes 66px and a relative time 50px. At the ≤720px breakpoint: (1) drop .idxWhen entirely — the day group header already says TODAY / YESTERDAY / MONDAY, the exact relative time is already in the row's aria-label, and it reappears in .readSrc the moment the note is opened; this alone returns 64–84px, taking row 1 from 118px to ~200px; (2) tighten .idxRow column-gap from 13px to 8px, returning another ~10px; (3) cap .idxTag with max-width 5rem and drop the data-quiet "Kept" pill at this breakpoint only — it is the resting state, it carries no ring already, and it stays in the accessible name. If the founder reads "one line each" as conceptual rather than literal, the stronger design is the two-line phone row the finding describes — text at full width with -webkit-line-clamp:2 over a 12px meta line at 0.44 alpha — but that is a founder call on the locked architecture, not a change to make unilaterally.
confirmed.done: Same fix.

confirmed.element: [data-act="d-delete"] in ?state=review; offerUndo() undoTimer; notebook.js:1042
confirmed.problem: In the hand, Delete is a data-quiet button sitting in the same weight and the same row as "Decide later". (3) Stop .deckNote outliving the truth: scope "every one of them can be put back" to the live window, or better, since decided[] is retained in state and reversal is a two-line pop, give the hand a persistent "put the last one back" that does not expire — that answers the missing bin properly instead of buying twenty more seconds. Drop the proposed two-step commit in the card footer: with real undo, a confirm step is friction Linear, Gmail and Things deliberately removed, and the proposed label is off-voice. confirmed.element: ?state=notebook → the When / What it is about toggle; data.js SUBJECTS; notebook.js idxRow, review card
confirmed.problem: Judged plainly, the grouping gestures at the structural charge rather than answering it. "What it is about" is opt-in and off by default, so the state every person lands in is still the day-grouped pile the last panel condemned. The subject appears in exactly two places: a 12px grey group header in the non-default view, and the read sheet's meta line. It is on no index row in the default view, absent from the review card entirely — so the one screen where a venue owner is actually deciding never says which couple the decision belongs to — absent from search results, and absent from the crossed ledger. The one genuinely venue-shaped element in the whole master is the dated subtitle "Saturday 18 July · in 2 days", and it is the least prominent text on a view most people will never switch to. The header states "in 2 days" for the wedding nowhere at all. The group headers also invert their own priority: the dated, urgent groups (Mara & Finn, The course) show a date and no count, while the standing groups (The studio, Enquiries, The house) show "5 notes", "2 notes", "3 notes" — the least urgent groups are the only ones you can size. Keep "When" as the landing state and earn the subject everywhere else instead. (b) Put note.about.label into every idxRow's ACCESSIBLE NAME unconditionally, in both groupings and in search and the crossed ledger — zero pixels, and it is the cheapest half of the fix. Show it visibly as a quiet ink-tint capsule only at desk width, and suppress it when the row already sits under a group header of that same subject; at 390 the lede is already trimmed to 118px against a 59px tag and an 84px time, so a capsule ahead of the lede there would eat the person's own words. (c) Put the subject and its countdown on the review card beside "Worth doing something about?", in the readSrc line where source and time already sit: "Spoken · 3 hours ago · Mara & Finn, in 2 days". This is the highest-value single change in the finding and costs one interpolation. (d) Wire N.next into head(): the data, the date and the fixture's own stated intention already exist and only the render is missing. Compose it from the fields rather than writing new copy: "The Orchard, events" then "Mara & Finn, Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" in the same register the group header already uses. (e) Give every group header the same two facts in the same order — count always, then date if it has one: "Mara & Finn · 6 notes · Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" and "The studio · 5 notes". Then update the gate: notes-interaction-check.mjs:690 stays valid, and add assertions that every idxRow name carries its subject, that the review card names the subject and its countdown, and that no two group headers in one list use different fact orders.
confirmed.done: Same fix, and the axis was rebuilt rather than re-labelled: one grammar for every name, one meaning for every slot (a date or No date), a count of what is waiting in each, and an order by what the venue is facing rather than by whichever date is nearest — so a college reading due today no longer outranks a wedding in two days.

The status chip is also the most contrasted object in each row, so the eye is pulled to "To decide" eleven times before it reads a single word anyone wrote.

Keep one line per row. Reclaim the space from the timestamp, which is the one fact that is genuinely redundant on a phone.

1. Hide `.idxWhen` inside `@media (max-width: 720px)` when the pile is grouped by When. It is not just low-value there, it states the same fact twice in two grammars — a standing-checklist defect. Measured pairs of group heading to row timestamp: Today→"35 minutes ago", Yesterday→"Yesterday", Yesterday→"Yesterday", Yesterday→"Yesterday", Monday→"2 days ago", Sunday→"3 days ago". Three rows print the group heading back at the reader letter for letter. The heading already carries the day; the exact minute belongs on the desk when the note is opened, not on every line of the pile. Keep `.idxWhen` visible under the "What it is about" grouping, where no heading carries the day, and keep the full timestamp in the row's aria-label either way so nothing leaves the accessible name.

"Saturday weddi…" becomes "Saturday wedding, Mara & Finn." — a whole recognisable sentence. "Bar restock: tonic ru…" becomes "Bar restock: tonic running low,…". Same row count on screen, same one line each, architecture untouched.

3. Then lower the trim floor in `trimRows()` from four words to one, so a row that still overflows loses its last word rather than half a letter. The four-word floor is what hands the row to the CSS ellipsis; with the space reclaimed it almost never fires, but the floor should not be the thing that reintroduces mid-word damage on a 320px phone or a long first word.

Add a gate assertion at 390px: no `.idxText` in the resting state carries `data-clipped`.

confirmed.element: button.headAct ("Private to you") + .topMeta ("Nobody else can read this") + .stays + the seam confirmation, ?state=notebook and ?state=seam

The rest of what you wrote stays private here.", then "Your note is still here, still private, still yours to edit." printed once under the note and again verbatim inside the confirmation card, and the announcement after sending reads "Sent to Tasks. refuted.why:
Drove ?state=notebook, clicked "What it is about", measured computed styles and geometry.

The two measurements are correct but the conclusions drawn from them are not, and the fix would regress the mode.

1. "The header is optically weaker than the content it governs." The type numbers check out (header 12.5px/600/rgb(17,17,17); row lede 14.5px/600/rgb(17,17,17)), but the finding omits the two hierarchy devices that are actually doing the work. The subject name HANGS LEFT of every title it governs: header text starts at x=130, row title text at x=163 — a 33px outdent, because the row's icon column occupies 120–160. It also carries 20px of clear air above it and a secondary ink-3 clause on the same baseline ("Saturday 18 July · in 2 days"). In the rendered index the four subjects — The course / Mara & Finn / The studio / Enquiries — read cleanly as group heads on the first scan. Outdent plus air plus a quieter trailing clause is exactly how Things, Bear and Linear separate a group head from its rows without inflating type. "The subject recedes below its own notes, so the list has no tier" is contradicted by the frame; size is not the only tier, and it is not the tier this list is using.

2. "Every row still reports capture recency, so the column speaks standup grammar." Confirmed as fact (.idxWhen carries note.when in both modes: "9 hours ago", "35 minutes ago", "3 days ago"), but the premise is wrong for this product. The standup charge from last round was about the GROUPING AXIS, which is what was changed. A capture timestamp on a note row is notebook grammar, not standup grammar — Apple Notes, Bear, Things and iA Writer all group by notebook/area/tag and still carry recency per row. Nothing about "3 days ago" beside a handwritten thought reads as engineering ceremony.

3. The proposed swap would make the work worse, on three counts. (a) It prints the header verbatim on every row it governs: all three rows under "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July · in 2 days" would read "in 2 days" in the right column. That is the checklist's own "facts restated / repeats itself" defect, and it inverts the finding's own hierarchy argument — a header whose every row repeats it is more redundant, not more governing. (b) It empties the column for the majority of the pile: three of the five subjects are standing (The house, The studio, Enquiries — 10 of 14 rows), so "blank for undated subjects" leaves most of the list with a dead right column. (c) It deletes the only recency signal in the notebook. Inside "The studio" the rows run 5 hours ago → 6 hours ago → Yesterday → 3 days ago → 3 days ago; that gradient is what tells a venue owner which thoughts are still warm, and it is also in the accessible name ("… Written. 35 minutes ago. In Tasks."), so the swap costs screen-reader users the same fact. The header and the row are stating two different, independent facts — what this is about, and how fresh it is — which is a list with two axes, not one axis stated in two grammars.

Refuted: the hierarchy half is overstated taste that ignores the outdent tier actually in the file, and the axis half rests on a false premise and a fix that would strip information from ten of fourteen rows.
