refuted.problem: Scanning down the left edge of one sheet the eye crosses three verticals inside 33px: 130 (wordmark, paper edge, row icon), 154 (the writing line), 163 (every note title). The writing line and the line it becomes are 9px apart, so the words shift right when a thought turns into a row. The flight layer proves it — sampled positions run x=154 at the field and x=163 at the landing, correcting sideways mid-arc to hit a rail the source never sat on. Everything aligns to its own container and nothing aligns to anything else.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on three independent grounds, each measured live at 1440x960.

1. THE PROPOSED FIX DOES NOT DO WHAT IT CLAIMS — it makes the named defect worse. I injected the exact rule (`.idxRow { grid-template-columns: 24px minmax(0,1fr) 76px 92px; column-gap: 10px }`) and measured: `.idxText` lands at x=164, not the promised 154. The row's content box starts at the index gutter (100 sheet + 30 gutter = 130; margin -10px and padding 10px cancel), so the text rail is 130 + col + gap. 24 + 10 = 34 gives 164 — one pixel FURTHER from the 154 writing rail than the 163 it set out to fix, while also fattening the icon column from 20px to 24px. Landing at 154 would require col + gap = 24 total, i.e. a 20px icon with a 4px gap to the text, which no benchmark named here would ship, or moving the paper's inner padding to 33px, or breaking the sheet gutter. None of those were proposed. A fix whose own arithmetic reverses its own premise cannot be confirmed.

2. "NOTHING ALIGNS TO ANYTHING" IS FACTUALLY INVERTED. x=130 is one rail carrying three of the objects the finding itself names, in exact alignment: head first child (wordmark) x=130, `.top` (the paper's left edge) x=130, `.idxMark` (every row icon) x=130. The finding lists that three-way alignment and then counts it as one of its three offending verticals. There are two structural rails on this left edge, not three: 130, the sheet gutter, which the wordmark, the paper edge and every row icon share; and 163, row text indented past its own 20px icon column with a 13px gap — the ordinary icon-list indent that Linear's issue rows, Things' checklist and Bear's note list all use. 154 is not a third rail competing with them; it is the paper's inner margin, on a raised bounded card, on the desk plane. The eye reads text on a bounded white card against that card's own edge, not against rows 250px below it — and the founder architecture locks these as TWO PLANES WITH DEPTH.

3. THE FLIGHT EVIDENCE IS BACKWARDS. I captured the ghost's bounding box every frame through a real Ctrl+Enter keep. Samples: t=12ms x=154 y=108, t=67ms x=160 y=596, t=134ms x=163 y=847, then held at x=163 through fade. It lands at x=163, which is exactly where `.idxText` sits — the flight lands precisely ON its target, not, as claimed, on "a rail the source never sat on." The lateral is 9px against 738px of vertical travel, a 0.7 degree deviation from vertical, interpolated monotonically by a single WAAPI translate. There is no "correcting sideways mid-arc"; there is no arc. Width is constant at 527px (scale computes to min(1, 1035/527) = 1), so nothing else in the motion draws attention to the 9px either.

The kernel — that a keep should feel like the words falling straight down — is a fair instinct, but it is already true to within 0.7 degrees, and the remedy offered would move the landing rail one pixel further out while coarsening the icon column. Taste stated as a defect, with arithmetic that refutes itself.

refuted.problem: The dock is centred on the sheet, which is the index's centre, while the entire desk plane is left-anchored. Measured at 1920 the dock spans 795→1207, centre 1001; the desk's centre is 488. The floating object that carries capture, search and the person's own avatar sits 513px to the right of the plane where capture happens, hovering in the middle of the empty field described in the first finding. At 1440 it is 273px off. The one element that is supposed to belong to the whole sheet visually belongs only to the table.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The finding's arithmetic is right and its conclusion is wrong. Measured live at 1024/1280/1440/1920, the dock's centre is 553/681/761/1001 — identical, to the pixel, to the centre of the sheet, the head, the index, the index head, and every index row. The only object on the sheet whose centre is 488 is `.top`, the desk paper, which is deliberately capped by `.top, .behind, .handTop, .handCard { max-width: calc(var(--measure) + 220px) }` with a comment in master.css explaining that the cap exists so a person's writing sits at a 31em measure, not so the composition acquires a left-anchored axis. So the dock is not "adrift from the plane it serves": it is centred on the plane it physically floats over — the index, which is full-width and for which `.index { padding-bottom: 92px }` reserves clearance — and on the head that names the notebook. The finding calls the dock centre "the index's centre" in its own first sentence and then asks it to abandon that centre. The dock carries search (an index control), voice, photo and the person's avatar; none of those belong to the desk paper.

The proposed fix makes the work worse, and I applied it to check rather than argue it. With `.dockWrap { justify-content: flex-start; padding-left: var(--gutter) }`, the dock's centre pins to 336 at every desktop width: at 1440 it is now 425px from the index centre it hovers over, worse than the 273px complained of, and it lands in the bottom-left corner directly beneath the pile's left edge, with the dock avatar stacked almost on top of the rail avatar — two "OR" discs in the same corner. The bottom two-thirds of the sheet foot goes dead, which is the opposite of what the sibling "empty field" complaint wants. At 390 it also breaks the phone dock, whose `.dock { width: calc(100% - var(--gutter) * 2) }` resolves against the now-padded wrap: measured left margin 16px, right margin 32px, dock centre 187 against a sheet centre of 195. That is the one width where the dock is the capture control, per the locked architecture, and the fix leaves it visibly off-centre.

The fix is also contingent, by its own words, on "the shared content column from the first finding" — a column that does not exist in the source. A change that only makes sense if an unaccepted restructure lands is not an actionable finding at a 9.5 bar. Whatever discomfort exists at 1920 comes from the sheet having no max-width at all (1802px wide), which is a question about the sheet, not about the one object holding down its foot.

refuted.problem: Wherever a person's own words appear beside a machine's version of them, the type ranks the machine first. In readback the verbatim is `.saidWas` at 13px / rgba(17,17,17,0.72) / 1.55 over a calc(31em + 6em) measure that computes to 481px — 82 characters, the widest measure anywhere in the product, on the smallest and palest reading type; the derived cards `.piece` are 17px at full ink. In the seam the picked words `.peelFrom span` are 15px/400 and the derived task wording `.peelField` is 17px/600. A product whose stated promise is that only the exact words a person picks ever cross sets those exact words as a caption and the derivation as the headline, twice, in the two flows that exist to prove the promise. This is the deepest defect on the sheet and it is a taste failure, not an oversight.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The CSS values quoted are real, but the premise built on them — "wherever a person's own words appear beside a machine's version, the type ranks the machine first" — is false in both flows once you drive them instead of diffing two rules.

READBACK. `.saidWas` and `.darkSaid` print the SAME string (`N.speech.transcript`, notebook.js:1017 and :1033). One state earlier, in ?state=voice, those exact words are set at `--t-34` — 34px, the largest type anywhere in the product, alone on the ink floor (master.css:507). The person's words are given the biggest type in the file; the derived pieces get 17px. The 13px `.saidWas` is the third appearance of that text, a held receipt labelled "What you said, once", not the first ranking of it. The measurement is also off: driven at 1440x960, box-sizing is border-box, so the content box is 449px and the widest rendered line is 75 characters, not 82 — and `.piece` (595px) and `.top` (527px) are both physically wider boxes.

SEAM. `.peelFrom span` is not the only place the picked words appear. At the moment the peel is open, the note is uncovered by architecture and the picked range renders in it as `.pick` at 17px / weight 400 / rgb(17,17,17), indigo-washed, 503px wide — measured. That is the same size as `.peelField` and heavier ink than nothing. The picked words are on screen at full reading type at the same instant as the derivation; `.peelFrom` is a second, smaller quotation of them inside the panel so the two can be compared without scrolling. "The derivation is the headline and the source is a caption" is not what is on the screen.

THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE, TWICE. (1) `.saidWas` at 17px/ink-1/measure inside a wash chip becomes near-identical to a `.piece` (white, 17px, ink-1) — two blocks of the same 174 characters at the same size and ink, stacked, one editable and one not, with only a 3.5% tint separating them. That is an invisible-affordance regression of exactly the kind the standing checklist names, and it grows the receipt from 111px to roughly 170px, pushing both pieces and the "Put both on the pile" commit down a 960px viewport. (2) `.peelFrom span` at 17px/600 becomes byte-identical in type to `.peelField`, so the static quote and the textarea a venue owner must find and edit read as the same object inside a 720px panel.

CONSTRAINT. The fix explicitly proposes to "let the tint carry the difference". The locked constraint is that state is ink DENSITY and FILL, never colour — density is the sanctioned mechanism and it is what is carrying the distinction today. The fix removes it and leans on background tint alone.

The closing law — "nothing derived may be larger or denser than the words it came from" — is already violated by the file's own correct behaviour: `.pick` (source, 17/400) and `.peelField` (derived, 17/600) sit at the same size, and that is right, because one is a quotation and one is an editable field. This is taste asserted as law, with the strongest counter-evidence (34px `.darkSaid`, 17px `.pick`) unlooked-at.

refuted.problem: Four uppercase 11px/0.075em labels of three different structural ranks are rendered identically in one view: a card title (TURN THIS INTO A TASK), two field labels (THE WORDS YOU PICKED, THE TASK WORDING) and a sheet section header (WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS). Caps stop signalling rank once they answer every labelling problem, and the seam is the flow where rank matters most. In the same card 13px runs at three trackings and two leadings — .act and .picker at -0.156px, .peelBoundary at -0.13px, .peelWhy at -0.078px, at 1.45 and 1.55 — because `--tr-13` is never declared and three rules silently fall back to a literal `-0.01em`. The stated "one tracking curve, by size, declared once" is not true of the file. And .peelBoundary, the boundary promise that opens the peel, is the one paragraph in the product without `text-wrap: pretty`, so it breaks as "the exact words you / pick and check below".
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The observations are partly true but every operative part of the fix fails measurement, and two of its factual premises are wrong.

TRUE: --tr-13 is undeclared (master.css:95-97), three rules use var(--tr-13, -0.01em) (392, 597, 605), and line 93 claims every letter-spacing is a token. Seam does render four identical 11px/0.825px/600/ink-3 caps labels.

1) THE TRACKING HALF IS A NO-OP. Declaring --tr-13: -0.010em and replacing the three call sites changes zero rendered pixels; the fallback already resolves to exactly that. Measured trackings at 13px in seam: .act/.picker -0.156px, .peelBoundary -0.13px, .peelWhy -0.078px. The widest gap is 0.078px per character, ~4.7px over a 60-char line, ~0.026px between the two the fix actually touches. Sub-pixel per glyph. This is a comment that overclaims, not a design defect at 9.5.

2) .topMeta IS 12px, NOT 13px. Computed in all four rooms: 12px / -0.072px. The fix instructs "change .peelWhy and .topMeta from var(--tr-12) to var(--tr-13) so 13px has one tracking" — that puts a 12px element on a 13px tracking and breaks the exact "one curve, by size" rule the finding invokes.

3) text-wrap: pretty ON .peelBoundary IS DEMONSTRABLY INERT. Applied live and re-measured line rects via Range.getClientRects(): before [384,128], with pretty [384,128]. Identical. The fix does not fix the break it names. (balance yields [264,249], but balance was not proposed.) The break is also not a defect: 384/128 of a 403px measure is a 32% second line, not a runt.

4) "THE ONE PARAGRAPH WITHOUT text-wrap: pretty" IS FALSE. .stays ("Your note is still here, still private, still yours") wraps to two lines in the same card with no pretty. Multiple other prose runs likewise.

5) THE CAPS FIX CONTRADICTS ITSELF AND MAKES THE WORK WORSE. It leaves .indexHead ("WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS") untouched, so the seam still shows two caps labels, not "the only caps label in the seam" as claimed. And the proposed replacement register — 12px / 400 / --ink-3 / no caps — is already the file's register for quiet facts (.topMeta, .pickCount, .stays, .idxDayTail, .indexHead .cnt). Demoting a field label into it removes the one cue separating a label from the 15px ink-1 content directly beneath it, trading a rank collision among labels for a rank collision between label and fact. Caps census across all ten states also shows seam is not the densest: ?state=nothing renders five (4x .specName + .indexHead), unaddressed.

Residue worth one line, not a finding: .peelBoundary (lh 1.45) and .peelWhy (lh 1.55) are two 13px paragraphs in one card at two leadings.

refuted.problem: The product's whole promise is the three seconds between a thought and it being safe, and the moment ends badly. Ctrl+Enter empties the field, and the flying-words layer carries the sentence 670px down the sheet to row 10 of 15, at the very bottom edge of the visible index, under a heading called "The house" that has nothing to do with what was written. At the resting 1440x960 it is on the last visible line; at any longer pile it is below the fold and the animation flies the words off the bottom of the screen. The head count ticks 14→15 and the chip ticks 8→9, so the only reliable confirmation of capture is two numbers changing in the header — not the words themselves.
refuted.why:
Driven in Playwright at 1440x960 against notebook.html, the finding's two load-bearing claims are false and its fix would break a tested contract.

(1) "At any longer pile it is below the fold and the animation flies the words off the bottom of the screen." Measured the opposite. Eight successive Ctrl+Enter captures, pile growing 15 -> 22 rows: the arriving row's position is i=9 on the first keep, then i=4 (top:594, bottom:634) on every keep after, never clipped by #index, never off viewport, always ~250px clear of the dock. The reason is in the source I read: groupsOf() breaks ties between no-date groups with `bag.get(b).length - bag.get(a).length`, so as "The house" accumulates the new notes that group climbs the order. Growth makes the landing more visible, not less. The escalation the finding rests on does not exist.

(2) "The only reliable confirmation of capture is two numbers changing in the header." False on four counts, all measured: #say announces "Kept. 15 notes, 9 waiting on a decision."; the undo strip reads "Kept on the pile. / Undo Ctrl+Z"; the row carries data-arriving with a 620ms arrive animation; and the flying words land on a row that IS on screen — rowT 837.5, rowB 877.4, dock top 878, elementFromPoint at the landing point returns .idxRow, unobstructed. The words are the confirmation, and they are visible.

The one accurate observation — the first keep lands the row on the last line above the dock — is a one-off caused by initial group sizes and self-corrects on the very next capture.

(3) The fix would make it worse. `scrollIntoView({block:"center"})` after every keep moves the pile under the reader on every single capture. Place-keeping across repaint is an explicit contract here: paint() captures and restores #index.scrollTop by design, with the rule stated in the source comment ("Nothing here may cost the operator their place"), and notes-interaction-check.mjs asserts it at lines 93-121. Yanking the pile to centre on each keep is the opposite posture from Things or Bear, where capture never disturbs where you are reading. The pinned "Just now" duplicate row is worse still: it prints a row under a heading that contradicts the grouping the round-3 charge is being judged on.

Residual worth noting but not this finding: if the reader has scrolled the pile down first, the restored scrollTop leaves the arriving row ABOVE the visible index (measured rowT 43 against idxT 303) and the ghost flies up into the desk. That is real, narrow, and the exact inverse of what this finding describes, so it cannot be confirmed as written.

refuted.problem: Four notes-copy.ts strings are never rendered and have been replaced by strings this master wrote: voiceStop ("Stop listening" → "Stop and read it back"), emptyBody ("The capture field is ready above." → "Nobody else can read what you write here…"), privacyLong ("Yours until you send something on" → "Nobody else can read this"), and offline. The offline substitution is not a rewrite, it is a different product: notes-copy says "Reconnect and try again" (the person retries) and the card says "Notes will put it on the pile the moment you reconnect" (it happens by itself). One of those two sentences is a lie to a venue manager whose note is sitting on a phone in a field. Grep confirms copy.privacyLong, copy.emptyBody, copy.voiceStop and copy.offline each have zero call sites.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The grep is right and the argument built on it is wrong; three of the four sub-claims are factually mistaken about which slot the notes-copy string belongs to, and the proposed fix would put two false sentences on screen.

1. OFFLINE — the headline claim, and it is wrong. `offline: "You are offline. Nothing has left Notes. Reconnect and try again."` lives in notes-copy.ts `errors` (notes-copy.ts:218), the hand-off error set, documented alongside `tasksUnavailable`, `replyLost`, `retryPending`, `sourceChanged`. It is the error for trying to SEND A NOTE TO TASKS while offline. notes-copy.ts has a separate `destination.offline` ("You are offline. Your note stays private here.") and no key at all for a note captured offline. notebook.js:1216 is not that fact: the card is headed "Held on this device", the desk above it reads "Written while the connection was down", and the state describes a note that was WRITTEN offline and is waiting to sync. Two different facts, not two grammars for one. There is no lie and no contradiction. Applying the fix would print "Nothing has left Notes. Reconnect and try again" on a card about a locally held note, i.e. it would tell the venue manager in the field to retry a Tasks send she never started, and would delete the one sentence that answers her actual question (does it sync by itself). The fix makes the product less honest, not more.

2. EMPTYBODY — the fix would state something false about the screen. I drove ?state=nothing at 1440x960: STATES.nothing replaces the top sheet's textarea entirely (notebook.js:1145-1155, no `topField`), so the rendered page is title, body, then two first-move buttons — there is no capture field above the body. On a phone capture is in the dock, below. Rendering "The capture field is ready above." verbatim would point at a field that is not there, and would trade two working first moves ("Write the first one", "Or say it") for a pointer, which is the standing checklist's own "empty states that repeat themselves instead of offering one first move".

3. PRIVACYLONG — no such key exists in notes-copy.ts. data.js invented the name for `capture.headerAssurance` ("Yours until you send something on"), a HEADER string. notebook.js:658 is the capture foot, whose notes-copy counterpart is `capture.privacyAssurance` ("Private until you send it on"). The finding is asking for a header string to be rendered in the capture slot, which is itself the placement change the fixture's own comment permits ("a direction may only decide where a string lives"). Also note data.js's `privacy: "Private to you"` is already not verbatim from notes-copy either, so the "verbatim fixture" premise the finding rests on does not hold at the source it cites.

4. VOICESTOP — the only sub-claim with force: "Stop listening" became "Stop and read it back" at :1024. It is a real deviation and it is two words. On a full-floor takeover the primary action naming its own consequence, where the next state is literally "What you said, once", is what Things and Linear do. The finding itself offers to withdraw it ("put 'and read it back' nowhere"), which is taste conceded as taste. Not a defect at 9.5.

5. THE GATE IS WRONG. data.js is a shared fixture read by render-a.js, render-b.js, render-c.js and notebook.js. I checked all four: none of them render voiceStop, emptyBody, privacyLong or offline. The fixture is a menu of the product's strings, not a manifest of one direction's screen. A gate that fails on any unused key would force copy into slots whose fact it does not state — exactly the three errors above — and would break the three sibling directions too.

refuted.problem: Every undo announces the past-tense sentence for the action it just reversed. Driven live: Ctrl+Z after a keep says "Undone. Kept on the pile."; after a send it says "Undone. Sent to Tasks." A person who is not looking at the screen hears the product confirm the exact thing they just cancelled. Reversibility is this product's safety claim and its announcement states the opposite of what happened.
refuted.why:
The quoted behaviour is accurate — I drove it and got `say="Undone. Kept on the pile."` after Ctrl+Z on a keep and `say="Undone. Kept in Notes."` after undoing K in the hand (notebook.js:144). But the reading of it is wrong and the proposed fix would make the product worse.

WRONG ABOUT THE BEHAVIOUR. "Reversibility ... its announcement states the opposite of what happened" mis-parses the sentence. The head of the utterance is "Undone."; the label is its object. A polite live region is spoken start to finish in order, so there is no moment at which "Kept on the pile" stands alone in the ear. Naming the reversed act is information, not contradiction: it identifies WHICH of several stacked acts came back, which is precisely what an eyes-off operator needs after the ten-second strip has timed out. This is the standard undo grammar shipped by every benchmark named in the brief and by the OS itself ("Undo Typing", "Undo Move"). It is not a defect that undo names its object.

THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE — three ways, all verifiable in the file:
1. "Put back." is ALREADY the verbatim announcement for closing an open note (notebook.js:468). Reusing it as the undo stem gives one sentence two meanings, breaking the "one noun for one fact" rule this programme just paid to establish.
2. "Nothing was kept." is ALREADY the verbatim announcement for discarding dictation (lines 1448, 1494, 1590, 1596). Saying it after undoing a keep is worse than ambiguous: I confirmed that undo restores the words live into the capture field (`field="Ring the florist about the arch"`, caret returned). Telling a venue owner "Nothing was kept" at the exact instant her words are sitting safe in the field reads as loss. That is the one failure this product cannot afford, and the fix introduces it.
3. "Tasks did not receive it." asserts a fact about another product's internal state that Notes cannot observe. The sealed one-way edge means Notes knows only that it did not send; claiming Tasks did not receive is an unverifiable outward promise.

ALREADY-CONSIDERED. The label string is shared deliberately between the pre-undo strip and the post-undo announcement, and the code comments at notebook.js:186 and :417 record that a previous round shipped the post-undo phrasing on the pre-undo strip and had to reverse it because it told the operator their note had gone back to the sheet while it was safely on the pile. The finding proposes re-splitting that seam with the strings that caused the earlier failure.

refuted.problem: Computed over every element in the resting 1440 view, indigo appears exactly twice: the wordmark dot and an 8% tint on whichever row the cursor is on. The one fact only this product has — that this note's words have already crossed a sealed one-way edge — is rendered in the same greyscale pill as "To decide" and "Kept". The accent is being spent on a browser state and withheld from the product's second promise, which is obeying three colours rather than spending them.
refuted.why:
REFUTED — the count is wrong, and the element it missed is the one that kills the argument. Computed over every element in the resting locked 1440 view, indigo appears three times, not twice: the rail mark dot (5x5 at 58,57), the cursor row's 8% tint, and — by far the largest indigo object on the page — a solid rgb(79,70,229) 1px ring around the entire 716x151 capture sheet (master.css:287, `.top:has(.topField:focus-visible)`), plainly visible in locked-notebook--1440x960.png. The accent is not "spent on a browser state"; it is spent on the product's first promise, drawn around the place a thought goes in three seconds. master.css:20 states that rule explicitly: "the one indigo — the live edge of whatever you are doing right now."

The pill claim is also wrong. "Kept" is not the same pill: it renders `data-quiet` (master.css:443) with no outline, ink-3, weight 400, and reads as unpilled in the frame. "In Tasks" and "To decide" share the outline, but pending rows carry the filled ink dot on their own mark (notebook.js:794, `.idxMark i`), which master.css:19 declares as the "waiting on you" signal and master.css:20 pairs with "in Tasks — an outlined chip, ink at full strength". Both states also differ in the accessible name (notebook.js:779). The selector cited, `.idxRow[aria-current]`, does not exist; it is `[data-cursor]`.

The crossing is already indigo, exactly where it is live: `.pick` on the picked words, `.pickBar` hairline, `.peelFrom` on the words printed above the wording they became, and `.readBody::selection` (master.css:587–625). Indigo means the crossing as it happens. The fix asks it to also mean a settled historical fact on every past row, which is the opposite reading of the same colour on the same screen.

The fix would make it worse twice over. At rest 3 of 14 rows carry "In Tasks", so three indigo pills would sit in the pile competing with the desk ring and the cursor; in the "What has crossed into Tasks" ledger every row is crossed and its tag is the lane name (notebook.js:781), so the proposed rule would not even reach the one surface the finding cares about. And taking the cursor row to "ink 4%" lands it on `--wash` (rgba(17,17,17,0.035)), which already carries both `.idxRow:hover` and `.idxRow[data-open]` — collapsing three distinct states onto one fill and regressing the gated single-tab-stop arrow walk so a keyboard cursor becomes indistinguishable from a hovered row.

refuted.problem: The desk column runs 130 to 846 (716px). The index rows directly beneath it run 120 to 1402 (1282px). That leaves 556px — 43% of the sheet — of permanently empty white to the right of every desk object, in every state and in all four finished rooms. The capture field, the opened note, the hand card and the peel all stop at the same ragged edge while the rows below go to the sheet wall. The two planes do not read as depth, they read as an unfinished right half with a full-bleed list under it. A discerning stranger looking at a 1440 screenshot sees a layout that ran out.
refuted.why:
The geometry is right and everything else about the finding is wrong. Measured at 1440x960: `.top` 130–846 (716px), `.paperStack` 130–1392, `.idxRow` 120–1402 (1282px). So the 556px band exists. But:

1. THE FIX RE-CREATES THE DEFECT ROUND 2 REMOVED, AND I PROVED IT. I applied the exact proposed fix in Playwright (`.top,.behind,.handTop,.handCard{max-width:980px}` + `margin-inline:auto` on `.paperStack`) and re-measured. `.top` becomes 980px (130–1110) — and the content does not move: `.topField` stays 154–681 (527px) and the 900-word `.readBody` in ?state=pressure stays 154–681. Every text-bearing rule on the desk is capped at `--measure` (31em) independently of the paper. So the fix does not remove 264px of white, it relocates it INSIDE the paper, framed by a border and a shadow, and drags "Put it back / Esc" 264px away from the column it belongs to while the foot rule spans 400px of nothing. Screenshot comparison at ?state=pressure is unambiguous: the current paper reads as a sheet on a desk, the "fixed" one reads as a mis-sized card with a paragraph in its left third. master.css line 269 names this exact failure as the thing that was fixed: "A 1262px card holding a 527px column is not a piece of paper on a desk, it is a big empty rectangle with a paragraph in the corner." The brief also lists "The desk paper is capped to its own content" as already landed. This finding proposes undoing a documented round-2 fix.

2. THE SECOND HALF OF THE FIX IS A NO-OP. `margin-inline: auto` on `.paperStack` changes nothing — `.paperStack` is already the full 1262px of the desk column; the paper is left-aligned inside it. Measured after applying it: `.top` still starts at l:130. The fix cannot "centre the desk over the index column" as written.

3. FACTUALLY WRONG ABOUT THE FRAMES. "The capture field, the opened note, the hand card and the peel all stop at the same ragged edge" is false. Measured right edges at 1440: capture field 681, paper 846, hand card 816 inside a 846 hand top, peel 884 — the peel deliberately juts 38px past the paper's right edge, which is the whole visual gesture of a second sheet peeled off the note. Four different edges, staged.

4. "43% OF THE SHEET" IS INFLATED. The band is 43% of the desk row's WIDTH, not of the sheet. In the resting state the desk is 187px tall inside a 924px sheet, so the empty region is ~556x187 = 8.5% of the sheet, and the head above it and the pile below it both run the full width. The reader's eye crosses one short band, not an unfinished right half.

5. IT IS ALSO NOT "PERMANENTLY EMPTY IN EVERY STATE". In ?state=seam the 373px-tall peel occupies that vertical zone and overhangs the paper; in ?state=review the desk carries the hand; in ?state=voice the floor is ink.

The genuinely open question the finding brushes past is the opposite one: at 1920 the index rows stretch to 1882px while the paper holds at 716, so it is the INDEX that has no measure of its own, not the paper that is too narrow. That is a different finding with a different fix, and it is not what was filed.

rounds.headline: Every seat rose, the spread closed to 0.4, and every seat answered the question that was put to them: the structural charge is answered, nothing holding this back is structural, and 9.5 is reachable inside the locked architecture and the three-colour lock. What is left, in the UI seat's words, is that the resting state is composed to about 8.5 and the transitional, secondary and phone states are composed to about 6 — the resting frame plus reflow, rather than every state designed as a frame.
rounds.body: Twenty-five findings confirmed, ten refuted. The desk became a two-column plane with the note's own facts in a margin beside the writing, and the peel opens into that margin. A phone can finally read a note and act on it. The index heading takes the step above the rows it heads. And one Ctrl+Z gives back a whole burst again: nothing is written to the DOM inside the input event, because Chromium ends the browser's typing history the moment the document is mutated during input.

wins.biggestWin: Make the desk a two-column plane and stop treating 45% of the top plane as margin. Right now the upper plane is 1000px wide doing 527px of work in every state, while the index directly beneath it is inked edge to edge — so the plane the architecture calls the desk optically recedes behind the plane it is meant to lift off. Put the note's own facts (kind, age, filing, word count, the In Tasks trail) in a 300px right column at x=937, and open the peel into that same column instead of floating it below the paper. That one change fixes four things at once: the void on the desk, the seam state's empty lower third, the peel's arbitrary left edge, and the density inversion between the two planes — and it gives the hand card somewhere to put meta so its height can be fixed and the review loop stops bobbing. On the standing charge: this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it. The subject is load-bearing — filing by house and couple, still-to-decide as the unit of state, the sealed one-way seam, the ledger of what crossed — and that charge is answered. What is holding it below 9.5 is not concept and not the three-colour lock; it is that the resting state is composed to about 8.5 and the transitional, secondary and phone states are composed to about 6. Nothing in my five findings needs a colour, a weight or an architecture change. 9.5 is reachable inside the locks; it needs one composition pass that treats every state as a designed frame rather than the resting frame plus reflow.

Give the index its typographic spine back. The group rule and the first sentence of every row under it are currently identical type — 15px/600/#111 both, measured — so the surface a venue owner spends almost her whole session in has no rank at all, only indentation and a hairline, and the gate's `rule >= row` assertion lets it sit exactly on the floor. Raise `.idxDay` to `--t-17` with `--tr-18`, leave the row lede at 15/600, and change the gate to `>`. That one change lifts every frame at every width in every room, and it is the change that turns a list into an index. I do not think this direction is an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it — the lede-plus-tail row (600 first sentence, ink-3 continuation), the subject rules that carry what the house is facing, and the per-group \"1 still to decide\" are a genuine point of view about setting somebody's own sentences, and they are better than Bear's. But this is not yet a type system, it is an excellent eight-step ramp sitting on ladders that are declared in prose and enforced nowhere, which is why four of my five findings exist and why the hero moment ships at browser-default 16px/normal without a single gate noticing. 9.5 is reachable inside the lock — nothing above needs a fourth colour, a third weight, or a change to the architecture — but only if the ladders become assertions rather than comments. Fix the fly first (it is a proven bug, not a taste call), the index rank second, then close the gate holes so round 5 cannot re-open them.

The failure-mode charge does not land: the subject axis ordered by what the house is facing, the ledger that reprints only what crossed, and the honesty states are product ideas a generic notes app does not have, so this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it. What is holding it below 9.5 is that the keyboard model stops at the happy path, and the single change that would move the score most is making the pick reachable and discoverable without a pointer: a roving sentence walker inside the note body (arrows move, Space picks, the same offerPick path downstream), with the primary control stating its precondition at rest — "Pick the words, then send" with a Space hint — instead of refusing after the press with an instruction only a mouse can obey. That one change turns the sealed edge from a mouse gesture into a model, removes the only place in the file where a labelled primary answers a person with something they cannot do, and teaches the gesture to a venue owner before they fail at it. None of my five findings need a colour, a weight or a change to the architecture, and none of them are structural: 9.5 is reachable inside the lock, and the honest distance is about a week of keyboard-and-repaint work, not a redirection.

Build the phone's read-and-decide surface. On desktop this is genuinely close to the bar — the subject axis, the grouping by what the house is facing, the seam ceremony, the empties and the not-yets are real design, not a notes app wearing wedding words, and the round-4 charge is answered there. On a phone it collapses to exactly that charge: a well-made list of wedding sentences you can add to and never act on, because .desk is display:none and nothing replaced it. A venue operator's phone is where the thought arrives and where the ten minutes between a ceremony and a dinner service actually is; a capture product that cannot read or decide on that device is missing a third of itself for its primary user. Nothing else on this list moves the score as far — fix the four smaller findings and it is an 8.4; ship the phone read/decide sheet with the same peel and this direction can reach 9.5 inside the locked architecture, which I believe it can.

Lock the vocabulary, then spend indigo on the edge. One editorial pass fixing findings 1 and 2 raises five surfaces at once, because the defect is not in any single string — it is that nobody owns the words. The state has five names, the verb \"keep\" has two opposite meanings, and the live announcements speak a sixth grammar nobody has ever proofread as a set ("Kept.", "Undone. Kept.", "Kept in Notes. 7 left.", "Open.", plus a 200-character legal sentence per keystroke). Print every rendered string and every accessible name and every announcement in one column, in the order a person meets them, and edit them as one document rather than as forty template literals. On the standing charge: this is not an extremely well-made notes app wearing wedding words. The subject grouping is genuinely what a venue is facing, the seam is a real product idea, and the honesty states are better than most shipped work — though six of the fourteen fixture notes are a software founder's notes (studio newsletter, teacher onboarding, student launch pricing, a cash-flow lecture) and two of the five headline groups exist only to hold them, so the pile a venue manager opens leads with a wedding and then a college assignment. Swap those for a venue's own standing work. And to answer the distance question plainly: 9.5 is reachable inside the locked architecture and the three-colour lock. Nothing holding this back is structural. What is holding it back is that the words were written surface by surface and the accent was never assigned a meaning.

Retime the arrival so the thought visibly travels and the row takes the words over on contact. Everything else here is craft debt; this is the only 1.5 seconds a stranger will carry away, and right now it is a fast blur followed by the same sentence printed on itself. On the standing charge, plainly: this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words pasted on. The sealed edge is a real idea, well built and honestly stated once ("Your note stays here. Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick"), the decision queue has a posture rather than a feature, and the offline and conflict states are the best-written English in the whole programme. What keeps it at 7.6 rather than 9.5 is not concept, it is that the product's own promises are kept everywhere except where they are most watched: the moment does not read, the keyboard walk chases a different list from the one on screen, and the sheet stops accepting a thought the moment you look something up. Fix those three and the remaining distance is small and cosmetic. One thing worth naming beyond my five: nothing on screen behaves differently because Mara and Finn are in two days. The heading says it, the product never acts on it, and that is the difference between a beautiful notebook for a venue and the notebook a venue could not work without.

It can reach 9.5 inside the locked architecture and the three-colour lock — not one of my five findings needs a colour, a weight, or a structural change, and the charge this direction was chosen to avoid does not stick: the subject axis ordered by what the house is facing, the group rule carrying "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days · 1 still to decide", and the sealed seam printing the picked words above the wording they became are venue ideas, not a generic notes app wearing wedding words. The distance is execution, not concept. The single change worth more than the other four together is to stop the pressure state being a photograph: delete the hard-coded desk block in STATES.pressure and render the 900-word note through readSheet() with a real openId. confirmed.element: 390px · .desk { display:none } · tapping .idxRow · ?state=review at 390
confirmed.problem: On a phone the product is capture-only. Tapping a note row tints it and does nothing else: the desk is display:none, so a note can never be opened, read in full, or crossed into Tasks. ?state=review at 390 renders the index alone — no card, no question, no Send to Tasks / Just keep it / Decide later / Delete — and its head still reads "7 left" while eight are pending, because the card that is not drawn is not counted. In review it is Send to Tasks / Just keep it / Decide later / Delete with the pips under the title, fed by the same .handTop markup so there is no second implementation. Render the peel as a second, smaller sheet inset further from the top so the note's source line and first line stay visible behind it — the lock says the note is never covered, and a full-bleed peel would break that. Add three gate assertions at 390 so this cannot regress: open a row and assert `.readBody` is visible; load ?state=review and assert all four `[data-act^="d-"]` controls are visible; assert the review head's number equals the notebook chip's number.

The product was capture-only on the device the thought actually arrives on.

confirmed.element: .handFoot [data-act="d-task"] and .peel [data-act="peel-send"], both visible at ?state=review after T

confirmed.element: .handBody and .peelLabel "THE WORDS YOU PICKED" on the T route, ?state=review
confirmed.problem: Pressing T in the hand auto-seeds the first sentence of the note, labels it "The words you picked", and announces "The words you picked: ...". Nobody picked anything. On this route .handBody is plain text with no mark, so the note above gives no visual account of which half crosses and which half stays — the selection route on the desk does mark it, so the two routes contradict each other on the one claim the product is sold on. confirmed.fix:
Three parts, in priority order.

1. Close the refusal gap first — it is the bigger defect. In `decide("task")` (notebook.js ~line 288), drop the `|| note.title` fallback and route through the same guard `startPeel` uses: with no pick available, say `N.copy.nothingSelected` and do not open the peel. Widen it to accept a range inside `.handBody` as well, and render `.pickBar` above `.handFoot` on the hand card the way `readSheet` renders it, so T on a card is either the confirmation of a real selection or a refusal, never an invention.

2. Mark the seeded range in place. 3. Do not author the label copy — the reviewer does not own it. State the constraint and let notes-copy.ts hold whichever string the founder picks: the label and the announcement must not assert an act the person did not perform. If step 1 lands, "The words you picked" becomes true on both routes and no new string is needed at all — which is the cheaper and better answer than adding a second noun for the same object. Gate it in notes-interaction-check.mjs, in the hand block: after pressing T, assert `.hand .pick` count === 1; assert the marked text equals the `.peelFrom` value; and assert that T on a card with no selection and no pick opens no peel and announces `nothingSelected`. Also extend the existing four-state "a person's own words are set identically" check (line 971) to confirm the `.pick` span inside `.handBody` does not change the type ramp.

confirmed.element: flyWords() ghost .fly (notebook.js ~245-270) and @keyframes arrive (master.css:323) — state=notebook, after Ctrl+Enter
confirmed.problem: Sampled every frame in a live browser: the ghost covers the whole distance from field to row in 138ms of a 460ms animation (top 108 -> 363 by t=138, left 285 -> 294) and then hangs motionless for another 320ms fading 0.84 -> 0, printed directly on top of a row that renders the identical words at full ink from frame one (@keyframes arrive only washes the row background, never its text). So 30% of the signature moment is travel and 70% is a stationary duplicate of the sentence dissolving over itself. The one thing a stranger would remember about this product reads as a smudge, not as a thought landing. The intention is written beautifully in the source comment and is not on the screen.

Fix the ghost first, because that alone kills the double-print with zero risk. In flyWords: duration 400, easing "cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)"; keyframes {transform: translate(0,0) scale(1), opacity: 1} / {opacity: 1, offset: 0.68} / {transform: translate(dx,dy) scale(s), opacity: 0}. Travel then occupies the whole duration and the ghost fades out across its last ~130px of motion, so there is never a frame where a static duplicate sits over the row. Also replace the dead scale term: s should be the type ratio, parseFloat(rowFontSize) / parseFloat(fieldFontSize) (15/16 here), not to.width / from.width, which clamps to 1 at every desktop width and is the reason the words never become the row's words. Keep transform-origin 0 0 and set the ghost's -webkit-line-clamp to 1 so a two-line ghost cannot land as a two-line stamp on a one-line row.

Do NOT ship the proposed ".idxRow[data-arriving] .idxText { animation: takeOver 120ms var(--curve) 290ms both }" as written. `arriving` is held for 620ms, and the input handler at notebook.js:1456 calls paint() the instant the draft crosses empty->live — the first character of the next thought, which is exactly the flow the caret-return exists to serve. The row remounts with data-arriving still set, takeOver restarts from its backwards fill, and the person's just-saved sentence blanks for 290ms after the ghost has already gone. Today that same remount only restarts a background wash.

If the hand-off is still wanted after the ghost fix, make it one-shot and repaint-proof by driving it from flyWords rather than from a selector that re-fires on every paint: pass the destination node in, and on the ghost animation's own timeline run row.animate([{opacity:0},{opacity:1}], {duration:120, delay:270, easing:"var-curve equivalent", fill:"backwards"}), cancelling it in the existing done() handler so a cut animation restores the text immediately. A WAAPI animation on the live node dies with the node and cannot be resurrected by a remount, which is the whole failure the [data-arriving] selector walks into. Leave the reduced-motion path untouched — `arriving` is never set there, so neither change reaches it.
confirmed.done: The travel is the moment, so the travel takes the time. It was covering the whole distance in 138ms of a 460ms animation and then hanging motionless for 320ms, which reads as a blur followed by the same sentence printed twice. The row also holds its breath until the words land on it.

(2) Fix the stale comment at notebook.js:522-524 so the next reader is not told the CSS solved something it clips. 2. STATES.pressure becomes `notebook()` with openId initialised to `N.long.id` on first entry only (guard it the way STATES.seam guards `seamTouched`, so closing the note does not immediately re-open it). 3. Carry the long-measure over: `.readLong` currently exists only in the deleted block, so readSheet must add it when the body exceeds a word threshold (or when note.id === "long"), or the 900-word measure regresses to the short-note measure and the state stops testing what it exists to test.

Then move the dead-control sweep out of the single resting-state block: loop it over all ten states, and add one assertion that after pressing the primary peel control the announced picked words are a substring of the body actually on the desk — that assertion alone would have caught (3) and would catch any future state that seeds a peel from a note that is not on screen.

For the typography, build the body once in readSheet so a note is set identically peeled and unpeeled. Always emit the `<span class="lede">` run and the rest run, then insert the `.pick` span inside whichever run contains the picked range, splitting it across both runs when the pick straddles the sentence boundary — the picked words keep the weight of the run they came from rather than flattening the note to 400.
