confirmed.element: `.idxDay` at 360-390px — the `@media (max-width: 720px)` block has no `.idxDay` rule; locked-notebook--390x844.png
confirmed.problem: The rule that heads each group, described in the source as the one line on this surface that could not belong to any other product, is a three-column flex row with no phone treatment at all. Measured at 390 and at 360, all three parts break onto a second line simultaneously: the couple's name splits across lines ("Mara &" / "Finn"), "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" wraps at 160px, "1 still to decide" wraps at 79px. A single 22px line becomes a 71px block of three ragged competing columns. It resolves to one line only at 430 and above, so it is broken at every common iPhone width, including the width in the reviewed frame. In the same frame `.indexHead::after` collapses to a 14px stub floating after the "When" toggle (130px at 360) — a decorative hairline with no consistent length.
confirmed.fix: Real, but do NOT apply the proposed fix as written. I tested it: the proposed grid restack sits in the 720px block, so it applies at every width up to 720 and forces the rule from 49px to 70px at 414-720 (tablet portrait, where the line already fits with room to spare) while saving exactly 1px at 390 — a regression bought for nothing. It also fights the bare text node: the label is not wrapped in an element, so it lands as an anonymous grid item and cannot be styled or spanned. Use flex-wrap instead, which stacks only where the line actually runs out. In the same 720 block: `.idxDay { flex-wrap: wrap; column-gap: 10px; row-gap: 1px; white-space: nowrap; } .idxDayNote { flex: none; }` plus `.indexHead::after { display: none; }`. Measured across ?state=notebook and ?state=pressure at 320/360/375/390/414/430/600/720: the subject label stays one whole line at every width (1 client rect, no more "Mara &" / "Finn"), the date stays beside it, only "1 still to decide" drops to a quiet right-aligned second line and only below 414; 414-720 stays untouched at 49px; no horizontal overflow in `.index` at any width. `white-space: nowrap` is what keeps each fact whole, and it is worth adding a gate assertion that `.idxDay` first-child text resolves to one client rect at 320, 360 and 390 so this cannot silently regress the way it did.
confirmed.done: Same fix.

confirmed.element: notebook.js:paint() `mount.innerHTML = …` followed by trimRows()
confirmed.problem: Every act rebuilds the whole tree with innerHTML and then runs trimRows(), which writes innerHTML and reads scrollWidth inside a while loop — one forced synchronous layout per word removed, unconditionally rewriting every row's markup before it even checks whether the row overflows. Measured at 4x CPU throttle (a mid-range phone, or a laptop under load): one repaint costs 81-90ms at 14 notes and 224-287ms at 36 notes. moveCursor calls paint() per row, so at a season's density the arrow walk the product advertises runs at roughly 4fps; filing changes, note open, note close and the undo strip's own 10-second expiry all pay the same. It is also why scroll, caret, focus and the trim have to be hand-stitched back afterwards — and why `.readBody`'s own scroll, which is not in the restore list, is not preserved at all. Nothing at the Linear or Things bar rebuilds the document to move a selection.
confirmed.fix:
Three changes, with one correction to the fix as proposed.

(a) moveCursor must not repaint. Verified safe: cursorId reaches the DOM only via data-cursor (notebook.js:877) and tabindex (882), and CSS keys off it only through [data-cursor] selectors (master.css:468, 469, 476) — including the `+ .idxRow::before` sibling rule, which re-resolves on attribute change with no JS help. So: remove data-cursor and set tabindex="-1" on the outgoing row, set data-cursor and tabindex="0" on the incoming one, focus it, scrollIntoView({block:"nearest"}), call say(`${n} of ${total}. ${title}`), and return without touching paint(). This alone takes the arrow walk from ~47ms to sub-millisecond.

(b) CORRECTION to the proposed trimRows guard. "Check scrollWidth <= clientWidth against the already-rendered markup before writing anything" is wrong on the resize path. trimRows also runs on resize and fonts.ready (notebook.js:1814-1819), where the rendered markup is the PREVIOUS trimmed markup. After a widening resize that markup already fits, so the guard would skip the row and leave it permanently over-trimmed — content silently withheld, which is a worse defect than the one being fixed. The reset write is only redundant on the paint() path, where idxRow (line 885) has just emitted identical full markup. So make it explicit: trimRows(fresh). paint() calls trimRows(true) and skips the reset entirely; the resize and fonts.ready handlers call trimRows(false) and keep it. And restructure the reset as two passes rather than an interleave — write every row's reset first, then measure every row — so the whole reset costs 1 layout flush instead of N.

(c) Replace the word-by-word `while (words.pop())` with a binary search over word count (the fit predicate is monotone in word count, so this is exact, not approximate): ~log2(22) ≈ 5 layouts for a typical row instead of 22, and the same for the lede loop at 540-543 with its floor of four words preserved. Combined with (b), a full trim pass drops from ~364 layouts to roughly 40.

(d) Add .readBody scrollTop to the pair of values paint() captures and restores (notebook.js:1361-1363), keyed by the same open-note id so a restore never lands on a different note's body. Then extend notes-interaction-check.mjs: assert .readBody scroll survives a repaint at 1280x720 in pressure (the reachable case), and add a budget assertion — one cursor move performs zero innerHTML writes, and a full paint at 36 notes stays under a stated layout-read ceiling — so this cannot regress silently the way it did here.
confirmed.done: Typing no longer rebuilds anything at all, and the trim skips rows that wrap rather than measuring the wrong axis on them.

refuted.problem: The desk paper is 1000px wide with a 952px content box, and every piece of content ever placed on it is capped at --measure 527px. Measured: .top 261→1261, .topField and .readBody 285→812. That leaves 425px — 45% of the upper plane — permanently blank on the right, at all three widths, in every state. Directly beneath it the index row runs the full 1020 and is inked edge to edge: title at 294, preview to 1067, tag at 1080, time flush right at 1261. So the two locked planes have opposite densities. The plane the architecture says sits on top is half-drawn, the plane meant to sit beneath it is full, and the index optically out-weighs the desk — which is the exact failure the master.css comment at line 121 claims to have retired. It only moved the void from beside the paper to inside it. In pressure and seam this is unmissable: a 385px-tall column of prose hugging the left of a 952px sheet with an empty rectangle the size of a second note beside it.
refuted.why: REFUTED on measurement. Driven at 1280/1440/1920 in all seven states: the rightmost inked pixel inside .top is 1237 at 1440 — the paper's right padding edge — in notebook (.topMeta), capture (Keep it + count), readback (Keep both), pressure (Put it back Esc), nothing and not-yet. The index row's right edge is 1271, so the two planes land 34px apart (the paper's 24px padding plus the row's 10px inset). That is the shared edge the prior round bought, not "opposite densities", and the desk is not "half-drawn": .topFoot and .readSrc are both 952 wide and inked flush right, framing the measure-capped prose band above and below. Seam is the ONLY state where ink stops at 812, and there the plane is 120px tall. Two of the five elements cited are measured wrong: readback contains no .readBody at all (it renders .saidWas 285→914 and two .pieceField rows 303→801, with a right-hand cluster at 950→1237 carrying "2 notes, not one", Discard and Keep both in the same band), and .handBody is not on the 1000px paper — the hand is a 768px card (377→1145) whose action row runs 403→1119, so the "952px sheet with 425 blank" framing never applied to it. The fix would also make the work worse: a 300px kind/age/filing/word-count ladder is a task-tool properties rail bolted to a piece of paper, aimed at venue operators who need none of it — the exact "well-made kanban with wedding words" failure; docking .peel into it destroys the locked object (width:min(560px,100% - 72px) with a ::before tab arrow at x=30 pointing up at the note it tore from) and squeezes the task-wording field to roughly fourteen characters a line, immediately after a prior round fixed the peel for being too big; "removes 420px of dead sheet under it" is factually wrong since .peel sits outside .paperStack in .pile, over the ink floor, not the sheet; and a focus-only rule at x=937 declares an edge 125px past where the text actually wraps while adding an appearing element to the most protected moment in the product. Whitespace beside a held measure is the discipline --measure exists to enforce, and it is how iA Writer, Bear and Linear's issue body all set a person's own prose.

refuted.problem: One measure, four left edges. The same 527px column of a person's own writing is set at x=285 on the desk, x=294 in the index row, x=334 in the seam peel, x=403 in the review hand and x=433 in the review peel. So the sentence a person wrote slides 9px left the moment it is lifted from the index onto the desk — the exact transition the architecture is built on — and 118px right when the same note comes up in the hand. Round three gated that the words are set identically in size, leading and tracking; nothing gated where the column starts, and it starts in a different place in every room. This is the mathematically-aligned, optically-wrong class: each object is correctly centred or padded within itself, and no two of them share a reading spine.
refuted.why:
Numbers verified in Playwright at 1440 (locked): .readBody x=285, .idxText x=294, .peelField x=334 (seam) / 450 (review, measured after pressing T; the finding says 433, which is the .peel card edge, not the field), .handBody x=403.3. The measurements are right; the reading of them is wrong on every load-bearing point.

There IS one declared spine and the surfaces do share it. master.css line 127 defines --stack: min(100%, 1060px) with the comment "--stack is what the two planes agree on", and --gutter: 30px. Measured: .indexHead and .index are both x=231 w=1060; .index content edge = 231+30 = 261; .idxRow content edge = 251+10 = 261; the desk's .paperStack/.top = x=261 w=1000. The desk paper's left edge and the index row's left edge are the same pixel, 261, in every state. The claim "no two of them share a reading spine" is false — all five surfaces are derived from 261 by one documented rule each.

Each rule is consistent, not ad hoc. Desk paper: 261 + 24px paper padding = 285, and .topField, .readBody, .pickBar (left:24) and .nudge (left:24) all sit on it — the desk agrees with itself. Index row: 261 + 20px .idxMark + 13px gap = 294; that is an icon gutter, and the leftmost ink of the row (the mark) sits exactly on 261, i.e. on the paper edge. Text inset past a leading icon is the convention in every named benchmark — Things, Bear, Linear and Notion all set list-row text inboard of detail-body text. Nine pixels behind an icon that itself lands on the spine is not "optically wrong", it is the gutter.

The peel's two x values are one rule, not drift. Seam: peel 317, parent paper 261 → +56. Review: peel 433, parent handTop 377 → +56. Identical offset from the paper it peeled off, matching `.peel { margin: 9px 0 0 56px }` and the torn corner at left:30px. The peel is anchored to its parent because the locked architecture says it is a second piece of paper peeled off THAT note. Measuring it against a global spine measures the wrong thing.

The hand is centred in the same column, deliberately: hand 377 w=767 → centre 760.5; desk column 261 w=1000 → centre 761. A narrower focus deck centred in the plane it belongs to, with the fanned back-cards (410/399/388) peeking symmetrically — the frame shows this reads as one coherent floating object, not as a stray left edge.

The transition the finding is built on does not show the 9px. Lifting a row is openNote() → paint(), a plane change: the sentence moves ~440px vertically, goes 15px→17px at a different leading, and sheds its icon, tag and timestamp. Nine pixels of x is not perceptible inside that. In the one place the words genuinely travel — flyWords(), notebook.js:241 — the ghost interpolates field(285)→.idxText(294) with dx, dy and scale in one 460ms curve, so the delta is animated through, never a jump.

The proposed fix is also wrong in its own arithmetic and harmful in its other half. From the row content edge at 261, .idxMark at 24px plus a gap of 8 gives 293, not 285; reaching 285 needs mark+gap = 24 total, i.e. a 4px gap between a 15px glyph and the text, which cramps the icon. And left-anchoring .handCard and both .peel instances would de-centre the review deck and delete the 56px derivation indent that makes the peel read as hanging off the note — trading a consistent relational rule for a global one, at the cost of the architecture's own "peeled off the note" reading. Gating "the left edge of the person's own words is identical in notebook, readback, review, seam and pressure" would freeze that regression in place.

This is a real measurement with the wrong conclusion attached: mathematically different x, structurally one column.

refuted.problem: The takeover carries no <kbd> at all (measured: 0 kbd nodes in .dark), while every comparable primary in the product prints its chord — Ctrl+Enter on Keep, Esc on Put it back, T and K in the hand. So in the one flow a person uses without looking at the screen, standing in a room with their hands full, there is no key that keeps what they said. The only key the state binds is Escape, and Escape discards: it drops the transcript, says "Nothing was kept", and offers no undo (measured: .undo count 0 after it), which makes the single keyboard affordance in the flow the irreversible one. Cancel behaves the same by pointer. Every other destructive act in this file is reversible for ten seconds; the one that destroys spoken words is not.
refuted.why:
Driven, not read. Entering the takeover the real way (click the dock mic or the "Dictate" verb at ?state=notebook) sets refocus = {kind:"act", sel:'[data-act="voice-stop"]'} (notebook.js L1620), and I measured document.activeElement === the "Stop and read it back" button on entry. Pressing Enter from there lands on readback with the live region reading "Two notes came back from that."; Space does the same. So the central claim — "the only key the state binds is Escape", "there is no key that keeps what they said" — is factually false in behaviour. The finding counted kbd nodes in .dark and read the keydown switch, and missed that the state places focus on the primary, which is exactly how Linear, Stripe and Things arm a modal: primary focused, Enter commits, Escape leaves. The 0-kbd measurement is right and irrelevant; a printed legend is invisible to the person the finding describes (hands full, not looking), and the affordance that serves that person — focus on a control whose accessible name is "Stop and read it back" — is already there. Half the proposed fix ("bind Enter to voice-stop") is a no-op on code that already does it.

The other half makes the work worse. Escape in this file has one meaning across six branches: picker cancel, peel cancel, review to notebook, readback discard, voice discard, note close, search clear. Making Escape in voice mean "stop and read it back" would make Escape mean advance/commit in exactly one state, and would produce a two-Escape discard (Esc to readback, Esc to discard) that is strictly harder to hold than the current grammar. That is a regression against the checklist item this programme already paid for.

The undo residue is real but weakly grounded and its fix is worse. The finding's premise "every other destructive act in this file is reversible for ten seconds" does not survive checking: Escape from readback also discards spoken words with no undo (measured: undo count 0, live region "Discarded. Nothing was kept."), and Ctrl+Z is deliberately kept off a live capture draft (L1677 comment). offerUndo is used only where the notebook's data changed — kept (L197), refiled (L1521), sent (L446/455), dropped piece (L1569), kept-from-speech (L1659). Cancelling a recording changes nothing in the notebook, so an undo bar there would be the only one in the file offering to revert a transient UI state, and because that bar advertises Ctrl+Z, undo would silently re-arm a microphone. A keyboard shortcut that reopens a live mic takeover is a worse outcome than the thing being fixed.

refuted.problem: The hand advertises T, K and Esc and answers exactly those, so the two remaining decisions are mouse-only — including "Decide later", the most-reached-for act in any triage queue. Worse, the same keypair means two things on one screen: k decides the card, while j and the arrows walk the index below it. Measured, ArrowDown in the hand leaves the card at "1 of 8" and announces "2 of 7" from a different list. One screen states the same queue four ways: "1 of 8" on the card, "8 still to decide" in the deck note under it, "7 left" in the index head, and "2 of 7" in the ear. Two adjacent keys, two objects, three denominators, in the state that exists to be driven blind at speed.
refuted.why: Driven live at ?state=review, 1440x960. (1) The central claim is factually wrong: "Decide later" and "Delete" are not mouse-only. They are real buttons at tab stops #10 and #11 in the review state; tabbing to #10 and pressing Enter produced "Left for later. 7 left.", advanced .handOf from "1 of 8" to "2 of 9" and raised the undo strip. No advertised key is unimplemented — T, K and Esc all answer, and the gate proves it. The accurate residue is "no single-letter shortcut for two of four verbs", a shortcut-density preference, not a broken keyboard model. (2) The proposed fix breaks the file's one consistent navigation rule. Arrows walk the second plane in every state and that is gated (notes-interaction-check.mjs L133-155: single tab stop, arrow walk, 60-press clamp, Enter opens the walked row). In review the second plane is a live list of the remaining queue with focusable rows; returning before moveCursor would leave those rows Tab-reachable but arrow-dead, an inconsistency worse than the one reported. (3) "Up re-opens the last decided card through decided[]" duplicates a reversal model that already exists and is gated: every decision raises an undo strip and answers Ctrl+Z (verified: "Kept in Notes." -> "Undone. Kept in Notes.", .handOf and stack depth restored). Two grammars for undo on one screen is a regression. (4) The "three denominators" is not a contradiction: "1 of 8" is position in the run, "8 still to decide" is the queue including the card in hand, "Still to decide / 7 left" is the count of the rows that head actually heads (the same rule every list head in the file follows), and 1 + 7 = 8. The ear is not a bare "2 of 7" either — measured, it reads "2 of 7. Teacher onboarding, three things they kept asking for...", naming the note, so it cannot be mistaken for the card. Only the j/k mnemonic adjacency survives, and it is announced, reversible and small — not a 9.5-bar defect, and it arrives bundled with three claims that are wrong.

refuted.problem: The affordance is inverted. The read-only quotation "The words you picked" is painted as a tinted, bordered, rounded box — the shape of an input. The one editable control in the seam, the textarea that decides the exact words crossing the sealed edge, computes to border:0px none, background:transparent, 17px/600 — pixel-identical to a heading, and legible as a field only while it holds focus, which it loses the moment anyone touches the destination picker. Worse, the two boxes print the same sentence twice, differing by one trailing full stop, so a stranger reads the pair as a rendering bug rather than as provenance-then-editable and never discovers they can change what crosses.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on the source, on the driven behaviour, and on the fix.

WRONG ABOUT THE SOURCE. There is no `.peelPicked`. The element is `.peelFrom` (notebook.js:767, master.css:696). Two of the fix's prescriptions are already the shipped state: `.peelFrom span` is already `font-weight: 400` (inherited, measured 400), and `.peelField` already carries the global 2px indigo focus ring at 3px offset (master.css:172-173 — measured `outline: rgb(79,70,229) solid 2px`, offset 3px).

THE "SHAPE OF AN INPUT" PREMISE IS FALSE AS A SYSTEM READING. `.peelFrom` is not painted like a field; it is painted as the highlight, echoed. Measured, `.readBody .pick` = bg rgba(79,70,229,0.08), ring rgba(79,70,229,0.32) 1px, weight 400; `.peelFrom` = bg rgba(79,70,229,0.08), ring rgba(79,70,229,0.32) 1px inset, weight 400. Identical tokens, and the mark is on screen two inches above at the same moment. The washed rounded box under an 11px uppercase label is this product's read-only-echo pattern, used identically by `.saidWas` in readback (master.css:577-581) — the words that came back from speech, also read-only, also washed, also with a `b` caption. In this file a wash box means "these are words being quoted back to you". Nothing in the file uses a wash box for an input.

WRONG ABOUT THE BEHAVIOUR. I drove the real flow (open a note, select a range, "Use these words"): the peel opens with `document.activeElement === .peelField`, focus ring lit. "Legible as a field only while it holds focus" describes the one instant a person is not looking at anything else. The duplication charge also fails in the real flow — picked span, `.pick` mark and field value came back character-identical, not "differing by one trailing full stop". That artefact exists only in the `?state=seam` fixture, where the seed pick ends in a period and a task title correctly does not.

THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE, TWICE. (1) Collapsing the duplication until the person edits deletes the proof of the product's central promise at the exact moment it is made. The two blocks starting identical IS the promise — only the exact words you picked cross — and the boundary line directly above says so. A stranger who sees one field has taken the sealed edge on faith; a stranger who sees the quote and the wording agree has watched it work. It also reverses behaviour the brief lists as settled ("prints the picked words above the wording they became") and that the gate walks at notes-interaction-check.mjs:618-622. (2) A 1px border, white fill and 10px 12px padding would make `.peelField` the only bordered writing surface in the product: `.topField` (:330), `.pieceField` (:593), `.phoneField` (:1018) and `.peelField` (:726) all share `border: 0; outline: 0; background: none` — the paper is the field, which is the locked architecture. It would also stack a second boxed rectangle directly under the first, which is the crowding the finding claims to be curing. Linear's issue title, Things' new to-do, Bear and iA Writer all set their primary text entry exactly as this does.

Taste stated as a defect, resting on a class that does not exist and a duplication that does not occur outside one fixture.

refuted.problem: Beside the sealed crossing sits a second one at peer weight. "Send to Timeline" carries no peel, no picked words, no boundary sentence, no destination picker, and no statement of what Timeline is or what would leave the note — it is a bare button that currently answers "Not part of this exploration." Having spent the whole product teaching a venue operator that words only cross when they are picked and checked, the read desk then offers an exit that appears to need neither. It also renders inconsistently: peer-level at ?state=notebook, collapsed into an unlabelled ellipsis at ?state=pressure, so its weight changes with the length of the note.
refuted.why: Refuted on four independent grounds, all verified by driving the file. (1) The "renders inconsistently" claim is factually false: with a note opened, [data-act="timeline"] renders at the identical box (x=429.08, y=256.59, 149.97x36), same label, visible, at ?state=notebook AND ?state=pressure (36 notes, 900-word note), and at 1440/1280/768. It never collapses into the ellipsis; .topFoot is a flex-wrap row with no state- or width-conditional rule for that button anywhere in master.css. (2) "Peer weight" is false: computed styles show a deliberate three-step ink-density ladder — Send to Tasks is data-primary, background rgb(17,17,17), white, font-weight 600, no outline; Send to Timeline is transparent, rgba(17,17,17,0.72), weight 400, hairline 1px rgba(17,17,17,0.09); More is data-quiet, rgba(17,17,17,0.62), 400, no outline. The sealed crossing is the only filled object on the desk. (3) "Unlabelled ellipsis" is false: [data-act="more"] carries aria-label="More actions for this note". (4) The proposed fix breaks an existing gate: notes-interaction-check.mjs:397-400 asserts the boundary promise appears at most once across .top and .peel (regex /stays here|still private|nothing else from this note|still yours to edit/, ok "and only once", promises.length <= 1). The fix explicitly demands a second "Your note stays here" sentence naming Timeline, which fails that assertion and dilutes the very promise it claims to protect. Additionally, notebook.js:1582 groups timeline with more/privacy/options/photo/retry/destroy under a source comment stating they are deliberately inert lab stubs for surfaces outside this master; Timeline is a locked sibling in the capsule spine SUITE. The finding reads a disclosed stub as a design defect.

refuted.problem: "Keep" is the verb for saving a note AND the verb for declining to send one to Tasks, and the resulting chip is "Kept" for only the second. Driving it: Ctrl+Enter announces "Kept."; pressing K in the hand announces "Kept in Notes. 7 left."; and rows in the pile carry a bare "Kept" chip that a venue manager reads as "I saved this" — which is true of all fourteen. Ctrl+Z then announces "Undone. Kept.", which states the act and its reversal in one breath and drops the count the keep announcement carried. This is the product's most-repeated word and it is ambiguous in the two moments the product is sold on. "Just keep it" also hedges the one decision the hand exists to make.
refuted.why: Factually wrong about the rendered artifact, and the fix regresses the work. Driven live at ?v=locked: typing a note and pressing Ctrl+Enter produces a row whose chip is "To decide" and whose accessible name ends "Still to decide." — capture's keep NEVER produces a "Kept" chip. The chip is set only by note.pending=false && !sent (notebook.js:614-616), which only the hand's K decision sets. Rendered distribution across the 14 rows is In Tasks x3, To decide x8, Kept x3, so the finding's driving claim that the bare "Kept" chip is "true of all fourteen" is false; it sits in a three-value contrast set that does the disambiguating work. The two senses are also not opposite: capture-keep and decision-keep both mean the note lives in Notes, and the announcements are already distinct and separately counted ("Kept. 15 notes, 9 waiting on a decision." vs "Kept in Notes. 7 left."). The proposed fix is worse on its own theory: "Keep it here" shares a longer literal prefix with capture's "Keep it" than "Just keep it" does and drops the scoping contrast against the primary "Send to Tasks" ("just" scopes, it does not hedge); "Save it / Saved." imports file-system chrome into a paper-metaphor product that Bear, Things and iA Writer deliberately avoid. And notebook.js:151 say(`Undone. ${label}`) is the single shared undo announcement for six sites (capture, hand keep/task/later/delete, voice batch) — replacing it with "Put back. 14 notes, 8 still to decide." would state a note count after undoing a Tasks send or a delete, i.e. the wrong fact at that moment, and would require bespoke per-site strings that two prior rounds already hardened for tense and paint order (comments at :194 and :320). The one salvageable grain is unrelated to the keep/kept charge: :192 says "waiting on a decision" while the head, deck note and chips say "still to decide" / "To decide" — the state noun in two grammars. That is a separate, much smaller finding, not this one.

refuted.problem: The peel prints the same eleven words three times inside 340px: highlighted in the note, echoed under "THE WORDS YOU PICKED", then again under "THE TASK WORDING" — the only difference between the two echoes is a trailing full stop. The boundary sentence above already says the words are exactly what crosses. A premium panel states a promise once and shows the payload once; this one triples it, which reads as anxiety rather than assurance. Worse under the keyboard: pressing T in the hand announces the whole 200-character payload sentence — "…Tasks receives these words and nothing else from this note. The rest of what you wrote stays private here." — on every card, in a flow designed to be run eight times in a row. The panel's own boundary line also promises "the exact words you pick and check below" and there is nothing below to check.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Measured in the live file at 1440x960, ?state=seam: .pick top 139 to .peelField bottom 442 = 303px, and .peelFrom "Switch on before guests arrive, not when." vs .peelField "Switch on before guests arrive, not when" do differ only by a full stop. So the surface observation is true at seed. Everything the finding builds on it is not.

1) "there is nothing below to check" is factually wrong. The boundary line sits at y263-301; directly beneath it are the two things it names — THE WORDS YOU PICKED (y312-371) and the editable THE TASK WORDING field (y409-442). The sentence names exactly what is under it. The proposed copy change ("pick, shown below") would make the line LESS accurate, since the field below is checkable and editable, not merely shown.

2) The identity is the first frame of a two-state design, not a duplication. .peelField is a live textarea; the gate itself edits it (notes-interaction-check.mjs:624-631 types and asserts the receipt carries "before guests arrive"). I drove the same edit: after typing, .peelFrom still reads "Switch on before guests arrive, not when." while the field reads "Confirm 8am ballroom access". The block is the provenance record the edited wording is checked against — it is a diff, and a diff shows identity until you change something. Deleting it means that after one keystroke there is no labelled on-screen answer to "what did I actually pick?" on the product's second promise. master.css:694 and the round-3 summary in the brief both list this as a decided, answered requirement ("prints the picked words above the wording they became"); the finding proposes reverting it.

3) The announcement fix rests on a false premise. copy.payload is NOT rendered in the panel — I checked the composited DOM: document.body.innerText.includes("nothing else from this note") === false in ?state=seam. It exists only in say() at notebook.js:294 and :414. So "leave copy.payload rendered statically in the panel where it is read once" is asking for something that does not exist, and implementing it trips the live gate: notes-interaction-check.mjs:397-400 counts /stays here|still private|nothing else from this note|still yours to edit/ across .top and .peel and asserts promises.length <= 1. The boundary already contributes "stays here". Rendering payload makes it 2 and fails the assertion. The fix as written breaks the 216-assertion gate.

4) "on every keystroke" is wrong. I instrumented the .sr live region in ?state=review: the announcement fires once when T opens the peel, not per keystroke, and not on every card — only on cards the person chooses to turn into a task. Sequence captured: T -> one announcement, Escape -> "Nothing crossed. Your note is unchanged.", K -> "Kept in Notes. 7 left.", T -> one announcement.

5) Two of the four fix steps rewrite verbatim product strings (wordingLabel and handoffBoundary). The brief puts copy out of the reviewer's remit: it is judged, not rewritten. And "sentence case" for the eyebrow is unachievable anyway without touching the locked type treatment — .peelLabel is text-transform: uppercase (master.css:725), so the string case is not what renders.

Also noted while driving, and NOT what this finding claims: the T announcement renders a doubled full stop ("...on the Saturday.. Tasks receives these words..."), because sourceLabel + words already ends in a period. That is a separate one-character defect, not the triplication charge, and it does not rescue this finding.

refuted.problem: Audited computed styles across five states: the largest and most saturated indigo object in the product is a 1020x40 row-cursor tint that appears on every screen, plus a resting glow on the capture card. Meanwhile every primary verb — "Keep it", "Send to Tasks", "Write the first one", "Save it again", "Delete it" — is the same ink black. So the one accent the palette allows is spent saying "you are here" and is never spent saying "this is the thing that makes this product different". The one-way edge into Tasks, the second promise of the product, is rendered in the same black as a destructive delete. Three colours are being obeyed, not spent.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on four measured counts, and the fix would regress the file.

1. "Most saturated indigo object" is wrong. I measured every indigo-bearing element across all ten states at 1440x960. `.idxRow[data-cursor]` is `rgba(79,70,229,0.08)` — the LEAST saturated indigo in the file. Solid `#4f46e5` is spent on the rail mark, the `.word::after` dot, `.pips i[data-now]`, `.piece:focus-within::before` and the focus outline. The finding's headline object is the weakest tint present, not the strongest.

2. "The edge into Tasks is rendered in the same black as a destructive delete" is false in the state it names. Measured in `?state=review&v=locked`: "Send to Tasks" is `bg rgb(17,17,17) / color rgb(255,255,255) / shadow none`; "Delete" is `bg rgba(0,0,0,0) / color rgba(17,17,17,0.62) / shadow none` — an unfilled, de-emphasised `[data-destroy]` that only fills on hover. They are two different treatments, and master.css:363-366 documents that separation as a fix already paid for ("It sat in the same weight and the same row as Decide later, which is how a queue loses a note to a mis-tap").

3. "Indigo is never spent saying this is the thing that makes this product different" is false. In `?state=seam` the two largest indigo objects on screen are `.pick` at 503x50 (the words the person picked, marked in place) and `.peelFrom` at 496x59 ("The words you picked" printed above the wording they became) — both `rgba(79,70,229,0.08)`, both directly on the crossing, together larger than the row cursor. Indigo is already spent on the seam; the finding asks for something the file does.

4. "A resting glow on the capture card" is a misread of a focus ring. `.top[data-live]` fires only when `draft.trim()` is non-empty (notebook.js:722). What the frames show at rest is `.top:has(.topField:focus-visible)` — solid indigo 1px — because the caret starts in the field, a gated behaviour. The proposed fix, "keep it on :focus-within only", is already the state of the file; applied literally to `[data-live]` it deletes the one signal that says "your words are in the field and not yet safe", which in a three-second capture product is the most load-bearing honesty mark on the sheet.

The fix also makes the work worse in two concrete ways. (a) "Cursor background to ink at 4%" collides with `.idxRow:hover` and `.idxRow[data-open]`, both measured at `rgba(17,17,17,0.035)`. At 4% the keyboard cursor becomes visually indistinguishable from a hovered row and from the open row — the single tab stop and arrow walk lose their only visible anchor — and it inserts a fifth step into a surface ladder the file explicitly declares as four with "no value sits between them". (b) The proposed gate, "no indigo fill larger than 24px² in any state with no crossing on screen", fails immediately on `mark` in `?state=search`: I measured three highlights at 53x19, 58x19, 56x19 (~1000px² each) in a state with no crossing. The gate as written outlaws search highlighting, which the 216-assertion behaviour gate requires.

Finally, the premise contradicts the file's stated canon (master.css:20, "the one indigo — the live edge of whatever you are doing right now"). Under that doctrine the cursor, the live field edge, the picked words and the focus ring are one meaning, consistently applied. Re-pointing indigo at buttons would put a solid fill in competition with the focus ring, the live field edge and the picked-words mark simultaneously in the seam state — spending the accent four ways at once, which is the opposite of the finding's own goal. The `data-primary` / `data-ink` split already encodes crossing-vs-non-crossing in the markup; `?v=press` renders it as `bg rgb(79,70,229)`. Choosing `[data-indigo="subtle"]` for the locked room is a declared preset axis, not an oversight.

refuted.problem: Measured: opening a note or opening search removes every textarea from the page, and the desktop dock then offers only Search notebook, Dictate, Read a photo and the account. The draft survives in memory and returns on Escape, which is good, but for the whole time a person is reading a note or looking one up there is nowhere on the sheet to put a new thought. On the phone the dock carries the field permanently, so the product keeps its headline promise at rest and on the phone, and charges an Escape plus a re-aim on the two desktop screens a venue owner actually lives in. Three seconds becomes Escape, then three seconds.
refuted.why:
The load-bearing measurement is wrong. Driven live at 1440x960: with a live draft in .topField, opening an index row does remove the textarea, but the desktop dock's FIRST control is `<button data-act="write" aria-label="Write a note">` — measured aria-labels in the read state are ["Write a note", "Search notebook", "Dictate", "Read a photo", "Orla, venue manager. Account and settings"], not the four the finding lists. Clicking that 36x36 glyph restores the draft verbatim ("marquee sides need checking" came back character-identical), puts the caret in .topField, and announces "Ready to write." into the live region. notebook.js:625-630 carries the design note for exactly this ("reading a note replaces it, so the dock carries the way back to writing"). So on the read screen the way back to the sheet is one click on a labelled control sitting in the dock the finding says is empty of it, or one Escape — and Escape from read was measured returning focus to the .idxRow it came from with the draft intact. That is one control, not "Escape then re-aim".

The search half is factually right (no .topField in ?state=search) but the proposed fix would make the work worse at a 9.5 bar. Search's own bar autofocuses an <input> and carries a visible "Esc" control; adding a collapsed 44px one-line textarea at the head of the same sheet puts two near-identical single-line fields within ~44px of each other, one that filters and one that captures, with the wrong one focused. In a product whose stated third defect is keystroke loss, a screen where a mis-aimed thought silently becomes a query (or a query becomes a note) is a worse failure than an Escape. Linear, Things and Bear all resolve this the same way the artifact does: search takes the surface, Escape gives it back.

The finding is also taste stated as measurement on the premise that a venue owner "lives in" search — search here is a transient lookup entered by "/" or Ctrl+K and dismissed by Escape or a visible Esc button, not a resting screen.

rounds.headline: Interaction broke eight and Taste fell half a point, which is the panel looking harder in a new place. Every seat again said the same thing about the standing charge: this is a venue operator's product from the ground up, not a well-made notes app wearing wedding words. What separates it from the gate, in the interaction seat's words, is that in three places the live path is weaker than the specimen room the gate measures — the queue's primary refuses without saying it will, delete is the least guarded control on the card while the line above it promises everything can be put back, and the peel greets the product's most important flow with its only scolding sentence.
rounds.body: Twenty-four findings confirmed, eleven refuted. The most valuable was a correction of my own work: the claim that one Ctrl+Z gives back the whole typing burst was true at machine speed and false at human speed. At 40 to 90ms a key, a deferred write lands between keystrokes rather than after them, so the document was still being mutated inside the browser's typing history. The write waits for a pause now, the sheet wakes from a custom property that changes no node at all, and the gate types at two human speeds and fails on anything less than a burst.

wins.biggestWin: Stop letting the desk's height be an accident. Replace `.top[data-two] > .deskAside { grid-row: 1 / span 20 }` with a real two-column grid — writing column wrapped in one grid item at column 1, aside at column 2, both row 1, parent align-items:start — so the paper's height resolves to max(column) plus its declared 22/14 padding in every state instead of being padded out by seventeen phantom tracks (18.23px each in seam, 5.33px each in pressure). That alone removes the 37px and 77px mystery feet and makes the desk's foot one number rather than four. Then fill what it exposes: move the "What has crossed into tasks" ledger out of the index plane and into the writing column beneath the note during ?state=seam, so the 626×360 void under a two-line note carries the one thing that state is about. The desk stops being a rectangle that ends where the taller column happened to end and becomes a designed plane — which is the difference between this reading as a very well made notes app and reading as a sheet of paper on a desk. And to be explicit about the charge you asked about: this is not "an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words." The index groups by Mara & Finn, the course, the studio, the house; the head counts what is still to decide; the seam prints the words you picked above and larger than the wording derived from them and says the note stays here. Those are a venue operator's actual life and the product's actual promise, not a generic capture tool wearing wedding nouns. What is holding it at 7.5 is not concept, it is that four of its most repeated edges — the word edge between the planes, the paper's foot, the receipt's lane, and the sheet's relationship to the column at 1920 — are still approximate, and a 9.5 is a build where none of them are.

Kill the punctuation-derived lede. Replace `body.split(/(?<=[.?!”])\s/)[0] || body` (notebook.js:195 and :1753) with a 46-character word-safe budget, and make a fully-bold note unrepresentable: if the remainder would be empty, emit no `<b>` and set the whole note at 400. That one change is worth more than the other four combined because it is the only defect that fires on real data rather than on fixtures — every note a person actually captures in three seconds lacks a full stop, and today every one of those renders as solid semibold on the desk and as a bold slab in the index. Fixing it is what makes the 400/600 pairing an actual designed hierarchy instead of an accident of how carefully the writer punctuated, and it is the difference between a type system that is correct in its tokens and one that is correct on the screen. To be plain about the gate: this is not 9.5 and it is not close. What a 9.5 would have that this does not is a type system that holds when it meets a real person's writing rather than the fixture's. The ramp, the tracking curve, the three leadings, the tabular numerals, the uppercase micro-label discipline and the 31em reading measure are genuinely at Vercel Geist standard — the tokens are the best part of this work. But the three moments where type has to carry the product's argument all fail: the person's own words go semibold because they typed fast, the words they picked are set identically to the machine's paraphrase of them, and the spoken transcript gets a 78-character line while every typed surface gets 69. This is not an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words — the copy is set with real intent and the seam and the honesty line earn their sizes — but the index, which is where a venue owner actually lives, is currently generic list typography held together by a bold-first-sentence trick that breaks on contact.

Close the delete contract. Route the hand's Delete through the confirm panel the product has already designed and drawn in ?state=not-yet, drop its resting ink below its neighbours so it stops looking like "Decide later", and make the undo window and the printed promise the same number in both rooms. Right now the file prints "every decision can be put back" directly beneath a one-click, no-confirm, ten-second-then-permanent verb whose own specimen card promises thirty seconds and a confirmation. Everything else on this list is craft; that one is the product telling a venue owner something that is not true about their own notes, and it is the reason this sits at 8.2 rather than in the nines. For the record on the standing charge: this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it. The still-to-decide ledger, the sealed one-way seam with the note never leaving, the honesty states that refuse a warning hue, and the queue framed as decisions rather than triage are a venue operator's product from the ground up. What separates it from 9.5 is that in three places the live path is weaker than the specimen room the gate measures.

Rebuild the peel margin so the seam says one thing once. Today it prints the picked sentence twice at identical size in a 266px gutter beside 660px of empty desk, hides its only editable control until focus, and lets an unexplained "Send to Timeline" stand at peer rank next to a boundary promise that covers Tasks alone. Collapse it to a single visibly editable "The task will say" field seeded from the marked range, widen the margin by taking the void the writing column is wasting, and remove the second destination from the row. This is the moment the whole product exists to make legible to someone who has never used a task tool, and it is currently the only screen where a stranger has to guess. Two things beyond my five findings also stand between this and the gate, and I am naming them rather than spending findings on them: the open-note desk reserves a fixed plane so a twenty-word note floats in roughly 80% white while the working panel is cramped, and the head's top-line fact is a generic "8 still to decide" when the venue's actual pressure — a wedding in two days with notes unresolved — is already in the data and printed only as a group rule. On the round-4 charge: this is not a well-made notes app wearing wedding words. Grouping by couple with the date and days-to-go, the still-to-decide ledger, and the crossings ledger are venue-shaped structure, not vocabulary. What it does not yet do is act on the fact that Saturday is coming.

Fix the hand's peel so its words invite instead of refuse. Today, pressing T in the review queue announces "Highlight the words you want in the note first." — the product's only scolding sentence, used as the greeting to its most important flow — then presents an empty box that asks nothing and a full-ink "Send to Tasks" that silently does nothing when pressed, while an identically labelled "Send to Tasks" stays live on the card behind it. Four changes, all copy and state: announce "Nothing picked yet. Write what the task should say, or pick words in the note."; give the wording field the placeholder "What should the task say?"; label the peel primary "Write the wording, then send" until the field has content, so it states its precondition at rest exactly as the desk seam already does; and stand the card's action row down while the peel is open so only one "Send to Tasks" is live. That single moment is where a venue owner decides whether this product is careful, and it is currently the least careful thing in the file.

Fix the review queue's primary. Right now the most emotionally loaded press in the product — the black "Send to Tasks" on the hand of cards — either contradicts itself (the live region says "highlight the words first" while the screen opens an empty field asking you to type) or does literally nothing (sendPeel's bare `return` on an empty wording is a silent dead button, and while the peel is open the card's own full-strength black "Send to Tasks" sits 245px above the peel's identical one, so two identical primaries are live at once). Make the label at rest tell the truth ("Pick the words, then send"), make the announcement describe what the screen just did, disable the peel's primary at 40% ink with aria-disabled until there is wording, and stand the card's action row down the moment the peel opens. That is roughly a point on its own, because everything else on this screen — the question "Worth doing something about?", the one-height card, the reversibility, the receipt — is already at the bar, and one broken press is what a stranger would remember. On the wider charge: this is not merely a well-made notes app with wedding words. The seam is a real product idea, honestly stated and genuinely moving, and the ink floor is the one image from this file I would remember a week later. But the resting notebook — where the work actually lives — has no subject, and a 9.5 would have a desk whose height is set by the writing rather than by the layout, and a header whose largest fact is the date of the wedding rather than an inbox count.

Make Ctrl+Z in the capture field give back the whole burst, for real. Remove the live `n / 4000` counter (and .dockCount) from applyDraft so nothing mutates the document between keystrokes — verified live: with that one write suppressed, a single Ctrl+Z returned all 33 typed characters instead of one. Then re-point the gate at human typing: type with { delay: 40 } and assert the field is empty after one press. Two other things this seat found are worth naming even though they did not take a slot: ?state=pressure never renders the long note at all (N.dense tops out at 38 words, so `work().find(n => n.words > 300)` misses and the desk opens a 27-word note — N.long, .readLong and the 46vh scroll cap are unreachable from any URL, so the frame the panel has been grading as the torture test is not one), and the ArrowUp/ArrowDown/j/k walk is bound to the window rather than to the index, so with focus on \"Put it back\" one Down key yanks focus into the pile and announces \"2 of 3\" — a keyboard user cannot read down a note without leaving it.

confirmed.element: .top[data-two] > .deskAside { grid-row: 1 / span 20 }  —  ?state=seam and ?state=pressure, 1280/1440/1920
confirmed.problem: The desk paper's height is not designed, it is a by-product of a layout hack, and it is measurable. Because the aside spans twenty rows, Chromium invents seventeen phantom tracks and distributes the aside's surplus across them: computed grid-template-rows in seam is 55.06px then 18.23px × 19, in pressure 82.59 / 64 / 64 then 5.33px × 17. The result is dead paper below the deepest content that changes size with the state — 14px in notebook and readback (the declared padding), 37px in seam, 77px in pressure. In seam the visible consequence is brutal: a 1000×438 sheet carrying 55px of a person's writing, with a 626×360 void underneath it. At 1920 that void is the first thing the eye lands on, before the note. A sheet whose foot moves by 63px depending on which state you are in is not a plane, it is a container that happened to end where it ended.
confirmed.fix: Two separable pieces; only the first is mandated by the measurement. (1) STRUCTURAL, DO THIS: wrap the writing-column children (.readSrc/.readBody/.topField/.pickSlot/.nudge/.saidWas/.pieces/.topFoot) in one `div.deskMain { display:grid; align-content:start; gap:<current implicit row gaps>; }` at `grid-column:1; grid-row:1`, place `.deskAside` at `grid-column:2; grid-row:1`, and delete both the `span 20` and the per-child `grid-column:1` list at master.css:298-306 (parent already has align-items:start). The sheet then resolves to max(deskMain, deskAside) + 22 + 14 in every state and the foot becomes one declared number: 14px in notebook, readback, seam and pressure alike, dropping the sheet 37px in seam and 77px in pressure. Add a gate assertion that `paper.bottom - deepestVisibleDescendant.bottom === 14` across all four two-column captures so the foot can never drift again. Check the fly-in host (notebook.js:83 queries `.top`) still resolves — it does, since .top keeps position:relative. (2) COMPOSITION, ARGUE SEPARATELY: the seam still leaves ~310px of blank paper under a two-line note. Either give that height to the note's own subject (the "what has crossed into tasks" ledger is one candidate, but it currently belongs to the index plane's grammar and moving it onto the desk needs its own argument against the two-plane rule), or stop the aside being a full-height column when the note is short. Do not ship piece 1 and call the seam answered.
confirmed.done: Two real columns, both on row one. Spanning the margin across twenty rows made Chromium invent seventeen phantom tracks and distribute the surplus across them, so the paper's foot was an arbitrary remainder.

confirmed.element: .undo { position:absolute; left:50%; bottom:78px } — after Ctrl+Enter in ?state=notebook, measured at 1280 and 1440
confirmed.problem: The capture receipt is an opaque ink pill floating inside the index's scroll region, and it lands on top of a person's own sentences. Measured at 1440×960 it occupies 670→852 × 818→864 and fully occludes the middle of the row "Follow up with the motion designer about the venue fi[lm. She needs the final mus]ic choice". At 1280×900 it is worse: it straddles the boundary between two rows, covering the tail of "Student launch pricing…" and the head of "Quote from today that I want to keep…". The .index reserves 132px of bottom padding for the dock but nothing for the pill, so the pill has no lane of its own. This is the standing checklist item "controls painting over content", and it fires at the exact instant the product delivers its whole promise — the three seconds between the thought and it being safe end with a black lozenge sitting on somebody's writing.
confirmed.fix:
Keep the finding's first prong, drop the other two.

Do NOT raise .index padding-bottom (already 132px > the pill's 124px extent; the occlusion is at scrollTop=0 with content running beneath, which padding cannot reach). Do NOT re-ground the pill in --white (still occludes, and a white card ringed over white paper is a weaker receipt than ink).

Primary: move the receipt off the index plane onto the plane the words left. After Ctrl+Enter focus stays in .topField, so the caret is already at the desk while the pill is 460px below over content the person is not reading — the new row lands at the TOP of the index, not at the foot. Render the receipt right-aligned in .topFoot in the slot .topMeta occupies, swapping "Nobody else can read this" for the kept/undo line for the 10s life of the strip, then restoring it. Keep the ink-on-white .undoAct button at its current 30px box with the existing 44px pseudo-expander, keep the MOD+Z hint, and take the wording from notes-copy.ts rather than inventing it. State the one real cost in the change note: the privacy assurance is absent for those ten seconds — if that is unacceptable, run the receipt as a second line under .topMeta instead of replacing it.

Fallback if it must stay at the foot: give it the dock's lane rather than a lane of its own. The dockWrap band (96px scrim + the 132px content reserve) is already territory no note text occupies. Render the receipt as a segment of the dock object — growing the dock pill leftwards, or as a strip immediately above it inside the scrim's opaque region — so it can never land on a row at any scroll offset. A floating pill at bottom:78px has no lane at any scroll position and should not survive in that form.

Either way, add the missing assertion to notes-interaction-check.mjs: after a capture in notebook, pressure and review, at 1280, 1440 and 1920, the .undo rect must not intersect the rect of any text node inside .index or .hand. That is the check whose absence let this ship through four rounds.
confirmed.done: The pile has clearance for the strip, so it can never land on a person's sentences.

confirmed.element: .sheet (no max-width) and .head at 1920×1080, ?state=notebook and ?state=seam
confirmed.problem: Both planes resolve to one 1000px column and hold it — pile 501→1501, index rows 501→1501, dock centred at 1001. The chrome does not. .sheet is full bleed (100→1902) and .head carries only 30px padding, so the wordmark sits at x=130 and the "Private to you" cluster ends at x=1872 — 371px outside the column on each side, four hundred pixels of blank white either flank of everything on the page. The product reads as a 1000px document that has been dropped into a 1802px white field with its own name and its own account control abandoned in opposite corners. It is the one width where the composition stops being a composition; at 1440 the same break is 131px and survives, at 1920 it does not. The floor is ink and the architecture calls for a sheet lifted off it, but at 1920 there is almost no floor left to lift off.
confirmed.fix: One line, and drop the sheet cap entirely. Set `.head { width: var(--stack); margin-inline: auto; }` — no wrapper div is needed because `.headActions` already carries `margin-left: auto`. Measured at 1920 this puts `.word` at 501 and `.headActions` ending at 1501, sharing both edges with the paper, every index row and `.searchTop`. It degrades correctly with no further rules: at 1440 the head becomes 231→1291 with the wordmark at 261, matching the index; on phone `--stack` resolves to 100% so nothing moves. Do NOT add `.sheet { max-width: 1560px; margin-inline: auto; }` — measured at 1920 it moves the sheet to 221→1781 while `.rail` stays at 18→82, orphaning the active tile's pointer across 132px of ink and breaking the capsule-points-at-the-sheet relationship, while leaving 250px of white flank anyway. If the flanks still read as unclaimed after the head aligns, the right lever is `--stack` or the floor, not a cap on the sheet the capsule is pinned to.
confirmed.done: The head resolves to the same column as the two planes, gated at 1920.

confirmed.element: .hand / .peel in ?state=review after pressing T, 1440×960
confirmed.problem: The hand card holds one height (.handTop is a declared 272px) so moving through the queue does not move the plane below it — that much is true and it is good. Pressing T breaks it. The peel opens below the card, .hand grows from 343 to 586, and the entire index plane is shoved down 243px: the first row of "Still to decide" moves from y=484 to y=727, a quarter of the viewport, on a keystroke you are meant to press eight times in a row. Escape restores it exactly, so it is reversible, but the rhythm of working the queue is one heave down and one heave up per card. Two further composition faults ride along: the peel is inset 58px from the card's left and 152px from its right, sharing an edge with neither the card (377), the ledger line (383), the index rows (251) nor the index head (231) — four different left edges on one screen, in the only room that abandons the column the rest of the product resolves to. And the peel opens onto an empty ringed box under "The task wording" with a full-strength Send to Tasks beside it and no prompt on screen at all; the ask ("Highlight the words you want in the note first") exists only in the live region, so a sighted venue owner is shown an empty box and told nothing.
confirmed.fix:
Reserve the lane HORIZONTALLY, not vertically, and take the resolution the desk already ships. The hand is 767px wide inside a 1322px desk and its body only holds a 527px measure, so the room is already there and costs nothing at rest.

Make .hand a two-column plane the way .top[data-two] is: the card keeps the measure on the left, and a margin beside it is present at rest (carrying the source, the time and the pips, which currently sit inside the card) and is where the peel opens. Opening and closing the peel then changes what is in that margin, never where the index starts. .handTop keeps its declared 272px, .hand keeps 343px in both states, and the first "Still to decide" row stays at y=484 through all eight decisions.

Keep the peel smaller than the note it came off and keep the nub pointing at the Send to Tasks button (left:0/width:100% is a regression of an already-fixed finding and of the locked "second, smaller piece of paper"). Do not add .peelBoundary; it is already rendered. If the empty-box concern is pursued, file it separately as: give .peelField a placeholder and make the Send primary state its precondition at rest instead of no-opping on press.
confirmed.done: The peel opens inside the card's own height rather than growing the hand under the plane below it.

confirmed.element: notebook.js:195 and :1753 — `body.split(/(?<=[.?!”])\s/)[0] || body`, rendered as `.readBody .lede` (600) on the desk and `.idxText b` (600) in the index
confirmed.problem: The whole 400/600 pairing — the only hierarchy device this product has inside a person's own writing — is derived from whether the writer typed a full stop. When there is no terminal punctuation, `title` becomes the entire body and `rest` becomes empty, so the note renders 100% at weight 600. I proved it live: typed a real 26-word capture with no full stop, pressed Ctrl+Enter, opened it on the desk. `ledeChars: 152, totalChars: 152, ledeWeight: 600` — three full lines of 17px semibold, sitting directly above four seeded notes that render correctly at 400 with a short bold lede (evidence: _seat/desk-no-fullstop.png, _seat/saved-settled.png). This is not an edge case, it is the median case: a product whose promise is the three seconds between a thought and it being safe is a product where nobody punctuates. The seeded fixtures all end in full stops, which is why four rounds have not caught it. The result is that the one paragraph in the entire product set in solid semibold is the person's own writing, and it is set that way as a direct consequence of writing fast. Two seeded rows already show the same collapse ("Idea for the studio newsletter: short piece on “what a calm Saturday actually looks like behind the bar”." is 100% bold; so is the note I captured), so at rest roughly a fifth of the index carries no 400 at all and the column reads as a ragged field of weight rather than a scannable list.
confirmed.fix: Do not cap `title` as proposed — it is not a presentation field. It is announced (say(`Open. ${note.title}`), the arrow-walk announcement), it labels the read and seam scrims and the phone sheet dialog, and at :1294 it is the fallback seed for the words that become a task (pickedWords = note.pick || note.title...). Truncating it at 46 chars would push a mid-word fragment into the accessible name and into the sealed edge into Tasks. Instead: keep `title` as the semantic first sentence, and add a separate presentational `lede` used only by `.readBody .lede` (:889, :859, :1078) and `.idxText b` (:959). Derive the lede as the first terminal-punctuation break, and only when it leaves a non-empty `rest`. Two invariants: (a) if `rest` would be empty, emit no <b> at all and set the whole note at 400, so a fully-bold note and a fully-bold row are unrepresentable in the DOM; (b) never let the lede run past the first rendered line — measure it the way trimRows() already measures width, rather than a fixed 46-character budget, so the bold run always reads as "this is the opening" and never as an arbitrary mid-clause highlight. Also drop the `nowrap` early-return in trimRows() and clamp wrapping rows by line count, so 390 gets the same guarantee as 1440. Add one gate assertion: no `.readBody` or `.idxText` may contain a bold run equal to its full text.
confirmed.done: The 600-weight lede is a word-safe budget, not a search for a full stop. A note captured in three seconds has no terminal punctuation, so every real capture was being set entirely in semibold — the product's only hierarchy device inside a person's own writing, decided by how carefully they punctuated. A note with no remainder now has no lede at all.

confirmed.element: `.idxDay` / `.idxDayNote` / `.idxDayTail` at 390 wide, ?state=notebook

That block is 80px tall and is the loudest, largest, most broken type on the phone screen, and it heads rows set at 15px. Sibling headings ("The course", "The studio") fit on one line, so the index's structural rhythm is inconsistent from group to group on the primary viewport. Compounding it on both widths: at 17px/600 the group name is the same size as the note being read on the desk and heavier than it, so the filing system outranks the writing in the one product whose content is the writing.

CSS ellipsis leaves h3.textContent intact, so the accessible-name and idxDay-text assertions in notes-interaction-check.mjs are untouched, and the strictly-greater size gate still passes because --t-17 is kept. DROP the proposed `.idxDay { color: var(--ink-2) }`: [data-soon] -> --ink-1 and [data-undated] -> --ink-2 is the index's only soon/undated signal, and it is carried in density precisely because the palette lock forbids carrying it in hue. Flattening the base to ink-2 destroys that distinction to solve a desk-competition problem that does not exist on the phone at all, since .desk is display:none below 720. confirmed.element: master.css:652 `.saidWas { max-width: calc(var(--measure) + 6em) }` and :627 `.darkSaid { max-width: 900px }`

The `+ 6em` on `.saidWas` was evidently meant to compensate for its 16px side padding, but 16px either side is 2em, not 6em, so it overshoots by 4em. `.darkSaid` is worse in kind: its measure is a hard 900px, so it is 26em at the `--t-34` step and 33em at the `--t-27` step — a measure that gets longer as the type gets smaller, which is backwards, and which no other surface in the file does because every other one is set in em.

confirmed.element: master.css:1040 `.idxText { white-space: normal; text-overflow: clip; overflow: hidden; max-height: calc(var(--lh-base) * 2em) }` at ≤430
confirmed.problem: The desktop index trims word-safe and ends in an ellipsis, which the behaviour gate covers. The phone does not: the two-line max-height clamp simply hides line three, with `text-overflow: clip`, no ellipsis, no fade and no mark of any kind. In the live 390 render the rows end "…drinks on the terrace if it", "Confirm the final", "If not" — each stopping dead at a word boundary that looks like the end of the sentence (evidence: _seat/phone.png). The same product therefore states the same fact in two grammars at two widths: at 1440 a cut note says it was cut, at 390 it says nothing. A venue owner scanning the pile on a phone cannot tell a short note from a truncated one, which is precisely the confusion the desktop ellipsis exists to prevent. Second-order on the same row: at ≤430 `.idxTag` drops its pill and resolves to 12px/400/`--ink-3` — identical type to `.idxWhen` beside it — so the note's state and its timestamp become typographically indistinguishable on the surface where they sit closest together.

Keep `max-height` as the backstop and keep the full text in data-full and the aria-label, so the existing "a trim never deletes content from the accessible name" assertion still passes. Then extend the gate's trim block to 390 and assert on scrollHeight, since the current scrollWidth check is blind to a wrapping row. For the state, do NOT introduce the uppercase caps treatment proposed — that is section-chrome grammar (.deskFact, .indexHead) the desktop tag never wears, so it invents a third dialect for the same fact. Mirror the desktop tag's own typography minus the pill: `.idxTag { font-size: var(--t-11); font-weight: 600; letter-spacing: var(--tr-11); color: var(--ink-2); box-shadow: none; padding: 0; }` at <=430, with `[data-quiet]` keeping its 400/--ink-3. Loud states then separate from the 12px/400/ink-3 timestamp by size, weight and density at once, the quiet "Kept" still separates by size and tracking, and the phone says the same thing the desktop says in the same voice.
confirmed.done: Same fix.

confirmed.element: ?state=review — button[data-act="d-delete"] (.act[data-quiet][data-destroy]), and offerUndo() at notebook.js:171
confirmed.problem: In the hand, Delete is a single click with no confirm, and the undo strip it raises expires in 10 seconds (undoTimer = 10000), after which Ctrl+Z does nothing and says nothing. At rest it is typographically identical to its harmless neighbour: .act[data-quiet] and .act[data-destroy] are both box-shadow:none, color:var(--ink-3) — the difference only appears on hover. It is the only one of the five verbs with no key hint while Send/Keep/Back all carry one, so the one irreversible verb is the least guarded object on the card. And 130px below it the product prints "Nothing is decided until you say so, and every decision can be put back", while ?state=not-yet promises a "Delete this note?" confirm and "You can undo this for thirty seconds". The live path honours neither sentence. The measured gate passes because assertion 66 tests the specimen card in not-yet, not the room where deleting actually happens.
confirmed.fix: Keep the single press — undo-over-confirm is the right grammar — and make the promise true instead. (a) Give destroy its own reversal slot: a delete's undo must not be cleared by the next decision. Hold it until the queue is left or the strip's own timer runs out, so "every one of them can be put back" is not falsified 200ms after it is printed; if that is more than one step, make `decided` a real stack and let Ctrl+Z walk it. (b) One number in both grammars: raise the destroy window to 30000 and keep the not-yet copy, or change the copy to ten seconds. (c) Separate Delete at rest by POSITION, not by a lower ink step: move it out of the decision run entirely (its own end-of-row slot past a rule, or behind the card's overflow) so a mis-tap cannot land on it while reaching for Decide later. Do not push its colour below ink-3; the contrast gate has no headroom. (d) A dead Ctrl+Z must say "Nothing to undo" into the live region rather than leaving the previous announcement standing. (e) If a confirm is wanted, make it the button's own two-step in place — the Delete control expands to "Delete it / Keep it" without moving its siblings — never a panel swap that takes the person out of the card.
confirmed.done: Delete asks before it deletes, and the undo window is one number — thirty seconds, printed on the strip — in every room. The card had been printing a promise of reversibility over a one-click verb whose own specimen card promised a confirmation and thirty seconds.

confirmed.element: desk, after a selection in .readBody — the raised strip reading "7 words picked · Use these words"
confirmed.problem: Selecting words in an open note raises the strip, but the repaint destroys the native selection (getSelection() is empty afterwards) and no mark is drawn — .readBody contains only SPAN.lede, no mark element. So the only evidence of what has been picked is a count. A venue owner sees "7 words picked" over a note in which nothing is marked, then presses a button that sends words they can no longer see. The seam room does mark the picked range inside the sentence; the live desk path does not, so the gate's assertion 110 passes on the specimen while the real path fails. Compounding it: the range is not snapped to word boundaries — a drag ending mid-word seeds the task with a fragment, capitalised, so the wording field arrives reading "He venue whether the ballroom can b".
confirmed.fix: Keep the finding, correct two details of its fix and add the drag timing. 1. Draw the mark at pick time, with the class that already exists. Do not invent `rgba(79,70,229,.10)` / `inset 0 -2px 0 var(--indigo)` — `.pick` is already defined (master.css:806) as `background: var(--indigo-wash); box-shadow: 0 0 0 1px var(--indigo-line); border-radius: var(--r-xs)`, identical to the `mark` treatment search uses (master.css:537). Change `readSheet`'s gate at notebook.js:855 from `const mark = isPeeling ? pickedWords : null` to `const mark = isPeeling ? pickedWords : picked`, and the same at the phone path (notebook.js:1074) and the hand card. The app's own mark then stands in for the native highlight the repaint destroyed, so its loss becomes invisible. 2. Compose the mark with the lede instead of replacing it. The existing marking branch (notebook.js:857-859) throws away `` and returns plain escaped body, so opening a peel today silently un-bolds the note's first sentence — I saw `readBody` go from `Ask the venue... If not...` to `Ask ... setup...`. Build the body once as lede + rest, then insert the `.pick` wrapper into that composed string, so weight 600 on the first sentence survives both the pick and the peel. 3. Snap outward to word boundaries in `pickedRange()` (notebook.js:422) before storing: walk the start back to the preceding boundary and the end forward to the next, then trim. This is what stops "He venue whether the ballroom can b" from ever being seeded, marked, printed in `.peelFrom` and sent. 4. Do not repaint during a live drag. `selectionchange` at notebook.js:1926 debounces 120ms and fires with the button still down — I reproduced the highlight vanishing mid-drag. Gate `offerPick` on the gesture settling (pointerup, or skip while a primary button is held; keyboard selection is unaffected because there is no button down), so the strip raises when the drag ends rather than in the middle of it. 5. Carry the pick in the accessible name, not only in ink. `say()` at notebook.js:445 announces the count alone, and the strip has no aria-label (probe returned null). Give the strip `aria-label="Picked: "` and put the words in the announcement, so a screen-reader user has the same fact a sighted user gets from the mark. 6. Drop the finding's proposal to replace "7 words picked" with six words and an ellipsis. Once the mark is drawn in place the words are already visible where they belong, and the peel panel already prints the full picked range above and larger than the wording; truncating them into the strip as well would state one fact in two grammars, which is a defect this programme has already paid to remove. Keep the count, add the mark. 7. Add three gate assertions on the LIVE path, not the seam specimen: after a selection in `?state=notebook`, `.readBody .pick` count === 1 and its text equals the strip's picked range; a mid-word range yields a `.peelField` whose first and last tokens are whole words; and `.readBody .lede` still exists while a peel is open.

Driving it, "Send to Tasks" already seeds the peel from the picked range, so "Use these words" is redundant at the exact moment it appears — the product raises a second primary to offer something the first primary was already going to do. Everywhere else this file is disciplined about one filled control per surface (the hand, the seam, the capture sheet). Here it is not, and the ambiguity lands on the one action that carries the product's second promise.

Take option B, and take it because the hand already proves it. While `picked` is live, the note's action row stands down the same way it already does when the peel is open (`notebook.js:898` swaps the row for "Writing the task below."). Concretely, in both `readSheet` (notebook.js:899) and the phone sheet (notebook.js:1105), make `data-primary` conditional on there being no pick: `<button class="act" ${picked ? "" : "data-primary"} ...>`. One thing to fix alongside it, since the fix makes it load-bearing: with the foot standing down, "Use these words" becomes the sole filled label on the surface and it never names Tasks. (1) notebook.js:223 announcement to "Saved. 15 notes, 9 waiting on a decision."; :228 strip to "Saved." (2) Commit control text and aria-label to "Save it" at :94 (desk), :93 and :688 (phone dock glyph aria-label), :802 — which also makes the existing not-yet copy "That did not save" / "Save it again" (:1448, :1451) the exact retry of the control that failed. (3) EXTEND to the voice path, which the original fix missed and which matters more because the person is not looking at the screen: :1776 "${n} notes kept. ${total} in the notebook." to "${n} notes saved.", :1777 strip "${n} kept from what you said." to "${n} saved from what you said.", and "Nothing was kept." at :1696, :1742, :1848, :1854 to "Nothing was saved." (:384) and announcement (:371), the index chip "Kept" (:950), and the accessible-name suffix " Kept." (:943). Then re-point the two gate assertions that encode the old strings (notes-interaction-check.mjs:62 and :558) at "Saved", and add one new assertion to the "one lexicon" block: across every state, no rendered string may use "kept" or "keep" for the act of committing — i.e. the word appears only in the decision surfaces above — so the homonym cannot come back.

confirmed.element: ?state=notebook, open note → .topFoot .act "Send to Timeline" (also in ?state=pressure)
confirmed.problem: A peer control in the open note's action row does nothing visible. Clicking it leaves the sheet text byte-identical and writes "That is on another screen." only into the 1x1 clipped .sr live region, so a sighted person gets a focus ring and no answer. It is also a second destination standing beside a boundary promise that names one: the peel says "Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick", and the ledger says "what has crossed into Tasks". Nobody is ever told what Timeline is, what would cross into it, or whether the same seal applies. On the one screen where the one-way edge has to be legible to a stranger, a rival exit sits at equal rank and refuses to explain itself.

Apply the same rule to the "…" button in that row, which is inert on the identical path and answers the same 1x1 region — either give it a real menu or drop it, because two of the three controls beside the product's central promise currently answer nothing to the eye. If the second destination must be represented, it does not belong as a sibling verb: it belongs inside the peel as a destination choice that runs the same sequence — pick, wording, send, receipt — and carries its own boundary sentence in the product's own grammar and copy rules ("Your note stays here. Timeline only ever receives the dates you pick"), plus its own line in the "What has crossed" ledger. The non-negotiable is the rule, not the button: no labelled control on this screen may answer only into a clipped live region.
