confirmed.element: .top[data-two] { grid-template-columns: minmax(0,1fr) 296px } — master.css, every desk state from 721px to about 1024px
confirmed.problem: The locked rule is that the writing keeps the measure and the facts sit in a margin beside it. Measured, the margin wins across the whole tablet band: writing column 203px vs margin 296px at 721 (about 24 characters per line), 250 vs 296 at 768, 342 vs 296 at 860, and it does not reach the 527px measure until 1100. 721px sits one pixel above the phone breakpoint, so the worst case is adjacent to the breakpoint rather than in a corner. At 1440 the column is fixed at 527 inside a 626px grid track, leaving a 99px dead gutter between the sentence and the margin rule, and in ?state=pressure 105px of empty paper sits under the action row because the aside spans rows 1/20 and sets the paper's height while the writing column ends early.
confirmed.fix:
Keep part one of the proposal, drop part two, replace part three.

KEEP. `@media (max-width: 1099px) { .top[data-two] { display: block } .top[data-two] > .deskAside { margin-top: 18px; padding-left: 0; box-shadow: none; border-top: 1px solid var(--line-soft); padding-top: 14px } }`. Applied and shot at 768: the sentence recovers the full 527px measure, the facts read as a quiet block under it, the action row returns to one line. Clear improvement, no sideways scroll.

DROP. `grid-template-columns: minmax(0, var(--measure)) 296px` with `justify-content: space-between`, and `.topFoot { grid-column: 1 / -1 }`. Applied verbatim at 1440 this is a regression on three counts I measured: the writing column falls from 527px to 496px, because --measure is 31em resolved against .top's 16px root rather than .readBody's own 17px, so the cap lands below the measure it is meant to protect; the action row spreads across the full 952px and strands "Put it back" in the far corner under the margin; and the paper grows from 337px to 398px, so the void the fix was meant to close roughly doubles.

REPLACE the height half with one line: `.top[data-two] { grid-auto-rows: min-content }`. Measured: pressure at 1440 goes 337.4 → 260 (paper now ends 14px under the taller column, which is the padding), seam goes 437.5 → 401, .readBody stays 527, nothing else moves. That kills the phantom rows at the source instead of re-laying the action row.

For the 99px gutter above 1100, do it by moving the slack outward rather than capping track one: leave `minmax(0, 1fr) 296px` and let the writing keep the wider track, or set the cap on .readBody/.topField in the element's own em so 527 is actually 527. Do not cap the track from .top.

If the collapse ships, notes-interaction-check.mjs:1101-1113 needs a width assertion added — that the writing column is never narrower than the margin beside it, checked at 721, 768, 860 and 1100 — otherwise the gate keeps passing on the state this finding is about.
confirmed.done: Below 1080 the margin folds under the writing instead of beside it, and the gate measures the two columns at five widths and fails wherever the facts outmeasure the words they annotate.

confirmed.element: ?state=notebook at 390 — .idxDay (three flex children, no narrow rule) and .idxText { text-overflow: clip; max-height: calc(var(--lh-base) * 2em) }
confirmed.problem: On the device this product exists for, the group heading is a three-line 76px ragged block: "Mara & Finn" wraps, "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" wraps, "1 still to decide" wraps, all at baseline-aligned mixed sizes. It is in the shipped 390 frame. Below it the row clamp deletes content silently — measured scrollHeight 87 against clientHeight 44, with text-overflow: clip, so the sentence simply stops with no ellipsis and no signal that there is more. trimRows() skips these rows deliberately (`if whiteSpace !== "nowrap" continue`), so the word-safe trim and the backstop ellipsis the desktop was given never run on the phone. The full text survives in the accessible name, which means a looker gets less than a listener.
confirmed.fix: Heading, in the ≤720 block: keep the subject at var(--t-17)/600 (the rank step is gated and was won in an earlier round) and give it the whole first line. `.idxDay { display: grid; grid-template-columns: minmax(0,1fr) auto; row-gap: 2px; padding: 16px 0 6px; align-items: baseline }`; the subject text takes `grid-column: 1 / -1; white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis`; `.idxDayNote { grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: var(--t-12); white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis }`; `.idxDayTail { grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; margin-left: 0; font-size: var(--t-12); white-space: nowrap }`. Every group then heads at one height (~66px) with the person's own words leading and the facts about the group on a quiet second line, instead of one 76px ragged block and four 52px ones. Rows: have render always emit the words inside `<span class="idxClamp">` within .idxText, with `.idxClamp { display: contents }` at desktop so the existing nowrap + ellipsis + scrollWidth measurement is untouched, and in the ≤720 block `.idxText { max-height: none; overflow: visible }` plus `.idxClamp { display: -webkit-box; -webkit-box-orient: vertical; -webkit-line-clamp: 2; overflow: hidden }` — measured to hold 43.5px and print the browser's own trailing ellipsis. Point trimRows at .idxClamp for its innerHTML writes (still measuring scrollWidth on .idxText) so the wrapper survives a trim, keep its nowrap skip so the phone stays CSS-clamped, and leave data-full and the aria-label untouched.
confirmed.done: The group rule is at most two lines on a phone, and a clamped row says it is clamped rather than silently hiding its third line.

refuted.problem: The two planes share a container edge and not a word edge. The paper and the index rows both run 261→1261 exactly, and the CSS comment is proud of it. But the thing a reader actually tracks down the page is the left edge of their own sentences, and that edge breaks: the note on the desk starts at 285 (paper 261 + 24 padding), every note in the index starts at 294 (row 261 + 20 mark + 13 gap). Nine pixels. It is not a rhythm and it is not a hang — it is a near-miss, which reads worse than a deliberate 30px indent because the eye registers the wobble without being able to name it. Worse, the offset is not even constant: it is 9px in locked and studio, 7px in quiet and press, so the product's most repeated alignment is a different wrong number depending on the room. Every time a note is lifted out of the index onto the desk, the words it is made of slide sideways by 9px — on the one transition the architecture is named after.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on three independent grounds, all measured live at 1440x960 in all four rooms.

1. The premise "285 is the single writing edge" is already false on the desk, in the states the finding itself cites. Measured ink lefts on the desk: .topField 285, .readBody 285, .emptyBody 285 — but ?state=readback puts .saidWas's BOX at 285 and its actual words at 301 (14/16px wash padding), and .piece's words at 303; ?state=not-yet puts .state p at 309; ?state=review puts .handBody at 403. The finding lists .saidWas "at x=285" as evidence of a writing edge, but 285 is that object's border, not its writing. The desk's real convention is not one writing edge — it is a nested-box convention where every inset object pays its own padding out of the measure. The index row is exactly that: an object with furniture (a 20px source glyph) whose text is inset by it. The proposed gate ("computed left of the desk's writing element equals computed left of .idxText to the pixel across all ten states") cannot even be written unambiguously, because in readback and not-yet there is no single "the desk's writing element" — it is 285 and 301 and 303 in the same frame.

2. The fix, applied literally, breaks the index grid. I injected the proposed CSS and measured. `.idxMark{position:absolute}` removes the mark from grid flow, so auto-placement shifts every remaining child one column left: .idxText lands in the 20px glyph column (measured box left 261, width 20px, overflowing), .idxTag takes the 773px column, .idxWhen shifts. The row's four fixed metadata columns — which master.css:495 explicitly exists to hold ("the right-hand verticals hold down the whole index instead of stepping in and out with the length of each timestamp") — collapse. The 285 ink position it produces is an accident of overflow, not alignment. And the mark itself lands at 244→264: 7px OUTSIDE the row's own background band (row border box 251→1271), so on hover and on the [data-cursor] row the source glyph sits half outside the wash and is bisected by the inset 1px indigo ring, and hangs left of the separator rules (261→1261) as a new ragged edge. A state-carrying indicator (the .idxMark i unread dot) would live outside its own row's highlight. That is strictly worse than a 9px inset.

3. The dramatic claim is factually wrong about the behaviour. "Every time a note is lifted out of the index onto the desk, the words slide sideways by 9px — on the one transition the architecture is named after." Nothing slides. openNote() (notebook.js:531) is a full paint() repaint with no shared-element transition; the row does not travel, it stays in place carrying data-open while the desk renders the full note. The two texts are also different objects at different sizes (15px one-line word-safe trim vs 17px prose at the 31em measure). There is no continuous column of sentences spanning the planes for an edge to wobble in.

Supporting: the real architectural edge is 261, and it is held exactly — paper border 261→1261, index row content 261, every group heading 261, "YOUR NOTES" 261, every source glyph 261→281. Both writing insets hang off that one edge by their own object's furniture. And the 9 vs 7 variance is not "a different wrong number per room": quiet and press run [data-index="tight"], a density preset that drops the row's secondary span and tightens column-gap 13→11. It is one system variable moving, not a stray value.

What is left is taste stated as a defect: a 9px difference between two texts on two depth-separated planes, at two sizes, never adjacent, both consistently inset from a shared 261 edge. Refuted.

refuted.problem: On the surface carrying the product's second promise — only the exact words a person picks ever cross — the words they picked and the machine's derived wording compute identically in every typographic axis. Measured in the live file: picked = `17px / 600 / 27.54px / -0.357px / rgb(17,17,17)`; derived = `17px / 600 / 27.54px / -0.357px / rgb(17,17,17)`; `identical: true`. The CSS comment above the rule states "They lead" and the round-5 brief states the picked words are printed "ABOVE and LARGER". They are above; they are not larger, not heavier, not longer-tracked, not any different at all. The only differentiation is an indigo wash box — and the box works against it: the picked words are boxed to a 240px column while the derived wording runs free at 266px, so the derived wording is the wider, more open, more display-like of the two. A reader glancing at the seam cannot tell by type which half is theirs, which is exactly the thing this screen exists to make obvious.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on four counts, three of them factual.

(1) "Not heavier" is false. Driven live at ?state=seam, `.readBody` — the note the words were picked FROM, sitting on the same screen at x=285 — computes `17px / 400 / 27.54px / -0.357px`. `.peelFrom span` computes `17px / 600`. The picked words are one full weight step above the note they came from. Every other surface carrying a person's own words is also 400 (`.topField` 17/400, `.pieceField` 17/400, `.handBody` 17/400). The picked words are the heaviest rendering of that sentence anywhere in the product. They only tie `.peelField` because `.peelField` is itself deliberately promoted to 600 as a task title — the single exception in the family.

(2) "Not any different at all" is false. `.peelFrom` carries `background: var(--indigo-wash)` = `rgba(79,70,229,0.08)` plus `inset 0 0 0 1px var(--indigo-line)`, and the `.pick` mark left in place on the range inside the note computes the identical `rgba(79,70,229,0.08)`. That fill is not decoration; it is the only thing on the screen tying the marked range in the note (left column) to the quote in the margin 690px away. It is also the only filled object in the entire peel. On top of that both halves carry explicit uppercase captions in plain English — "THE WORDS YOU PICKED" and "THE TASK WORDING". A reader is told which half is theirs, shown it in the same ink that marks it in their note, and given it first. The claim that only type could carry this is taste asserted as defect.

(3) The width argument does not survive the render. `.peelFrom` measures 266px wide — exactly the same as `.peelField`'s 266px. The 240 the finding quotes is the span inside 11px of chip padding. In the frame both blocks wrap at the same word onto the same two lines ("…guests arrive, / not when"). There is no perceptible measure difference to make the derived wording "wider, more open, more display-like"; that is 26px of inset described as a hierarchy inversion.

(4) The fix would make the work worse and reintroduce a gated defect. `.peelFrom span` holds the person's verbatim words, quoted from `.readBody` in the same viewport. Setting it to `--t-20 / --lh-base / --tr-21` renders one sentence at two sizes and two leadings simultaneously, side by side. That is precisely the fault a prior round fixed and memorialised at master.css:415 ("The same sentence was rendering at four different leadings depending on which surface it happened to be on, which is a thing a reader feels and cannot name") and which the locked round-gate states as "A person's own words are set identically on every surface". Worse, the behaviour gate at notes-interaction-check.mjs:988-999 samples `.peelField` and not `.peelFrom span`, so this would land as an ungated regression of a gated principle. Dropping `.peelField` to 400 demotes the one editable, actionable object in the peel — the wording that becomes the task and is sent — to ordinary prose weight, beneath the authority of its own label. And removing the indigo wash severs the mark-in-note ↔ quote-in-margin correspondence, which is the strongest thing this screen currently does.

(5) The relationship is already gated and already at its settled value: notes-interaction-check.mjs:1184-1192 asserts "the words a person picked are not demoted beneath the machine's version" (`picked >= wording`). Equality is the deliberate resolution of an earlier round in which the picked words were smaller and lighter, recorded in the CSS comment at :797. The finding argues the gate should be strictly greater; it offers no evidence a reader misreads the current screen, and the frame shows the opposite.

refuted.problem: On desktop the moment the thought becomes safe is a filled pill that says "Keep it" with Ctrl+Enter on it. On a phone, where this product is actually used at a venue, that same act collapses to a bare tick in a strip of eight same-sized glyphs (search, dictate, photo, tick, rule, Notes, Tasks, Timeline, avatar), with a naked number floating beside it. The aria-label says "Keep it" so assertions 96 and 97 pass, but a person mid-thought who has never used the product has to work out which of eight glyphs commits, and the number next to it is unexplained. This is the one screen where capture latency is measured in seconds of hesitation rather than milliseconds.
refuted.why:
REFUTED — the premise is factually wrong about the rendered phone dock, and the fix would break the locked phone architecture.

Measured live at 390x844 (Playwright, ?state=notebook, typed "Marquee lights need PAT certs", then tapped the tick). Every item in .dock, with computed fill:

  phoneField   17,744  356x45  color #fff
  search       17,791   36x36  bg transparent, stroke rgba(255,255,255,0.62)
  dictate      55,791   36x36  bg transparent, 0.62 white
  photo        93,791   36x36  bg transparent, 0.62 white
  dockCount   131,797   21x24  0.62 white, aria-hidden="true"
  KEEP        154,791   36x36  bg rgb(255,255,255), glyph rgb(17,17,17)
  dockRule    222,800    1x18
  Notes/Tasks/Timeline 229/265/301, 36x36, 0.62 white (Notes 0.14 wash)
  avatar      343,794   30x30  white, letters "OR"

1. "A bare tick in a strip of eight same-sized glyphs" is false, and the finding contradicts itself by stating background #ffffff in its own element line. Seven controls in that bar are 62%-alpha white strokes on #111111 ink; the keep control is a solid #ffffff disc carrying an ink glyph. It is the single highest-contrast object on the bar by a wide margin (18:1 vs a 62% stroke), it is 36px against a 30px avatar, and the only other white object sits 189px away at the far right, past a rule and three suite tiles, and carries initials rather than a glyph. The clipped dock screenshot makes this unarguable: the eye lands on the white disc first.

2. It is not a permanent member of the strip — it is an ENTRANCE. notebook.js dock(): `const live = Boolean(draft.trim())`; the keep glyph and the count are emitted only when a draft exists. The resting phone frame (locked-notebook--390x844.png) shows seven controls and no white disc. The moment the first character lands, a new white object appears immediately beside the field the thumb just typed into. A person mid-thought does not "work out which of eight glyphs commits"; one thing changed on the bar, and it changed because they started writing. That is the Things / Bear / iA Writer phone-commit pattern exactly — a filled glyph, no word — and it is at benchmark, not below it.

3. "A naked number overlapping its left edge" is wrong: the count ends at x=152, the keep disc starts at x=154. A 2px sibling gap, not an overlap.

4. The proposed fix breaks the locked architecture. "Collapse the three suite tiles behind the existing .dockRule into a single overflow while a draft is live" removes the suite from the merged capsule-and-dock during the product's central state. The locked line is that on a phone the capsule and dock are ONE ink object carrying capture, the verbs, the suite AND the account — four rounds were spent un-fragmenting exactly this (master.css:1051 comment: two stacked floating objects taking 163px of an 844px screen). It also makes the seal into Tasks vanish and reappear on the first and last keystroke of every draft, re-laying-out the foot of the phone under a moving thumb mid-capture. On a product whose claim is that nothing shifts while you write, that is a regression, not a fix.

5. It is not "a width reallocation". The verbs row ends at x=190 and the suite rule starts at x=222: 32px of slack inside a 356px inner width. A worded "Keep it" pill with its tick needs roughly 50-60px more than the 36px disc, and fails outright at 360px. That is precisely why the fix has to evict the suite — the geometry proves the trade, and the build already chose the side that keeps the locked object intact.

6. The counter half of the fix would make things worse, not better. Showing the number only past 90% means it materialises with no prior grammar at the one moment a person is under pressure; the continuous count is what makes a climb toward a ceiling legible. And .dockCount is aria-hidden="true", so a 90%-only rule gives a screen-reader user nothing at either threshold — the fix as written proposes no live region to replace it.

Post-commit behaviour was also driven and is clean: field cleared only after the note was safe, focus returned to .phoneField, status announced "Kept. Undo Ctrl+Z", the row appeared in the index, keep glyph and count both withdrew. Nothing here is the defect described.

refuted.problem: The one editable thing on the seam — the words that will actually cross into Tasks — is set at weight 600 in ink-1 with no border, no background, no rule, and no hover rule at all. Directly above it sits "THE WORDS YOU PICKED", a block of identical weight and colour that is not editable. Two blocks that look the same, one of which can be changed and one of which cannot, with nothing at rest or on hover telling them apart. It is reachable and it takes an indigo focus ring once you get there, but discovery requires guessing. The readback flow already solved this: .piece draws a 2px rule via ::before that turns indigo on :focus-within. The seam did not inherit it.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on measurement, on the analogy it rests on, and on the consequence of its fix.

1. The central factual claim is false. The finding says the picked block and the wording field are "two blocks that look the same... identical weight and colour" with "nothing at rest telling them apart." Measured live at ?state=seam, 1440x960: `.peelFrom` computes to `background: rgba(79,70,229,0.08)` with `box-shadow: rgba(79,70,229,0.32) 0 0 0 1px inset`, 8px/11px padding, indented to x=982. `.peelField` computes to `background: rgba(0,0,0,0)`, `box-shadow: none`, flush at x=971. One is a filled, ringed, indigo-tinted panel; the other is bare ink on white paper. The locked-seam frame shows this plainly — the picked words sit in a lavender card, the wording sits on the sheet. That is one of the loudest at-rest distinctions on the whole panel.

2. It also ignores the labels. Each block carries its own 11px caps ink-3 label directly above it, measured and visible in the frame: "THE WORDS YOU PICKED" (`.peelFrom b`, y=187) and "THE TASK WORDING" (`#peel-label`, y=285). The field's label is also its accessible name via `aria-labelledby="peel-label"`. "Nothing telling them apart" is contradicted twice over, and the boundary copy above ("the exact words you pick and check below") points at the field in words.

3. The `.piece` analogy is misread. The 2px rule lives on `.piece` — the readback CARD (master.css:672) — not on `.pieceField`, the textarea inside it, which is built exactly as bare as `.peelField`: `border:0; outline:0; background:none` (master.css:668). The rule exists because the readback stacks N sibling white cards on white paper at 9px gaps and each needs an edge. The seam has one card, `.peel`, and it already carries `var(--ring), var(--paper)` in its own plane. The seam did not fail to inherit anything; the analogous element is the card, and the card is treated.

4. The fix would make the work worse. `.topField` — the primary capture field, the object the entire three-second promise runs through — is constructed identically bare (master.css:361). So is `.pieceField`. So is `.searchBar input`. "Editable surfaces are paper, not boxes" is the product's idiom, and line 415 documents the companion rule that a person's own writing is set identically on every surface. Boxing only the seam field would hand the least-important field in the product the strongest editable affordance in it, while the capture field stays bare — an inconsistency a Linear or iA Writer would not ship.

5. The geometry fails too. In the two-column desk the peel column is 266px wide and `.peelBoundary`, `#peel-label`, `.peelField` and `.peelRow` are all flush at x=971; only the filled picked panel indents. A 2px rule plus 6px left pad would indent the wording alone, creating a third indent level in a 266px margin and breaking the peel's left spine — while duplicating an indent language the picked panel already owns.

The one true residual — no `:hover` on the field — is not a defect at this bar. Focus is a 2px indigo outline at 3px offset (measured), cursor is `text`, and the field carries a caret and live `field-sizing: content`. Bear, iA Writer and Linear's own issue body all present editable prose with no hover fill. Hover-as-discovery is taste stated as a defect here, and the taste points the wrong way for a product whose sheet is meant to read as paper.

refuted.problem: Five verbs in one row, three of which a first-time user cannot tell apart. "Just keep it" announces "Kept in Notes. 7 left." and "Decide later" announces "Left for later. 7 left." — identical counts, no statement of what changed, and nothing on screen says one removes the note from the queue for good while the other returns it. "Back to your notes" is a third flavour of not-now. Only two of the five carry keys, so the queue's advertised keyboard model covers less than half its own row. "Delete", the single destructive verb, sits inline at the same weight and 60px from "Decide later", fires with no confirmation, and the product's own catalogue in ?state=not-yet shows a delete confirmation sheet that this flow never uses.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Four of the five load-bearing claims are factually wrong about the file, and the structural half of the fix would make the queue worse.

(1) "Only two of the five carry keys." False. DOM dump of `.handFoot .act`: `d-task` renders `<kbd>T</kbd>`, `d-keep` renders `<kbd>K</kbd>`, and `notebook` renders `<kbd>Esc</kbd>` — three of five, and all three are wired (notebook.js:1899-1910 for t/k, :1836-1842 for Escape). "Covers less than half its own row" is arithmetically false. Delete deliberately carrying no single-letter hotkey next to K is correct design, not a gap.

(2) "Delete ... fires with no confirmation" — as a defect this is already handled by a stronger mechanism than the one proposed. Driven: clicking Delete announces "Deleted. 7 left." into the live region, raises an undo strip reading "Deleted. / Undo / Ctrl+Z", and Ctrl+Z restores the card (live region then reads "Undone. Deleted.", `.handBody` is the same note). The precondition is stated at rest, before any press, in the deck line: "Nothing is decided until you say so, and every decision can be put back."

(3) "The product's own catalogue in ?state=not-yet shows a delete confirmation sheet that this flow never uses." Misread. That tile's own body copy is "It has not been sent anywhere, so deleting it here deletes it everywhere. You can undo this for thirty seconds." The catalogue prescribes an undo model, which is exactly what the hand implements. Routing a per-card queue decision through a modal — in a flow whose whole model is one-key reversible decisions at pace — is the Gmail/Linear anti-pattern and would make it worse. (Real residue: the strip window is 10s, notebook.js:171, against the catalogue's stated thirty. That is a different, smaller finding.)

(4) "Nothing on screen says one removes the note from the queue for good while the other returns it." False after the moment. Keep sets `pending:false, reviewed:true`; later sets `pending:true`. Driven: the strips differ ("Kept in Notes." vs "Left for later."), the index row's accessible name differs ("... Kept." vs "... Still to decide."), and returning to the notebook after deferring one note shows the header chip "1 still to decide" with aria-label "1 still to decide. Go through the notes waiting on a decision."

(5) "Replace 'Back to your notes Esc' with the existing .handFoot exit only" is incoherent — that button IS the `.handFoot` exit, and the behaviour gate asserts exactly one of them (notes-interaction-check.mjs:737, `.handFoot [data-act="notebook"]` count === 1). The fix asks to replace a control with itself.

Also wrong on measurement: Delete does not sit "at the same weight" undifferentiated — it is the only icon-bearing control in the quiet group and carries `data-destroy`, which fills to solid ink on hover while every neighbour only washes. And the row is already grouped by a `<span class="spacer">` splitting the two decisions from the three non-decisions.

What is left after all that is one small copy nit: both announcements end in the same "7 left" and neither names what changed. That is a two-string edit, not the "four ways to not decide" structural charge, and it does not clear the bar for a finding at 9.5.

Separate defect noticed while driving, offered for another seat rather than as support for this one: finish the queue with one note deferred and the end state reads "Everything is decided. 8 notes went through. 0 became tasks and the rest stayed here", while the chip one click away reads "1 still to decide" — a header/body contradiction and a deferred note counted as resolved.

refuted.problem: One promise, six sentences, five of them visible within a single screen: "Private to you" (header), "Nobody else can read this" (capture foot), "Your note stays here. Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick and check below." (peel), "Your note is still here, still private, still yours to edit." (confirmation), "3 so far, and every note stayed here" (crossed eyebrow), and the announcement "Sent to Tasks. Your note stayed here." A confident product states a boundary once, exactly, where the boundary is crossed. Repeating it in six grammars reads as a product reassuring itself, which is the one register a venue owner will read as a reason to doubt. Two of the six are also invented strings that do not exist in notes-copy.ts: the shipped generic register says "Private until you send it on" and "Yours until you send something on", and the lab has substituted "Private to you" and "Nobody else can read this" — the latter lifted from the wedding register's empty state, so the venue-operator surface is now reading a couple's line.
refuted.why: REFUTED on measurement and on the source. (1) The headline count is false. I drove the file in Playwright at 1440x960 across notebook, capture, seam, review, nothing, search and pressure, walking every text node matching the promise vocabulary and recording visibility plus viewport position. Maximum co-visible is TWO in ?state=notebook (header badge "Private to you" at top 40, .topMeta "Nobody else can read this" at top 199) and THREE in ?state=seam (header badge, .peelBoundary, .cnt eyebrow at top 554). Every other state shows exactly one. Not five, not six. The finding counted across states that are never on screen together, and two of its six are a live-region announcement (aural, never co-visible with anything) and a string that lives in a different state. (2) The provenance claim, which is the finding's only hard evidence, is wrong about the product. "Private to you" IS the shipped header string: src/modules/notes/app/workspace/NotesWorkspace.tsx:909 renders plus Private to you, in the same slot, with the same lock glyph and the same sibling "Notes options" button as the lab's .head [data-act="privacy"]. The lab mirrors the shipped header exactly. It is absent from notes-copy.ts because notes-copy.ts governs the capture and hand-off flow, not the header badge. Worse for the finding: capture.privacyAssurance ("Private until you send it on") and capture.headerAssurance ("Yours until you send something on") have ZERO call sites in NotesWorkspace.tsx, so the two strings it wants "restored" are on no shipped screen at all. Applying the fix would make the lab DIVERGE from the shipped product. The "lifted from the wedding register" charge also fails: the wedding privacyAssurance is "Only the two of you can see this", which is the couple's line; "Nobody else can read this" names no couple and is not verbatim from either register. (3) Two parts of the fix make the work worse. Deleting the .topFoot assurance removes a line that only renders when the field is empty (notebook.js:101 and :803) and is replaced by the character count plus "Keep it" on the first keystroke, so it costs nothing while writing and answers the one question a first-time venue owner has before typing a private thought into a new product. Trimming the sent announcement rewrites receipts.sent, which is "Sent to Tasks. Your note stayed here." verbatim at notes-copy.ts:242, and the brief forbids rewriting shipped copy. (4) This is a restatement. docs/design/labs/notes-2026-08/log.html:670 and :1332 already refuse the same premise, citing the same NotesWorkspace header. Residue, stated for honesty and not rising to a finding: in ?state=seam the .cnt eyebrow "3 so far, and every note stayed here" does sit about 400px under .peelBoundary, so one clause is genuinely doubled there, under a heading that already reads "What has crossed into Tasks". That is a one-clause taste call, not a defect at a 9.5 bar, and the finding argued it only as the sixth item of a pile-up that does not exist.

refuted.problem: The loudest object in the resting header is a count of unfinished work, and it is the only filled shape in the header. Driven live at 390 and 1440: capturing one note moves it from "8 still to decide" to "9 still to decide". The product's entire promise is the three seconds between having a thought and it being safe; the reward it hands back for keeping a thought is a bigger guilt number, in the highest-contrast object on the page. The press room paints that same pill indigo, so the product's one accent colour is spent on the size of your backlog. Things, Bear and iA Writer all put the count of what you have, never the count of what you owe, in the resting chrome. This is the header of a queue tool, not of a place where thoughts are safe.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven live at 1440 and 390, and read in master.css/notebook.js.

What is true and worth nothing: the chip is the only filled shape in the head (109×26, ink fill, white, 12px/600 — the SMALLEST type in the head row, not the largest), and capture does move it 8 → 9 (measured at +120ms and +900ms; index pending marks move 8 → 9 with it).

Four things kill it.

(1) Factually wrong about the artifact. The claim is that the resting chrome carries "the count of what you owe, never the count of what you have." Both are on screen at rest, four inches apart: `.indexHead` reads "YOUR NOTES · 14 notes" — the count of what you have, in larger type than the chip, at the head of the plane the person actually lives in. The frame locked-notebook--1440x960.png shows both.

(2) Factually wrong about the named benchmark. Things 3's resting sidebar badges are counts of what you owe (Today, Inbox). Bear counts what you have; iA Writer counts nothing. One of the three cited actually does the opposite of what the finding says all three do, so the "queue tool, not a place where thoughts are safe" argument rests on an invented consensus.

(3) Half the fix is already shipped, in the room the finding is scored against. Computed style at rest and while typing in `v=locked`: `.top` (the capture paper) carries `rgb(79,70,229) 0 0 0 1px` — indigo IS on the capture field's live edge, and the chip in locked is ink, never indigo. The indigo chip exists only in `v=press`, which is the declared `data-indigo="forward"` knob whose stated thesis in master.css is "spends it on the primary action too, so the next move is the loudest object on the sheet" — and in press indigo also lands on `.undo` and the open row, so "the product's one accent colour is spent on the size of your backlog" is not true even there. Faulting a variant knob at its designed extreme while the locked direction already does the proposed thing is not a defect.

(4) The other half of the fix makes the work worse, twice over.
 · Demote to a quiet ink-60% text link: `[data-act="review"]` returns exactly one element on the notebook — the chip. It is the ONLY door into the hand of cards, and therefore into the product's second promise, the seam into Tasks. Making the sole entrance to the review queue the quietest thing in the head is a regression against the first-contact priority (a venue owner who has never used a task tool), and log.html:524 already records this artifact being punished for review being hard to enter and leave.
 · Suppress the count for the 10s of the undo strip: driven, the instant you keep, the new row appears in the index with the pending dot and the accessible name "…Still to decide.", AND the per-group tail (notebook.js:1008) restates "N still to decide" in the same grammar, summing to the head. Freezing the head at 8 while nine rows are marked still to decide and the group tails sum to 9 is precisely "facts stated in two grammars or contradicted between header and body" from the standing checklist, breaks the code's own invariant ("the head can never state a number the body below it disagrees with", notebook.js:138), and breaks the gated assertion "the head's count and the index agree" in notes-interaction-check.mjs:83. It reintroduces, deliberately, the exact defect a prior round paid to fix.

Also, the stated goal of the fix is already met: the immediate answer to keeping a note IS "Kept." and nothing else. The undo strip reads "Kept. / Undo / Ctrl+Z" with no count in it; the live region leads "Kept." before any number; and the reward the person actually watches is their own sentence flying into the row it became, not a 12px number moving by one.

Taste stated as a defect, built on two factual errors, with a fix that would break a gated invariant.

refuted.problem: The sheet you write on and read on is a fixed box that ignores what is on it. Opening notes from ?state=pressure: card 337px carrying 83px of words (75% empty), card 272px carrying 83px (69%), card 244px carrying 55px (77%). At ?state=seam the card is 438x1000; the person's own words occupy 527x55 at the top left — 6.6% of the sheet — while the apparatus about those words occupies 266x365 in the margin and roughly 70% of the plane is nothing at all. On the one screen whose whole subject is a person's words crossing into Tasks, their words are the smallest thing in frame. That is why this reads as a very good form rather than as paper: iA Writer and Bear make the page equal the writing, and here the page is a container the writing rattles inside.
refuted.why:
REFUTED — the finding is factually wrong about the source, and its fix is already shipped in a tighter form.

1. There is no fixed or minimum height on `.top`. Computed at 1440x960 in every state: `min-height: 0px`, and `height` resolves to exactly the content box — notebook 153.078px, capture 159.062px, pressure 337.391px, readback 408px, seam 437.516px. Five different heights across five states is the definition of "height set by its contents". The instruction "remove the fixed/min height on .top and give it height: auto" removes nothing that exists and sets a property that is already in force.

2. The desk already breathes with the writing, live. Driving the file: rest 153px / field 55px, index top 305. Type a sentence → 159 / 59, index 311. Add six lines → 324 / 224, index 476. Ctrl+Enter → back to 153 / 55, index 305. `.topField` carries `field-sizing: content; min-height: calc(var(--lh-read) * 2em); max-height: 42vh; overflow: auto` (master.css:364) — content sizing, a floor, and a cap so a 900-word note scrolls inside the desk instead of pushing the index off screen. That is the proposed fix, verbatim, already there — and at a two-line floor rather than the four the finding asks for. `min-height: calc(var(--lead-3) * 4)` would make the resting desk taller and emptier, the opposite of the complaint. `--lead-3` is also not a token in this file; the leading ladder is `--lh-tight/--lh-base/--lh-read`.

3. "Set the margin column to align-self: start and let the card's height be max(words, margin) rather than a constant" describes what the file already does twice over. `.deskAside` has `align-self: start` (master.css:308) and `.top[data-two]` has `align-items: start` (297). The seam card is 437.5px because `.deskAside` measures 365px and `.readBody` 55px — the grid row is already max(words, margin) plus padding. There is no constant to remove.

4. The residual observation — that at the seam a 55px line of words sits beside a 365px margin, leaving a tall void under column 1 — is true but is the two-column desk the panel already settled and the brief lists as worthless to restate ("everything true ABOUT a note sits in a margin beside it, and the peel opens into that margin"). Shortening that void means shortening or relocating the margin, which is the locked architecture. The finding's own fix does not touch it.

Taste stated as a defect, resting on measurements read as evidence of a fixed box when they are evidence of content sizing.

refuted.problem: Ninety-five percent of the time in this product is the resting notebook, and the resting notebook has no subject. The single most emotionally loaded fact on the screen — "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" — is a ~13px grey subtitle beside a group heading, weighted the same as "3 hours ago". The one thing promoted to the black pill in the header is "8 still to decide", which is an inbox count: a task-manager idea, borrowed. Strip the sentences out of the rows and this frame is a superb generic capture tool. The seam and the review question ("Worth doing something about?") are genuinely of this domain and rescue the product from the charge, but the state a venue owner actually lives in does not: nothing on it knows a wedding is in two days.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on measurement, on prior art, and on the fix.

FACTUALLY WRONG ABOUT THE FRAME. Driven live at 1440x960, ?state=notebook&v=locked, computed styles read off the DOM. The resting notebook's default grouping is by subject (`let group = params.get("group") || "about"`, notebook.js:60), so the first thing in the index plane is `<h3 class="idxDay" data-soon>` reading "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July, in 2 days · 1 still to decide", sticky at the head of the pile at y=305. Measured: the subject is 17px / 600 / #111 — the largest step anywhere on the sheet, equal to the "notes" wordmark and larger than the workspace name (15/400/72%). The date is NOT a "~13px grey subtitle weighted the same as '3 hours ago'": it is 13px / **600** / rgba(17,17,17,**0.72**) (master.css:480, `.idxDay[data-soon] .idxDayNote { color: var(--ink-2); font-weight: 600 }`), whereas "35 minutes ago" is 12px / **400** / 0.62 and the group's own "1 still to decide" tail is 12/400/0.62. Three distinct steps, three densities, two weights. The hierarchy the finding asks for — subject loudest, date second, count last — is exactly what is already rendered. And the subject is stated a second time on the same resting frame: the filing chip on the desk reads "Mara & Finn".

ALREADY HANDLED, AND GATED. notes-interaction-check.mjs:745-778 asserts "the pile opens on what each note is about", "and on the thing the venue is facing, not the nearest date" (subjects[0] must contain "Mara & Finn"), "a dated subject says when the venue is actually facing it" (must contain "Saturday 18 July" and /in \d+ days?/), and "every group's slot means the same thing". The source comment records this as a prior round's fix: "Shipped as an opt-in it was an answer filed in a drawer: the product still opened on the calendar of when you typed." The charge "nothing on it knows a wedding is in two days" is answered by the sentence sitting at the top of the plane in the largest type on it.

THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE. (a) Putting "Mara & Finn, Saturday 18 July" at 17/600 in the header duplicates the sticky index heading 240px below it verbatim — the same fact in two places in two grammars, which is on this programme's own standing defect list, and it displaces "The Orchard, events", the one thing a header is for. The head already carries wordmark + rule + workspace + chip + two actions at 1440; .headName ellipsises at min-width 5ch as it is. (b) Promoting `.idxDayNote` to the heading step hits every group, not the dated one: three of the five resting groups say "No date", so the change prints a 17px statement of absence three times down the pile. (c) Stripping the fill off "8 still to decide" leaves the resting screen with no filled control at all — that chip is the single route into the hand, which is locked architecture ("the review queue is a hand of cards"), not a borrowed inbox count. Demoting it to a 13px grey line makes the one action on the screen read as a label.

What survives is taste stated as a defect: a wish that the fact lived in the header rather than at the top of the pile. The fact is on screen, at the top, in the largest type, in the heavier weight, in the denser ink, and gated. Nothing here is a defect at 9.5.

refuted.problem: The whole product disappears behind an ink floor and nothing is announced: #say is empty on entry and document.activeElement is still <body>. A keyboard user has to Tab blind to find that the trap holds Cancel and Stop and read it back; a person who is not looking at the screen — the entire reason dictation exists for someone carrying chairs across a marquee — gets no confirmation that it is listening. The exit is handled well ("Nothing was kept." on Escape), which makes the silence on the way in look like an oversight rather than a choice. Separately, the legally required disclosure sits 342px below the words at the far bottom-left corner, at the smallest step and the faintest density on the darkest surface in the file: it survives verbatim, but it is placed where a design puts something it hopes is not read.
refuted.why:
Factually wrong about the behaviour, and its fix is already the shipped code. Driving the real entry path (click Dictate from ?state=notebook, 1440x960) gives #say = "Listening. Speak whenever you are ready. Stop when you are done." and document.activeElement = BUTTON[data-act="voice-stop"] "Stop and read it back" — exactly what the proposed fix asks for. The source is notebook.js:1734-1738, which calls say(...) then sets refocus to '[data-act="voice-stop"]'. The finding's measurement (#say empty, activeElement ) reproduces only on the deep-link ?state=voice URL, a lab addressing convenience for capturing frames, not a path a person can reach. Tabbing from entry walks Cancel -> Stop -> Cancel -> Stop, a closed trap; the "Tab blind to find what the trap holds" claim is false. Both halves are already in the measured baseline the brief says not to spend findings on: notes-interaction-check.mjs:272 asserts "listening is announced" and :686 asserts "focus lands inside the takeover" on voice-stop, plus :279 asserts the transcript itself is

— a live region reading the person's own arriving words back, which is the real confirmation for someone not looking at the screen. The two novel additions both make the work worse. Announcing elapsed time every fifteen seconds puts a second polite region in competition with darkSaid; the phone-in-a-pocket user's confirmation is hearing their own words, and periodic "Still listening, thirty seconds" chatter queues against and delays exactly that. The disclosure relocation misdescribes the layout: it is not isolated in the far bottom-left corner but is the left member of .darkFoot, flex-aligned bottom with Cancel and Stop (measured y=868 against Cancel at y=882, same decision band, 62ch measure over three lines) — it sits with the controls you read when deciding to stop or cancel. 12px is not "the smallest step" (--t-11 exists and is in use on .idxTag), and white at 0.62 on ink is already cleared by the composited AA check in the measured gate. Moving it under the LISTENING marker would push legal boilerplate into the headroom the design keeps clear for the person's own words as they arrive, and "72% ink" invents an alpha with no basis in the stated palette.

refuted.problem: The product's second promise is demonstrated by printing the same sentence twice with no difference in rank. Measured, both are 17px / weight 600 / 27.54px leading; the only distinction is the indigo tint behind the upper one. In the default seam the two strings are also character-identical ("Switch on before guests arrive, not when"), so a venue owner reads her own sentence, then reads it again under a different label, and nothing on screen tells her what the second one is for or that she may change it. The answered-findings list records that the picked words print "above and LARGER" than the wording derived from them; they do not.
refuted.why: REFUTED. The measurement is right and everything built on it is wrong. Live at ?state=seam the two strings are NOT character-identical: picked = "Switch on before guests arrive, not when." and wording = "Switch on before guests arrive, not when" — notebook.js:349/473/1296 seeds the wording via .replace(/^[a-z]/,upper).replace(/[.]$/,""), stripping the full stop. So the fix's own guard, taskWording.trim() === pickedWords.trim(), does not fire in the very state the finding names; it is dead code in its worked example. "The only distinction is the indigo tint" and "nothing on screen tells her what the second one is for or that she may change it" are both false: the panel carries the boundary line "Your note stays here. Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick and check below.", then the caps label THE WORDS YOU PICKED over the chip, then the caps label THE TASK WORDING over the field, and the same words are marked in place inside the note body (.pick verified present). The "above and LARGER" wording is the round-summary prose, not the artifact's contract; the codified promise is notes-interaction-check.mjs:1183-1192, "the words a person picked are not demoted beneath the machine's version", rank.picked >= rank.wording, which passes. The proposed fix would make the work worse: it demotes the editable, sendable payload (the field is what "Send to Tasks" sends) to 17/400 beneath a read-only echo at 20/600, on a surface whose job is "check this before you send it"; it prints the same sentence at 20/600 in the margin while the identical words sit at 17/400 marked in .readBody one column away, breaking the answered principle that a person's own words are set identically on every surface; and it deletes a control by swapping the field for a static line. Residual, pointing the opposite way and belonging to a different finding: .topField, .pieceField and .handBody all set a person's words at weight 400, while the peel is the only surface setting them at 600 — both the chip and the field.

rounds.headline: The second plane gets its two edges, and picking gets a keyboard
rounds.body: Twenty-three findings survived the refuter. The three costliest were one omission each: a sticky group rule with no lead-out that cut the row travelling under it through the x-height at most resting scroll offsets; a 600-weight lede budget so generous that two thirds of the index was semibold and a heading could end on the word she; and a second promise — that only the words you pick cross into Tasks — that could only be kept with a mouse. All three are closed. The note is now a pick surface with a real tab stop, walked sentence by sentence with the arrows and extended with shift, feeding exactly the same picked state a drag feeds. What crosses is what is marked, in both rooms, on every control. Deferring a card no longer counts as deciding one. The read-back hands back your own words once, with the caret in them. Reduced motion holds the arrival rather than deleting it.

wins.biggestWin: Give the index plane its two edges. Every one of the three costliest defects is the same missing decision: the second plane has no designed top edge and no designed foot. Fix the top with a 16px white-to-transparent lead-out under the sticky group rule (plus scroll-padding-top so the keyboard cannot park a row under it) and the foot with a hairline, one closing line naming what the plane holds, and shrink-wrapped trailing white — with the phone's padding-bottom taken from the real dock height and the same fade above it. That single move kills the row-guillotine at every scroll offset, un-clips the last note on the phone, and turns the 400-700px voids in search, seam and review from an unfinished page into a terminated plane. It also, for the first time, makes the desk and the index read as two objects with different jobs rather than one list with a box on top. Everything I found is craft debt of this kind, not a limit of the direction: nothing on my list needs the architecture or the three-colour lock touched, and none of it is more than an evening of CSS. This is emphatically not "a well-made notes app with wedding words" — the head leads with the couple and the days left, the groups are the house's own nouns, and the seam's boundary sentence is the actual promise rather than a feature. One more round closes the gap; 9.5 is reachable from here.

Cap the 600-weight lede to one earned budget and give no lede at all when the note has no short syntactic head. Right now 67% of the index's rendered characters are semibold at 1440, and on the phone three of six visible rows contain no 400 type whatsoever — the 400/600 pairing, the only hierarchy this product has inside a person's own writing, is spent on nearly everything and therefore signals nothing. One change in `ledeOf` (require a terminal stop within 48 characters that leaves a remainder, else return null, and delete the 46-character prefix branch) takes the index from a wall of bold to roughly a quarter bold, makes every semibold run a complete clause instead of a fragment ending on 'she', and makes the phone index legible as a list of notes rather than a list of headlines. It is the difference between a type system that has a hierarchy and one that only claims to. Everything else on my list is bounded craft debt one round closes; nothing here needs the architecture, the palette or a third weight, so 9.5 is reachable — this finding is most of the distance.

Make the hand modal. Applying inert to the sheet and rail while the queue is open, putting initial focus on the card's primary (it is currently on BODY), gating the index's arrow/j/k/Enter bindings on state !== "review", and suppressing the index cursor while a card is up removes four separate defects in one change: the tab escape out of the queue, the single keystroke that decides a card and walks the index at the same time, the "Open. <note>" announced for a note that never opened, and the two lit selections contradicting each other in the frame. It is the only finding on my list that damages a primary flow rather than a secondary keyboard path, and the peel already contains the exact pattern to copy. Two notes on the round as a whole. First, the failure mode this direction was chosen to avoid is not present: the head leads with Mara & Finn, Saturday 18 July, in 2 days and how many are still to decide, the pile groups by what a note is about rather than when it was typed, and the queue's question is "Worth doing something about?" — that is a venue's week shaping the product, not wedding vocabulary painted onto a notes app. Second, the 1.5 I am withholding is craft debt, not a limit of the direction: all five findings are bounded edits inside the locked architecture and the three-colour lock, and none of them require a new surface. One more round closes them.

Give picking a keyboard route and make it the only door into the seam. Turn the note body into a sentence-pick surface — one tab stop, sentences walked with the arrows and taken with Space, feeding the same `picked` state the mouse feeds — then delete the blank-field fallback in the hand so T cannot open the seam from nothing. That single change closes the largest hole in the product's second promise (today the sealed edge is only sealed if you own a mouse), removes the cause of the two-behaviours defect in the primary, and makes the most important cross-product moment in the suite operable and legible without a pointer. On the failure mode this direction was chosen to avoid: it is not true here. The subject axis, the head that leads with Mara & Finn and Saturday 18 July, \"still to decide\" as the state noun, and \"Nobody else can read this\" are venue-shaped and could not be swapped for engineering standups. The structural charge is answered. What stands between this and 9.5 is craft debt — five closeable defects, two of them named on the standing checklist — not a limit of the direction, and one more round can close all of it.

Put the words behind a gate as strict as the one the pixels already pass. notes-audit.mjs governs colour, weight, contrast, radii and motion; nothing governs the lexicon, and every finding above is what that gap produced — two verbs for keeping, four grammars for one queue, two meanings for "put back", two typographies for thirty seconds, a hardcoded wedding string in a generic panel, an invented privacy claim stronger than the product's own, and a strip that reports decisions nobody made. Build a lexicon check that (a) fails if any user-visible string in notebook.js is a literal rather than sourced from N.copy, (b) asserts one verb per act and one noun per state across rendered text AND every say() and offerUndo() argument, not only rendered text, and (c) runs BANNED_IN_COPY over the announcements too, with "cross" added. Seed it with the true privacy line and it takes findings 2, 3, 4 and 5 in one pass. The remaining distance to 9.5 is craft debt, not a limit of this direction: the three-colour lock is spent well and reads editorial rather than impoverished, the seam and the "IN TASKS AS" line are the work of a studio that understands this product, and the charge that this is a well-made notes app with wedding words on it does not land. What has not happened yet is the words being treated as the architecture's other half rather than as its finish.

Rebuild the readback as the one place the product proves it can be trusted without looking. It is currently the weakest surface in the build and it sits immediately after the boldest gesture — the floor going to ink, which is the one genuinely memorable moment this product has. Three changes in one pass: land focus and the caret in the first .pieceField instead of dropping it on document.body; announce what came back in the person's own words plus the next move rather than a bare count; and delete the duplicate .saidWas transcript so her sentences are printed once, in the fields she can edit, reclaiming the dead right half of the desk. That single surface converts the product's most emotionally exposed moment from something you must look at and re-read into something that hands you back your own words and tells you where you are. Nothing else on the board buys as much confidence per line of code, and it is the difference between a beautiful capture tool and one a venue owner will speak into while carrying chairs across a lawn.

Rebuild the head for the phone band. It is the single change that moves the most, because it fails at 360, 390 and 414 — effectively every phone — on the surface the locked architecture names as the product's home, and it fails invisibly: `.sheet { overflow: hidden }` converts the overflow into amputation rather than scroll, so the 276-assertion gate reports green while "Private to you" is cut mid-word, the "Notes options" button sits entirely off-sheet and still tabbable, and the lead fact the last round was spent adding (Mara & Finn, Saturday 18 July, in 2 days, 1 still to decide) computes to zero width and is announced to a screen reader but drawn nowhere. Give the head two rows below 720 with `.headNext` on its own line at `white-space: normal`, fold `Private to you` into the "…" menu below 400, and add a gate assertion that no focusable element's rect exceeds its nearest overflow:hidden ancestor. Ship the three-line reduced-motion fix in the same pass. Neither defect is something this direction cannot do — both are craft debt one round closes, and I found nothing structural: the subject spine, the "still to decide" count, the seam's boundary sentence and the wedding-facing head are things a generic notes app has no reason to build, so the "well-made notes app with wedding words" charge does not stand against this build.

confirmed.element: .idxDay (position: sticky, top: 0, background: var(--white)) over .idxRow inside the .index scroller — master.css ~line 524ff; reproduced at ?state=pressure, index.scrollTop 300, and at 390 on the phone at any mid-scroll rest
confirmed.problem: The group rule is opaque across its own 52px band and nothing else. Any scroll offset that leaves a row mid-transit under it cuts the row horizontally through the x-height: you see the bottom halves of the letters of somebody's own sentence, cleanly sliced. At scrollTop 300 the row under "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July" reads as a strip of severed glyphs; at 455 it happens to land clean. So the defect is present at most resting positions, not a few. This is the same failure the code already reasoned about horizontally — the comment at .idxText says a half-sliced letter "reads as damage rather than as a truncation" — solved on the x axis and left open on the y. It is the single most frequently visible flaw in the build, and it lands on the one object the whole product exists to protect.
confirmed.fix:
Drop the ::after rewrite entirely — it deletes the group hairline and scrims the person's own words. Keep only the scroll offset, and set it to the real band height rather than 68px (measured: 51.6px at 1440, 43.8px at 390, but the phone rule wraps to two lines).

In master.css, one line on the scroller: `.index { scroll-padding-top: 56px; }`, and in the 430-and-below block `.index { scroll-padding-top: 76px; }` to cover the wrapped rule. Verified: 18 obscured cursor positions at 1440 and 21 at 390 both go to zero, worst-case hidden fraction 100% → 0% and 51% → 0%, with no change to any resting frame.

Then fix the assertion that let it through. notes-interaction-check.mjs:153 should stop counting the attribute and measure the pixels: after each of a run of ArrowUp presses, assert the cursor row's box is not overlapped by any `.idxDay` whose rect is stuck to the scroller top, at 1440 and at 390. The current sentence, "the walked row is visible without a pointer", is the right sentence; it just needs to be true.

confirmed.element: .idxRow[data-cursor] { background: var(--indigo-wash); box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--indigo-line); } — master.css line 537, painted unconditionally; ?state=notebook at load, and after Ctrl+Enter
confirmed.problem: The loudest object inside the resting sheet is a keyboard cursor that nobody has moved yet. At load, before a key is pressed, a full-width indigo band with an indigo ring sits on row one — so the eye's first stop inside the paper is a cursor, not the person's newest words and not the field they are meant to write in. It gets worse after a capture: the cursor holds its note by id, so the moment you keep a thought, the new row appears at the top of the group unemphasised while the indigo band stays on the row below it. The strongest ink in the index points at the note you did not just write. And the paint is not even the index's own: `var(--indigo-wash)` + `var(--indigo-line)` is verbatim the pair used for `mark` (search hits) and for the picked sentence in the seam, so at rest the pile wears the exact visual language of "these are the words that will cross into Tasks". Indigo is currently doing five jobs (focus ring, keyboard cursor, arrival flash, search hit, picked words); in a three-colour lock it can afford one or two.
confirmed.fix:
Two changes, and drop the `--wash` fallback the finding proposed.

1. Scope the paint to focus: `.index:focus-within .idxRow[data-cursor] { background: var(--indigo-wash); box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--indigo-line); }`, and move the `::before` rule-suppression (line 538) and the `.idxMark i` halo (line 545) inside the same guard so the hairline and the dot halo do not go missing on a row with no visible band. Leave the roving tabindex, the `data-cursor` attribute and moveCursor() exactly as they are, so interaction-check line 153 still passes.

2. Give the unfocused cursor NO paint at all rather than `var(--wash)`. `--wash` is already `.idxRow:hover` and `.idxRow[data-open]`; a third meaning on the same tint makes a resting row read as hovered and an unfocused cursor indistinguishable from the note currently on the desk. Nothing else in the file paints an unfocused keyboard position, and it does not need one.

3. On keep, move the cursor to the row that arrived, so the emphasis and the arrival flash are the same row: set `cursorId = note.id` in keepDraft() beside `arriving = note.id` (notebook.js:287), and `cursorId = made[0].id` beside `arriving = made.length ? made[0].id : null` in the readback path (line 1891). Guard both with `if (!document.querySelector('.index')?.contains(document.activeElement))` so a keyboard user mid-walk in the pile does not have their place stolen by a capture.

confirmed.element: .headNext span ("Saturday 18 July, in 2 days, 1 still to decide", right edge 817) and .chip ("8 still to decide", left edge 830) — 13px apart in .head at 1440
confirmed.problem: The head ends one sentence with "1 still to decide" and starts the next object with "8 still to decide", thirteen pixels later, in the same baseline. Two different numbers of the same phrase, at two different scopes (this wedding vs the whole notebook), with nothing in the composition saying which is which — at a glance it reads as one broken string. And the chip is full ink on white, the heaviest object anywhere above the sheet, so it wins the first fixation: the eye's opening move in the product is a count it has to disambiguate, not the couple and the date the head was rebuilt to lead with. The group rule for Mara & Finn already prints "1 still to decide" on the right of its own row, so the head's copy of it is the third statement of the same fact on one screen.
confirmed.fix:
Keep the head clause - it is the round-5 lede and the scoped count is the correct one to keep. Fix the unscoped object instead, in two moves, both cheap and neither touching architecture, palette or weights:

1. The chip names its scope in its own words, in the visible label and in the accessible name, so the two counts can never be read or heard as one. It is the only one of the two with no subject, and 8 contains the 1, so the scope word has to be the notebook, not a repeat of the wedding. On-voice candidate from the product's existing nouns: "8 in the notebook still to decide" (aria: "8 notes in the notebook still to decide. Go through the notes waiting on a decision."). Exact wording is notes-copy.ts's call; the requirement is that the chip states its scope.

2. Put a .headRule hairline before the chip, as already exists between the wordmark and the workspace name, so the chip reads as a new object rather than the tail of the sentence beside it. Change no spacing: the strings are already 24px apart glyph to glyph and the fix's own target is met.

Then add the assertion the gate is missing: the head's scoped clause and the chip may never render the same phrase without the chip naming its scope - i.e. assert the chip's text and aria-label both contain the scope noun whenever .headNext also prints a count.

confirmed.element: `.idxText b` — `ledeOf()` at notebook.js:210-216; every room, every state that renders the index
confirmed.problem: The 600-weight lede has two budgets and neither works. If a note's first sentence ends inside 88 characters the whole sentence goes semibold; if it does not, an arbitrary 46-character prefix goes semibold. Measured live at 1440 in ?state=notebook: 67% of the index's 1,498 rendered characters are set at 600, the mean bold run is 66% of row width, and four of fourteen rows carry a 100-plus-character semibold run with no 400 text visible at all (105, 105, 104, 80 chars). At 390 it collapses completely — three of six visible rows show zero regular type inside the two-line clamp, with bold runs of 105, 196 and 104 characters against a ~56-character window, so on the primary capture device the 400/600 pairing does not exist. The 46-character path is worse in kind: a note I typed live rendered as 'ring the florist about the ceremony arch **she** | said she would confirm the width by friday' — semibold ending on a dangling pronoun, creating an emphasis unit that is not a unit. The only hierarchy device this product has inside a person's own writing is either spent on everything or applied to a fragment. Bear and Things bold a title; this bolds a paragraph prefix.
confirmed.fix: Keep a lede on every note; make it short and make it a unit. In ledeOf: (1) accept a terminal stop only if it is <=48 characters AND leaves a non-empty remainder; (2) otherwise prefer the last clause boundary — comma, colon, semicolon, en/em dash followed by a space — within the first 41 characters; (3) otherwise fall back to the last word boundary at 34, not 46; (4) then step back over a trailing weak word (article, pronoun, preposition, conjunction, auxiliary) so a lede can never end on "she", "the", "before"; (5) return null unless at least three words of remainder survive. I ran this over the live fixture: bold share falls from 67% to 21.0%, every lede is a readable unit ("Bar restock: tonic running low,", "Quote from today that I want to keep:", "Teacher onboarding,"), and the live capture keeps a lede ("ring the florist") instead of losing hierarchy. Separately, in trimRows at notebook.js:646-660 the head.pop() stage is what produces the 97.2% tablet reading: replace it, when lede plus one word of remainder will not fit, with dropping to the existing no-lede path (render the row whole at 400) rather than shortening the lede into an ellipsised fragment. That fixes the tablet and honours the finding's own principle that a shortened lede is a fragment, without deleting the budget.

confirmed.element: `.undo` (master.css:599) — notebook state, for 30 seconds after every Ctrl+Enter, 1440x960
confirmed.problem: The confirmation that a note is safe covers a note. Measured live after a capture: the strip occupies x 642-880, y 818-864, and the row 'Follow up with the motion designer about the venue film. She needs the final music choice…' sits at y 829 — 238px of a person's own sentence is blacked out for the full undo window. The comment directly above the rule asserts the opposite: 'Outside the pile's own scroll region, so it can never land on a person's sentences.' Moving it out of the scroll region stopped it scrolling with the rows, not overlapping them; the index's `padding-bottom: 132px` clears the dock and only takes effect at scroll-end, so at scroll-top a row is always underneath. This is the standing checklist's 'controls painting over content', unfixed, in the exact moment the whole direction exists for.
confirmed.fix: Keep the mechanism, fix the number, and drop the conditional. 58px is wrong: .index bottom is 942 and the strip top is 818, so clearing the band needs 124px — at 58px the box still ends at 884 and rows still show under the strip. Toggling on data-undo also reflows the pile twice per capture. Instead move the existing clearance from inside the scroll box to outside it, permanently: `.indexWrap { padding-bottom: 132px }` and `.index { padding-bottom: 0 }`, mirrored per breakpoint (128px at the 1063 query, 148px at 1069, 22px at 1165). Verified by injection at 1440x960: index bottom becomes 810, zero visible rows under the strip at scroll top / mid / end, scrollable distance identical at 352px both ways (so no pile height is lost), no layout jump when the strip appears or expires, and it additionally stops the floating dock cutting the 'Bar restock' row at scroll-top — a second occlusion present in the shipped build. Leave .undo at bottom:78px, and delete the master.css:596-598 comment claim.

confirmed.element: .readBody — pickedRange() / document selectionchange; [data-act="peel"]
confirmed.problem: The second promise of the product is reachable only with a pointer. pickedRange() reads document.getSelection() inside .readBody, and .readBody is neither focusable nor contenteditable, so shift+ArrowRight eight times leaves getSelection().toString() empty and .pickBar at 0. Only 3 of 14 fixture notes carry a fallback pick, so for the other 11 the desk's primary refuses with "Nothing picked yet. Pick the words in the note that should become the task." — an instruction a keyboard or screen-reader user physically cannot follow. The hand degrades gracefully on the same intent (T opens the peel with an empty field and says "Write what the task should say, or pick words in the note"); the desk blocks outright. One product, two grammars for the same act, and the sealed edge is closed to anyone not holding a mouse.
confirmed.fix: Two changes, both in the file's existing grammar. (1) Give the desk one tab stop and a drawn keyboard pick. Add tabindex="0" to .readBody, keeping the deskOf label as its accessible name so the desk gains exactly one stop and the index's single-stop discipline is untouched. In the same escaped-string pass that already inserts .lede and .pick (notebook.js:938-942), split note.body on sentence boundaries and wrap each run in <span class="sent" data-i="n"> — no new escaping path, so the bracket-safety already gated stays gated. Inside .readBody: ArrowDown/ArrowUp move a drawn sentence cursor, Space toggles the cursored sentence into the pick, Shift+ArrowDown extends across sentences, Escape clears. Distinguish cursor from picked by fill and density only — the cursor a hairline ink outline, the picked run the existing .pick wash — so the three-colour lock holds and state is never carried by hue. Route the result through offerPick() rather than a parallel path, so the .pickBar, the primary's label swap to "Send to Tasks", and the drawn mark all come for free, and announce with the string offerPick already uses ("N words picked. Begin to make them a task."), so no new copy enters the product. (2) Make the desk's refusal match the hand's invitation. In startPeel (:500-511), delete the early return and the 4.2s nudge; when no words are picked, open the peel with an empty .peelField, focus it, and say the line decide("task") already ships verbatim: "Nothing picked yet. Write what the task should say, or pick words in the note." One grammar for one act across both surfaces, and the primary never dead-ends. Gate both: extend notes-interaction-check.mjs with a real keyboard pick — Tab to .readBody, ArrowDown, Space, assert .pickBar count 1 and .readBody .pick count 1 with no page.evaluate selection anywhere — and assert that pressing the desk primary opens a .peel on all 14 notes, not 3. The existing synthetic-Range assertion at :1026 should stay but be renamed so it never again reads as proof of a keyboard route.

confirmed.element: startPeel() early-return branch when words is falsy — [data-act="peel"] on a note with no pick
confirmed.problem: Pressing the read note's own primary with nothing picked repaints and drops focus to <body> — verified for both a click and an Enter press. Every other repaint in this file restores place through refocus; this branch sets none, so a keyboard user who presses the note's main action is dumped to the top of the document and has to Tab back through the filing chip, both verbs, both group buttons and the index to reach the note again. It is the exact defect the standing checklist names (repaints that annihilate focus), and it lands on the one press most likely to be a first-timer's first attempt at the seam. The replacement instruction then self-destructs: the .nudge is removed on a 4200ms timer whether or not it has been read, and after it goes the button still reads "Pick the words, then send" with no route to what that means.
confirmed.fix: In the words-falsy early return of startPeel() (notebook.js:503-513) set `refocus = { kind: "act", sel: '[data-act="peel"]' }` before paint(), mirroring cancelPeel at :530, so the press returns focus to the control that was pressed on both the desk and the phone sheet. Delete the 4200ms setTimeout entirely rather than shortening it: its repaint is itself a focus-annihilating repaint (verified — focus parked on "Put it back" is dumped to body 4.2s later with no user input), and the nudge is already cleared on the next pick (:490), on a successful peel (:514) and on close/open (:579, :590), so the instruction dies when it has been acted on instead of on a clock. While the nudge stands, keep it and the button label telling the same story rather than letting the sentence vanish and leave "Pick the words, then send" pointing at nothing.

confirmed.element: #q with .idxRow[data-cursor] painted behind it
confirmed.problem: While the caret is in search, the index still paints its indigo keyboard cursor on the first result (rgba(79,70,229,0.08) plus an indigo ring) — the same mark that means "press Enter to open this" everywhere else in the product. From #q it means nothing: ArrowDown does not move it, ArrowUp does not move it, and Enter opens nothing (.readBody stays 0) with no announcement at all. A person types three letters, sees the note they want highlighted, presses Enter and the product does not react. The fastest path in a capture product — type, arrow, Enter — is drawn and not wired; the real route is two Tab presses past the Esc button.
confirmed.fix: Make search a combobox, not a focus move. In the single keydown handler, above `if (typing) return;` (notebook.js:2008), add a branch for `state === "search" && e.target.id === "q"`: ArrowDown/ArrowUp call a walk that sets cursorId along walkOrder() and say()s "n of m, {title}" but keeps `refocus = { kind: "field", sel: "#q" }` — do NOT call moveCursor() as written, because it sets `refocus = { kind: "row", id }` and would yank the caret out of the field mid-query, ending the person's typing. preventDefault so the arrows do not jump the caret to the ends of the input. Enter (no modifier) calls openNote(cursorId) — the same path the row's own Enter takes, with the same "Open. {title}" announcement — and does nothing when visible() is empty, so a no-hit query still dead-ends only into the existing emptyMove exits. Wire the field as the combobox that the paint already implies: role="combobox" with aria-expanded and aria-controls on #q pointing at the index list, aria-activedescendant set to the cursor row's id, and an id on each .idxRow, so the announcement is the real one a screen reader makes rather than a second story told through the live region. Keep the row's tabindex="0" so the existing single tab stop and its arrow walk are untouched. If the walk is not wired this round, the fallback is narrower than "suppress data-cursor": suppress only the paint (`data-cursor`) while state === "search", leaving the tabindex="0" seeding intact so the index keeps its tab stop, and let :focus-visible mark the row once Tab actually reaches it.

confirmed.problem: The file's own comments claim "Three leadings, declared" and "Every letter-spacing in this file is a token from it."
