Measured across ten states: 17px reading text renders at five different leadings (1.22, 1.45, 1.58, 1.62, 1.28), 11px at three, 12px at three, 13px at two; 1.22 / 1.38 / 1.50 / 1.55 / 1.58 / 1.60 / 1.64 are all off the declared three-step ladder. `--tr-13` is never defined in `:root`, so `.nudge` and `.peelBoundary` silently take the hardcoded -0.01em fallback and sit off the tracking curve, giving 13px text three trackings (-0.156px, -0.13px, -0.078px). Same class of defect the file says it fixed for `.readBody`/`.handBody`, left standing on every surface that was not in that one selector list.
confirmed.fix:
Two moves, both inside the locked constraints.

1. Make the declaration true. Either collapse to the declared three, or declare what is actually needed and name it. Collapsing is the stronger answer and costs almost nothing visually: .emptyBody 1.58, .peelWhy 1.55, .specWhy 1.55, .state p 1.55, .darkNote 1.6 and expressive .readLong 1.64 all become `var(--lh-read)` (1.62 — max delta 0.07 ratio, under a pixel a line); .idxText's literal 1.45, .peelSent 1.45 and mobile field 1.5 become `var(--lh-base)`; .emptyTitle 1.22, .darkSaid 1.38 and expressive .handBody 1.56 / .readBody 1.6 are the only genuine outliers — if display leading really wants to be tighter than 1.28 at 27px and 34px, add ONE token `--lh-display: 1.22` and give .darkSaid and .emptyTitle that, rather than the finding's two. Four steps, all named, beats three claimed and eleven shipped.

2. Kill the dead token and the literals. Define `--tr-13: -0.010em` in the :root curve (it sits correctly between --tr-14 -0.012em and --tr-12 -0.006em) and drop both fallbacks at lines 812 and 820 — or, cheaper and more honest, point .nudge and .peelBoundary at `--tr-14`, which is the declared step for 13px text everywhere else in the file, and delete --tr-13 entirely. Replace the three hardcoded uppercase literals — 0.04em at 221 and 588, 0.05em at 649 — with `var(--tr-cap)`, so the curve's one uppercase step is actually the only uppercase step.

3. Close the blind spot so this cannot come back. Extend notes-audit.mjs check 9 from a `=== "normal"` test to a ladder test: read the declared `--lh-*` and `--tr-*` values off :root at run time (do not hardcode them, so the check tracks the tokens), then fail any text-bearing element whose computed line-height / font-size is more than 0.01 from a declared ratio, and any whose computed letter-spacing is more than 0.01px from a declared em step at its own size. Report it as a tenth check with its own zero, alongside the nine. Run it across all ten states and all four rooms including [data-type="expressive"] and the 390 breakpoint, which is where four of the eleven stray ratios live and where a locked-room-only pass would miss them.

refuted.problem: The paper never responds to how much is on it. In search with one hit, the last row bottoms out at y=205 and the sheet runs to y=942: roughly 700px of blank white with the dock floating in the middle of nothing. In seam it is ~390px, in review ~180px plus the dock band. The second plane has no foot — it does not end, it evaporates — so in exactly the states where the index is short, the architecture stops reading as two planes with depth and reads as one card sitting on an empty page. Horizontally the same thing: at 1920 the sheet is 1802px wide holding a 1060px column, 371px of dead paper each side, and the ink floor collapses to an 18px picture frame, so "one white sheet lifted off an ink floor" disappears at the width most venue owners' desktops actually run.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on all four legs — measured, not argued.

1. The horizontal premise is factually wrong. The ink floor does not "collapse to an 18px picture frame at 1920". It is 18px at every width, by declaration: `.floor { padding: var(--inset) }` with `--inset: 18px`. Measured at 1440x960 (the canonical approved frame the whole programme has been reviewed against): sheetX 100, right inset 18, top 18, bottom 18. Measured at 1920x1080: identical, 18/18/18. Nothing changes with width except the paper margin beside the column (131px -> 371px). The finding invents a width-dependent failure that the box model does not have.

2. The horizontal fix makes the work worse and breaks a deliberate detail. Applying `.sheet { max-width: 1560px; margin: 0 auto }` at 1920 was measured live: the rail-to-sheet gap goes from 18px to 139px. The floating capsule is then stranded in open ink, and `.railTile[data-active]::after` — the 7px arrow at `right: -12px` whose whole job is that "the capsule points at the sheet it opened" — points at 139px of nothing. The screenshot of the modified state shows the L-frame relationship the architecture locks coming apart. The finding trades a taste complaint about margin for a broken adjacency.

3. The vertical content already exists, at the head. `.indexHead` names the plane, prints its count, and draws a hairline to the column edge (`::after { flex: 1; height: 1px; background: var(--line-soft) }`). Rendered text, captured live: notebook "YOUR NOTES · 14 notes"; search after typing marquee "FOUND · 1 of 14 notes have “marquee” in them" — which is verbatim the closing line the finding proposes; seam "WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS · 3 so far, and every note stayed here"; review "STILL TO DECIDE · 7 left". Printing that same fact again under the last row states one fact twice on one plane, which is the "facts stated in two grammars" defect on the standing checklist. The plane does not "evaporate" — it is named and ruled at its head, where you read it before you scan, not after.

4. The vertical mechanism does not do what the finding claims it does. I applied `.indexWrap { flex: 0 1 auto }` to the seam state at 1920 and measured before/after: sheet height 1044 -> 1044, sheet bottom 1062 -> 1062, dock top 998 -> 998. The only change is `.indexWrap`'s own invisible box bottom, 1062 -> 688. Not one visible pixel moves and no white is capped. The trailing white is a property of `.sheet { height: 100% }` — the locked "one white sheet lifted off an ink floor". Capping it means shrinking the sheet itself, which is redesigning the locked architecture, and in search it would make the sheet and the capture dock jump vertically on every keystroke, under the hand of someone mid-thought, in a product whose promise is three seconds from thought to safe.

5. "The dock floating in the middle of nothing" is wrong. Measured in all four states, the dock sits at top 998 / bottom 1044 — pinned 18px above the sheet foot, exactly where the locked architecture puts it ("a floating dock at the foot of the sheet").

The finding's own numbers are also off: at 1920 the search last row bottoms at y=228 and the sheet at y=1062, not 205 and 942.

What survives is a taste preference: a one-hit search reads sparse. Linear, Things and Bear all keep the list region's frame on a single result rather than reflowing the surface, and the head already says "1 of 14". Taste stated as a defect, with a fix that is measurably inert vertically and actively damaging horizontally.

refuted.problem: On the primary device the pile's scroll padding is 22px and the ink dock over it is 103px tall and fully opaque. At the end of the pile the last note ("Photographer recommendation from the Hendersons…") has its meta line sliced by the dock's top edge: "Kept · 2 days ago" is cut through the baseline and the row cannot be brought clear by any amount of scrolling. So the oldest note in the notebook can never be seen whole, and its tap target is partly under an opaque control. This is controls-painting-over-content at the one place the checklist says to look, on the device the product's three-second promise is actually kept on.
refuted.why:
REFUTED — the described clipping does not happen, and the measurements it rests on are wrong.

Driven live at 390x844, `?state=notebook`, `.index` scrolled to `scrollTop = scrollHeight` (789 = max, confirmed):
- `.dock` / `.dockWrap` are at y=740, height 95 — not "9,732 372x103". The finding is 8px and 8px out on the two numbers its whole argument depends on.
- The last row's meta line is two elements, `.idxTag` "Kept" and `.idxWhen` "2 days ago", both bottoming at y=734.2. The dock top is 740. They clear the ink by 5.8px and are fully painted. There is no cut baseline. A 3x crop of y 640–840 shows "Kept" and "2 days ago" whole, with white between them and the dock's rounded top edge.
- The only thing under the dock is 5.2px of the row's own bottom padding (row box bottoms at 745.2). `elementFromPoint(200, 738)` returns the row button; the row exposes ~80px of a 44px requirement, so "its tap target is partly under an opaque control" is not a hit-target defect the measured gate would or should catch.
- Same result at `?state=pressure` (36 notes, scrollTop 2679 = max): meta bottoms at 733.8, dock top 740, clears.

The clearance is not an accident. `.sheet` is `calc(100dvh - 68px - var(--inset)*2 - env(safe-area-inset-bottom))` and the dock is `bottom: calc(var(--inset) + env(safe-area-inset-bottom))`, so the sheet foot and the dock move together; the 22px `.index` padding plus the coarse-pointer 12px row padding is 34px against a 27px dock-over-sheet overlap. I re-derived it with a 34px safe-area inset: dock top 706, last glyph 700.2 — the same 5.8px clearance. The overlap is the locked architecture ("a floating dock at the foot of the sheet"), and the sheet height is already tuned so the pile's last line lands above it.

The proposed fix would also make the work worse, and contradicts itself. `padding-bottom: calc(var(--dockH) + 20px)` = 115px on a 654px-tall index means the last note comes to rest ~88px above the dock: a hole of dead white a seventh of the screen tall at the end of the pile, on the one surface where density is the product, and it breaks the reading that the ink floats over the paper by making the paper stop short of it. And if content is padded fully past the dock, no row is ever "in transit" under it, so the second half of the fix — a fade-to-white lead-out for rows meeting the ink edge — has nothing left to fade.

refuted.problem: The file declares 'Three leadings' and 'One tracking curve, by size, declared once. Every letter-spacing in this file is a token from it.' Both claims are false in the shipped locked room. Six leadings render off the 1.28/1.45/1.62 ladder: 1.22 (`.emptyTitle`, verified at 32.94px/27px and 20.74px/17px), 1.38 (`.darkSaid`), 1.5 (phone `.phoneField`), 1.55 (`.peelWhy`, `.specWhy`, `.state p`, verified at 18.6px/12px), 1.58 (`.emptyBody`, verified at 26.86px/17px and 23.7px/15px), 1.6 (`.darkNote`); the type rooms add 1.56 and 1.64. That is more off-ladder values than on it. Tracking leaks in five ways: `0.04em` hardcoded on `.railAvatar` and `.dockAvatar`, `0.05em` on `.darkTag`, an undefined `--tr-13` falling back to `-0.01em` at master.css:812 and 820 (a ninth value on an eight-value curve), `.spec .emptyTitle` setting 17px with `--tr-21`, and every `kbd` dropping to 11px while inheriting its 13px parent's tracking — measured at -0.0142em where the curve says 0. In the resting notebook alone, 11px renders at three tracking values, 13px at two, 15px at two. The measured gate passes because it checks families and weights, not the two ladders the file's own comments certify.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The source facts are real but the finding's central claim is false, one of its "verified" measurements is attributed to the wrong selector, and its fix is a rendered regression.

MEASURED, not read. Driving the locked room at 1440x960 and enumerating every text-bearing node's computed lineHeight/fontSize:
- notebook: 1.28 / 1.45 / 1.62 and nothing else
- seam: 1.28 / 1.45 / 1.62 and nothing else
- review: 1.28 / 1.45 / 1.62 and nothing else
- not-yet: 1.28 / 1.45 / 1.62 + 1.55
- voice: 1.28 / 1.45 / 1.62 + 1.38 (34px display) + 1.6 (12px caption)
- nothing: 1.22 / 1.45 / 1.55 / 1.58 + 1.28
"That is more off-ladder values than on it" is false in every rendered state of the shipped locked room. Three of the six states render the three-value ladder exactly and nothing else. The finding counted declarations in the stylesheet and reported them as if they were pixels on a screen.

FABRICATED VERIFICATION. It claims `.peelWhy` "verified at 18.6px/12px". `.peelWhy` is `font-size: var(--t-13)` (master.css:879), so 1.55 renders at 20.15px. 18.6/12 is `.specWhy` (:915). And `.peelWhy` does not render in `?state=seam` at all — the seam measures 1.28/1.45/1.62 only. A measurement was asserted for a selector that was not measured.

THE TRACKING "LEAKS" ARE MOSTLY THE FILE'S OWN TOKENS DOING CORRECT WORK. Per-size in the resting notebook, measured: 11px carries 0em (`--tr-11`, on `.idxTag`/`.groupBtn`), 0.075em (`--tr-cap`, uppercase micro-labels), 0.04em (the two monograms), -0.0142em (kbd). Two of those four are declared tokens serving lowercase versus uppercase at the same size, which is required typography, not a leak. Likewise the curve is deliberately keyed one notch off the size ramp (13px uses `--tr-14`, 15px `--tr-16`, 17px `--tr-18`, 20px `--tr-21`) — which is why no `--tr-13` exists. The residual deltas are 0.026px to 0.16px per gap: the kbd inheritance is -0.156px per gap on a two-character keycap, roughly 0.3px across the whole key. Sub-pixel. Not visible to any reader at any size, in any frame.

THE FIX MAKES THE ARTIFACT WORSE, in four places:
1. `1.38 to --lh-read` puts 34px `.darkSaid` at 1.62 — 55px leading on the display line of the voice takeover, the most cinematic surface in the product. 1.38 is correct display leading; 1.62 is a reading leading and would wreck it.
2. Collapsing 1.5/1.55/1.58/1.6/1.64 to one `--lh-prose: 1.56` flattens the phone capture field, the empty body, the dark note, and the entire `[data-type="expressive"]` room (1.56/1.6/1.64) onto one number. That room exists to prove the ramp can breathe; the fix deletes the thing it demonstrates. Smaller type needs proportionally more leading — the file's actual practice is a size-indexed leading curve, which is better typography than the comment it is being measured against.
3. `--tr-cap` (0.075em) on `.railAvatar`/`.dockAvatar` adds a 0.825px trailing letter-space to a two-letter monogram centred by `place-items: center` with no compensating indent, shifting the glyphs off optical centre on the one element that is on screen in every state. The current 0.04em is the correct compromise, not a leak.
4. `.darkTag { font-size: var(--t-11) }` is a rendered redesign smuggled into a hygiene finding — and dropping reverse type on ink from 12px to 11px is the wrong direction for reverse type.

THE PROPOSED GATE IS UNSOUND. "Every rendered letterSpacing/fontSize ratio must equal a declared token" fails correct CSS: em letter-spacing computes to an absolute length and inherits, so every legitimate nested size change produces a non-token ratio. That gate would force a letter-spacing declaration on every nested element or ban size changes inside tracked parents.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY LEFT is a stale word in a code comment and one dead `var(--tr-13, -0.01em)` fallback worth 0.026px per gap at master.css:812/820. The comment's operative certification — that leading is declared rather than left to the browser, "because leading left to the browser is leading that shifts by a pixel" — IS gated: notes-audit.mjs check 9 fails any element computing `line-height: normal`, zero across ten states and four rooms. This is a lint of a stylesheet's prose, not a defect in the artifact, and nothing in it is visible in any of the eleven frames.

refuted.problem: 'still to decide' renders seven times on the resting notebook screen carrying six different numbers, in three registers, with nothing naming the scope of any of them: a 13px/400 grey clause inside the header sentence ('…, in 2 days, 1 still to decide'), a 12px/600 white-on-ink pill ('8 still to decide') 40px to its right, and five 12px/400 grey group tails (1, 1, 3, 2, 1). The pill is the loudest object in the header band and carries the least scoped fact on screen, while the number about the couple actually named sits in the quietest register beside it. A venue owner has to derive that 1+1+3+2+1 equals the 8 in the pill; the type states no such relationship. ?state=review compounds it — '1 of 8' on the card, '8 still to decide.' on the strip, and 'STILL TO DECIDE · 7 left' on the index head, three numbers and three grammars inside one 500px column.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The count is right (7 prints on ?state=notebook: 1 / 8 / 1 / 1 / 3 / 2 / 1) but every load-bearing claim under it is false, and all three edits destroy information.

1. The central premise of the fix is factually wrong. "At notebook.js:722 delete the trailing clause — the pill already states it." It does not. notebook.js:719 computes `work().filter(n => n.pending && n.aboutKey === "mara-finn").length` = 1, scoped to the named couple; the chip at :731 uses `counts().pending` = 8, global. 1 ≠ 8. Deleting :722 deletes the couple-scoped number — the very number the finding itself argues is the most valuable thing in the band ("the number about the couple actually named") — and leaves only the unscoped 8. The fix contradicts its own diagnosis.

2. "nothing naming the scope of any of them" is false in the rendered DOM. The 13px clause lives inside `.headNext`, whose 600-weight lede immediately preceding it is "Mara & Finn" — subject and number in one sentence. Each `.idxDayTail` sits on its own group rule, whose label is the group ("Mara & Finn", "The course", "The studio", "The house"). Six of the seven have their scope named by adjacency. The seventh is the only object in the header band that belongs to no group, which is what makes it the global one. The finding's own proposed principle — "let position carry scope" — is already what is implemented.

3. The sums check out: 1+1+3+2+1 = 8, and the index-count agreement is a gated assertion (notes-interaction-check.mjs:91-96, "the head's count and the index agree"). Total-above-breakdown is a legible, standard reading, not a derivation the reader is left to perform. The chip is a `<button data-act="review">` with an aria-label that states the action; it is the loudest ink object because it is the only *action* in the band, which is correct, not inverted.

4. The ?state=review claim is wrong about what is on screen. Driven live: the card prints "1 of 8" (`.handOf`), the strip prints "8 still to decide.", and the index head prints "Still to decide / 7 left" above a list of exactly 7 visible rows. The 8→7 relationship is not inferred, it is shown twice — by "1 of 8" and by the row count directly beneath "7 left". Rewriting it to "7 after this one" duplicates the card's position readout and invents a grammar no other index head uses (`count` is a slot, "N left").

5. The tail edit makes the work worse and trips a checklist item. A bare grey numeral in an unheaded right column, whose accessible name says a full sentence the eye cannot see, creates an accessible name richer than the rendered text — the inverse of the name/rendered-text agreement this build gates — and drops the product's single state noun ("still to decide", matching the "To decide" row tags) from the visible layer.

6. "Relabel the pill 'to decide across everything'" is off-voice chrome and out of the state-noun set the rest of the surface is gated against.

The one true residue is much narrower than the finding: at 1440 the eye does see "…in 2 days, 1 still to decide" and a black pill "8 still to decide" 40px apart, and the Mara & Finn group rule already prints "1 still to decide" a third time. That is a stutter worth one small edit, not the three-part rewrite proposed — and it collides with the head design a prior round explicitly established.

refuted.problem: The one sentence a person needs in order to trust the voice flow is the smallest and dimmest type in the product: 12px at `--on-ink-2`, leading 1.6, ragged over three lines in the bottom-left corner of a 1440x960 field of ink, while the transcript above runs at 34px and most of the screen is empty. It is also the only text block in the file measured in `ch` (`max-width: 62ch`) — precisely the anti-pattern the token comment 600 lines above condemns by name ('Calibrated in em rather than ch… 31em… self-scales with the type ramp, which `ch` does not'), so it alone does not scale with the ramp. The result is that in a product whose second promise is that nothing leaves, the only notice about something leaving is typeset in the register every reader has been trained to skip. The palette and contrast gates pass it because 0.62 white on ink is 7.7:1; the gates cannot see that it reads as boilerplate.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Drove ?state=voice in all four rooms at 390/768/1440/1920 and built the proposed fix live to see it.

Two of the finding's load-bearing facts are wrong. (1) "the transcript above runs at 34px" — in the locked and quiet rooms `.darkSaid` computes to 27px, not 34px, and the frame the finding cites (locked-voice--1440x960.png) is the 27px one; 34px exists only in studio/press (`[data-type="expressive"]`). (2) "the smallest and dimmest type in the product" — `--t-11: 11px` exists and is used in roughly ten places, and `.undoFor` (master.css:611) is 11px at the identical `--on-ink-2` on ink. On this very screen `.darkTime` (master.css:652) is 12px at `--on-ink-2` — the same size and the same alpha as the disclosure. The disclosure is mid-ramp, not the floor of it.

The `ch` charge has no rendered consequence. `--t-12` is declared once at master.css:83 and never redefined in any of the five media queries, so `.darkNote` has no ramp to fail to scale with; 62ch is a fixed 493px against a fixed 12px. It is a consistency nit dressed as a defect. Worse, the prescribed swap makes the thing it complains about worse: `var(--measure)` at the prescribed `--t-13` is 403px, narrower than the current 493px, so the block rags to 4 lines at 1440 and 5 at 390 instead of today's 3 and 5.

The fix, built and screenshotted, is a regression on three counts. Its own stated goal fails: `.darkSaid` is `max-width: var(--measure)` at 27px = 837px centred at x=302, while a 13px block at `var(--measure)` is 403px centred at x=519 — so the moved note does not share the transcript's column or its left edge, it floats indented under the middle of it. It severs the transcript from `.darkWave`, the live listening indicator that currently sits directly beneath the words, pushing static legal text between the two live elements. And it moves the notice from a `flex: none` foot that is permanently pinned outside the scrolling body into `.darkBody`, which is `overflow: auto` and vertically centred — the one place a legally required always-on notice should not live.

The current placement is a decision, not an oversight. The source carries the argument (master.css:664-668): the contrast was deliberately raised from `--on-ink-3` to `--on-ink-2` because "the one thing on this screen that must be readable is the sentence saying the words are leaving the device," and notes-interaction-check.mjs:285-287 gates its presence and its content. Sitting on the same band as Cancel and Stop and read it back puts the notice at the point of decision, which is where Stripe and Apple put the same class of sentence. "It reads as boilerplate" is taste stated as a defect, and the only concrete remedy offered makes the composition worse.

Evidence: C:/Users/ethan/signal-studio-workspace/_wt-design-notes/_disc_voice_1440.png (as shipped) and C:/Users/ethan/signal-studio-workspace/_wt-design-notes/_disc_moved_1440.png (the proposed fix, built).

refuted.problem: The review queue is the only takeover in the product that is not modal, and it fails three ways at once. Tab from the hand walks straight out of it into the seven index rows behind (rail → head → 5 hand acts → .idxRow → dock search); nothing is inert. Pressing k with focus on one of those rows fires BOTH bindings in one keystroke — the top card is decided ("Kept in Notes. 7 left.", queue 1 of 8 → 2 of 8) AND the index cursor walks a row, two unrelated planes changed by one key. Pressing Enter on a row behind the hand announces "Open. Teacher onboarding, three things they kept asking for…" while .readBody count stays 0: the product speaks an event that did not happen. And the frame shows two lit selections at once — the card in the hand and the indigo keyboard cursor on the first row of STILL TO DECIDE. The peel is correctly modal and gated as such; the hand, which binds bare letters, is not.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The load-bearing claim is factually false, and the proposed fix would break the hand it is trying to protect.

1) "Pressing k fires BOTH bindings in one keystroke ... two unrelated planes changed by one key" — false. notebook.js:2015-2027: the review branch runs `decide("keep")` then `return`s, before the ArrowUp/`k` cursor branch at :2031 is ever reached. Only one binding fires. I drove it: focus the first `.idxRow` behind the hand, press `k` — say = "Kept in Notes. 7 left.", queue 1 of 8 → 2 of 8, and the row the cursor was on ("Idea for the studio newsletter") is now the card in the hand (`.handBody` = "Idea for the studio newsletter…") and has left the index (idxRow count 7 → 6). The cursor did not "walk"; `indexOf()` at :1123 re-seeds `cursorId` because the row it was holding is no longer in the list. That is the correct place-keeping behaviour, not a double-fire. The finding read a re-render as a second keybinding.

2) "Apply inert to .sheet and .rail exactly as startPeel does" — this would inert the hand. `startPeel` does not do that; the inert loop at :1627-1631 keys on an overlay (`.dark, .phoneSheet`) and inerts what is behind it. In review there is no overlay: the hand is `s.desk`, injected inside `<main class="sheet">` (:1607-1615). `.sheet[inert]` kills d-task, d-keep, d-later, d-delete and the Esc button. The fix as written is inoperable.

3) The premise "the only takeover that is not modal" contradicts the locked architecture. Review is not a takeover — it is the locked two-plane sheet doing its job: the desk carries the card, and the index below carries the rest of the queue, headed "Still to decide · n left". The only stated takeover is dictation ("dictating takes the whole floor to ink"), and that one IS inert-gated. Gating the arrow/j/k walk on `state !== "review"` would remove the ability to read ahead in your own queue, which is a real affordance, not leakage.

4) "Suppress data-cursor on .idxRow while a hand is open" makes it worse. The index keeps its single tab stop either way (tabindex="0" at :1040); suppressing the wash leaves a focusable row with no visible keyboard position — master.css:535-537 records that exact regression being fixed ("the row it is on has to be visible without hovering"). "Two lit selections" is also taste stated as defect: one is the card on the desk, the other is a tab-stop marker, drawn in ink density and indigo wash, not a competing selection.

The only residual truth is a much smaller, differently-shaped defect (see sharpenedFix), and it does not support the charge as filed.

refuted.problem: The way back states two things it does not keep. First, it prints "for 30s" as a static string: measured at t=0 it reads "for 30s" and at t=+9s it still reads "for 30s", then at 30s the strip vanishes with no announcement, and Ctrl+Z afterwards changes nothing and says nothing. The only reversible moment in a capture product carries a number that never moves. Second, at 390 the same strip renders <kbd>Ctrl+Z</kbd> — confirmed display:block, text "Ctrl+Z" — on a device with no Ctrl key, and the strip's Undo button is 11 tab stops from the capture field. So on the phone the product advertises a keyboard chord as the route back and nothing else.
refuted.why:
Half two is factually wrong and already handled. master.css:1197 hides `.undoAct kbd` under `@media (pointer: coarse)`. Driven in a real phone context (hasTouch/isMobile, 390x844): `matchMedia("(pointer: coarse)")` is true, the kbd computes `display: none`, and the visible strip children are ["Saved.", "Undo", "for 30s"]. The screenshot shows an ink-on-white "⟲ Undo" pill, 76x30 at y=641, sitting directly above the dock — one tap, and the only advertised route. The finding's "confirmed display:block, text Ctrl+Z" was measured in a narrow DESKTOP window, where pointer is fine and a Ctrl key genuinely exists, so the chord is correct there. The tab count is also wrong: measured 8 stops from the phone field to the Undo button, not 11, and forcing the strip earlier would need a positive tabindex or a DOM reorder, an anti-pattern for a transient status region on a surface where the route back is a thumb.

Half one is factually accurate — "for 30s" is static at t=0 and t=+9s, the strip expires silently, and an expired Ctrl+Z on an empty field says nothing — but the proposed fix is a regression. `.undo` carries role="status"; ticking `.undoFor` inside it mutates a live region once a second and fires roughly thirty polite announcements per save, which the fix does not guard. With a live draft, notebook.js:1921 deliberately declines to preventDefault so Ctrl+Z belongs to the field's own undo stack, so "changes nothing" only holds when there is nothing to undo. And the single unmoving number is the calm the strip is selling: none of the named benchmarks ship a ticking undo countdown, and the fixed thirty is a prior round's gated fix (notes-interaction-check.mjs:577 and :1354). A countdown clock plus an unsolicited "that can no longer be undone" thirty seconds after a save trades a settled promise for a nervous one.

refuted.problem: Standing-checklist item found: clamps that cut mid-word. The desktop row trim is genuinely word-safe (trimRows pops whole words). The phone's two-line row is not: it is `max-height: calc(var(--lh-base) * 2em)` plus `overflow: hidden`, with an absolutely positioned `::after` ellipsis and a white gradient pinned bottom-right. At 390 that slices the last visible word through the glyph — "Bring the worke", "If no", "a w" — and pastes an ellipsis over the wound, detached from the text with a visible gap. On the cursor and hover row the gradient is removed (`background: none`), so the ellipsis overprints the half-drawn letters with nothing masking the cut. On the one surface a venue operator actually reads while walking the building, a person's own words are cut mid-letter.
refuted.why: Factually wrong about the behaviour and the pixels. .idxText at 390 is white-space: normal, so lines break at WORD boundaries; max-height 43.5px against a 21.75px line box contains line 2 whole (bottom 209.5 vs box bottom 211.25) and hides line 3 entirely. Measured across all 8 states at 390 (14 + 36 + others), scrollWidth never exceeds clientWidth on any .idxText — there is no horizontal clip, so no glyph is ever sliced. The three quoted examples are invented: the real line-2 endings are the complete words "worked", "not" and "way". The hover/cursor claim is backwards: screenshotting the worst-overlap row (line 2 ending at 359.6 of a 365 edge) at 3x, the rest state fades the last ~6px of "way" while the hover/cursor state with background:none renders "a way…" complete with the ellipsis adjacent and nothing overprinted — the state called the wound is the cleaner of the two. Accessible names carry the full text on every row in every state (verified, zero misses), so nothing is silently deleted. The proposed fix is a regression: popping whole words off a wrapped two-line row can only remove the person's words from the one surface designed to give its width to them, and it adds a 36-row measure loop on every resize to reproduce a break the browser already makes at a word boundary. What is left is a conventional fade clamp softening a final glyph — taste, not a defect.

refuted.problem: Keeping one note produces two verbs in the same second: the undo strip prints "Saved." while the live region announces "Kept. 15 notes, 9 waiting on a decision." and the row paints the tag "Kept". The announcement also invents a fourth grammar for the queue that appears nowhere on screen — "waiting on a decision" — against "8 still to decide" (head chip), "Still to decide" (section), "To decide" (row tag) and "7 left" (section count). The undo window is typed two ways: "30s" on the strip, "thirty seconds" in the delete dialog. The measured gate governs colour, type and contrast; nothing governs the lexicon, so the transient and spoken layers speak a dialect the page does not. "Put it back" compounds it — it closes a note in the detail view and means undo in the review strip, while the same escape is labelled "Back to your notes" in the hand.
refuted.why:
Driven live at 1440x960 (?state=notebook&v=locked, typed a note, Ctrl+Enter) and at ?state=review (K), plus the source. Two of the finding's four factual predicates are false, and the prescribed fix is inverted on the one true residue.

(1) "the row paints the tag 'Kept'" — FALSE. makeNote sets pending:true, and notebook.js:1029-1034 tags a pending note "To decide". Measured after capture: TOP ROW TAG = "To decide", accessible name = "…Written. Just now. Still to decide." "Kept" is the tag for the opposite state (reviewed, not pending). So there is no three-way verb collision on the row.

(2) "'Put it back' … means undo in the review strip" — FALSE. The review strip's control is literally `Undo Ctrl+Z` (notebook.js:800); measured strip text = "Kept in Notes. Undo Ctrl+Z for 30s". "Put it back" occurs exactly once, on the detail view's escape (:988), matched by closeNote()'s say("Put back.") (:593). The deck note's "every decision can be put back" is prose about reversibility, not a control label. And the label is load-bearing: the locked architecture is two planes with depth where reading LIFTS a note out of the index onto the desk — "Put it back" is the only word in the product that names that lift. The proposed relabel to "Back to your notes" would make an object-return read like the room-exits in search/review/peel and flatten the founder-locked depth metaphor into generic chrome. That fix makes the work worse.

(3) The fix's direction is backwards on the one real residue. The control the person presses is labelled "Save it" (:103, :871, phone aria-label "Save it"). So the strip's "Saved." is on-verb with the button; the outlier is say("Kept. …") at :250, which borrows the review lexicon where "Kept in Notes." / tag "Kept" mean decided-and-not-pending — precisely NOT the state of the note just captured. offerUndo("Kept.") as proposed would push the wrong verb onto the strip and collide capture with review, announcing a still-pending note with the word reserved for a decided one.

(4) "waiting on a decision" is not a dialect invented for the spoken layer. It is the consistent accessible-name form in three places: the head chip's label (measured: "9 still to decide. Go through the notes waiting on a decision."), the desk landmark aria-label "Notes waiting on a decision", and the capture announcement. The chip's own label leads with the visible words and only then explains in a sentence. "Delete it from the codebase" would leave the landmark named "Notes still to decide" — clipped, and a regression in the aria layer.

(5) "30s" vs "thirty seconds" is register, not contradiction: `.undoFor` is a tabular-figure meter on a transient strip (`class="undoFor tab"`), the delete dialog is prose. Numerals in meters, words in prose is standard practice, and the invariant prior rounds gated is one NUMBER in every room, which holds. notes-interaction-check.mjs:577 and :1354 both assert `.undoFor` contains "30s"; the fix would break two gated assertions and make a glance-read strip longer, to satisfy a preference.

What survives is one word in one string, not a lexicon failure, and this finding gets it the wrong way round.

refuted.problem: "Cross" is the founder's architecture word for the sealed edge, promoted intact into product chrome and into the spoken layer. A venue manager does not say a note crossed; she says she sent it. It reads as the designer enjoying the metaphor, and it is weaker than the sentence three inches above it in the same panel, which says the same thing in the product's own voice: "Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick and check below." The master's claim that no lab vocabulary reaches product chrome is not true of this word.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on five counts, three of them factual.

1. "Cross" is not lab vocabulary. It is the shipped product's own boundary lexicon. The real Notes product chrome says it verbatim: src/modules/notes/app/workspace/NotesWorkspace.tsx:959 — "Only the task wording you approve crosses over. Everyone in that project can see the task. The note stays here, private, unchanged." And notes-copy.ts's own contract test (notes-copy.test.ts:100) asserts `/only ever/` on the boundary sentence under the label "the boundary sentence must bound what crosses", with the module header at :22 stating "the privacy sentences name what crosses and what does not". The finding's central claim — that the master's "no lab vocabulary in product chrome" is untrue of this word — inverts the fact. The gate it invokes (notes-interaction-check.mjs:1247–1256) tests for `fixture|exploration|extension of the`, i.e. lab-apparatus words. Separately, notes-interaction-check.mjs:1070 gates "and the crossing has one verb" — the lab already adjudicated this lexicon deliberately and locked it.

2. The cited empty twin is misread. notebook.js:1494 "Nothing has crossed" is a `.specName` — a lab caption in the ?state=nothing annotation gallery, headed "EVERY OTHER EMPTY IN THIS PRODUCT / one first move each", sitting alongside captions like "A dead end is a defect" and "An empty ledger explains the promise it exists to keep". I drove ?state=nothing: the product-facing headline in that card already reads "Nothing has left Notes yet." The finding proposes to replace it with "Nothing has gone to Tasks yet." — a rewrite of a caption that is not chrome, of a headline that already avoids the word.

3. The ledger sub is misquoted. Driven at ?state=seam it renders "3 so far, and every note stayed here", not "3 so far". The finding's proposed sub ("3 so far. Every note stayed here.") is the shipped line with a full stop swapped in, presented as a repair.

4. The redundancy claim is wrong about the geometry. The boundary sentence sits on the desk directly above the peel field, in the peel panel; the ledger heading heads the index plane below. Different planes, different jobs: the boundary states a rule about what will happen; the ledger names the record of what did. They are not the same sentence twice.

5. The fix would make it worse. "Send" is already the person's verb in this product — the primary reads "Send to Tasks", the undo strip announces "Sent to Tasks.", N.copy.sentReceipt fires on send. Retitling the ledger "What you have sent to Tasks" collapses the exact distinction the sealed edge is built on: you send, only the picked words cross, the note never moves. The finding's own fix has to bolt "Every note stayed here" and "They get listed here" back on to recover the meaning "cross" carries for free — which is the tell. And adding "cross"/"crossed"/"crossing" to BANNED_IN_COPY is a category error: that list is documented at notes-copy.ts:20 as "no engineer vocabulary" (extract, payload, endpoint, sha256, dto) and the ban would fire on the module's own legally-load-bearing privacy sentences it is documented to protect.

The one arguable grain — that "send" and "cross" name one event in two grammars — is not what this finding argues, and it is a deliberate, gated distinction rather than a slip. Taste stated as a defect.

refuted.problem: The seam pulls its heading, boundary sentence, cancel and primary from N.copy (generic register, verbatim from notes-copy.ts) and then hardcodes the field label as "What the task will say" — the wedding register's string — in a venue operator's room. One panel, two registers. N.copy.wordingLabel ("The task wording") is loaded and used 0 times, and the destination reads a bare "To" rather than N.copy.destinationLabel. A hardcoded product string also sits outside the ban-list test that governs every other string in this flow, so it is the one line in the seam that can drift without a test failing.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The one true atom does not survive contact with the rest of the finding.

What is true: notebook.js:911 hardcodes "What the task will say", that string is verbatim the wedding register's `handoff.wordingLabel` in notes-copy.ts:272, and `N.copy.wordingLabel` ("The task wording") is loaded in data.js:336 and rendered zero times by the master. Everything the finding builds on that is wrong.

1) The singularity claim — "the one line in the seam that can drift without a test failing" — is false, and false inside the same function. peelPanel() renders four other user-visible literals that are in neither register and in no copy object: "Done" (:892), the placeholder "What should the task say?" (:913), "To" (:915), and the primary's precondition state "Write the wording, then send" (:918, repeated at :1712). "Nobody else can read this" (:110, :872) is another. So the panel is not one literal among sourced strings; the label is one of five, and the placeholder sitting eight pixels below it is the same species of string.

2) The "ban-list test that governs every other string in this flow" does not exist. I read the gate. Every string check in notes-interaction-check.mjs runs on RENDERED text, not on provenance: the one-lexicon test (:1065-1071) and the no-lab-vocabulary test (:1247-1258) both evaluate document.body.innerText, so they cover a hardcoded string exactly as they cover a sourced one. The seam's own block (:397-424) gates the boundary with a literal in the test — `.includes("the exact words you pick")` — not against N.copy.handoffBoundary. So every neighbouring string is equally free to drift; nothing in 276 assertions ties rendered text to the copy object. The finding's coverage asymmetry is invented.

3) The destination half is factually wrong. destinationLabel IS used at :915 as the picker's accessible name, and line 409-415 of the gate asserts it: `/Which project/.test(p.getAttribute("aria-label"))`. Driven live in all four rooms, the picker's accessible name is "Which project: The Orchard, events" while its visible text is "To / The Orchard, events". Printing "Which project" visibly beside the project name it already names would be redundant chrome on a button that currently reads as a sentence. That half of the fix makes the work worse.

4) The mechanical half of the fix reverts a decided round-5 improvement. Rendering N.copy.wordingLabel puts "THE TASK WORDING" back over the field — the exact state the round-5 seat condemned (log.html:1884: "a labelled empty box with no question in it", label "The task wording") and whose fix (log.html:1885 step 2) was to make the peel ask. The finding itself concedes "What the task will say is the better line". A fix whose first instruction is to render the worse line is not a fix.

5) The remaining half — "change generic wordingLabel in notes-copy.ts" — rewrites a verbatim product string in the shipping product source. The brief puts copy out of the reviewer's remit ("judged, not rewritten"), and a prior refuter already killed a finding on this exact ground (log.html:1678, point 5).

6) There is no rendered defect. Driven at 1440x960 in ?v=locked|quiet|studio|press, the panel reads: TURN THIS INTO A TASK / "Your note stays here. Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick and check below." / WHAT THE TASK WILL SAY / [field] / To The Orchard, events · Never mind · Send to Tasks. The string names a task and sits beside "Turn this into a task" and "Send to Tasks" — same noun, same register, no wedding vocabulary ("your list", "which plan") anywhere near it. "One panel, two registers" is a provenance fact no reader can detect. Taken at its most charitable — move the literal into data.js under the existing key — the fix produces a byte-identical screen and changes nothing about feel, discoverability or trust. That is below the 9.5 bar, which is about what is on screen, not where the string was declared.

refuted.problem: On the phone the act the whole product exists for is a white circle containing a bare tick, unlabelled, sat beside a naked "58" with no unit, in the same size and shape class as the mic, the photo glyph, the three product-switch tiles and the avatar — eight peer objects in one dock at the exact instant a thought is unsaved. Desktop gets "Save it Ctrl+Enter" in words; the phone, where a venue owner most often captures and where she is least able to guess, gets the least legible object on the screen. The bare number is uninterpretable to anyone who has not seen the desktop's "113 / 4000". The accessible name is correct, so this costs sighted first-timers only, which is the audience the product is sold to.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on the measurements, on the constraint, and on the fix.

1. The central visual claim is factually wrong. I drove the file at 390x844, typed a 61-character draft and measured every object in the dock. The keep control is the ONLY solid-white-filled object in the verbs row: bg rgb(255,255,255), color rgb(17,17,17), 36x44, border-radius 50%, sitting in a dock whose background is rgb(17,17,17). Its supposed peers are not peers: search, mic and photo are unfilled, rgba(255,255,255,0.62) on ink; the three suite tiles are 36px rounded SQUARES (border-radius 10px) at rgba(255,255,255,0.14); the avatar is a 30px disc carrying letters, in a separate grid column (.dockRow[data-suite]) behind a rule, with a 39px gap between the commit at x=154..190 and the first tile at x=229. The crop confirms it by eye: the white disc is the loudest thing on the phone, not "the least legible object on the screen". Fill, shape and isolation are doing precisely the work the finding says is absent, and doing it inside a three-colour lock where fill is the only remaining lever.

2. The proposed fix breaks the locked architecture and regresses behaviour. "Suppress the three product tiles and the avatar for the duration of the draft" un-merges the capsule from the dock in the exact state the phone is designed around ("on a phone the capsule and the dock merge"), and makes the suite plus the account vanish on the first keystroke and return on the last — live chrome reflowing under a thumb at typing speed, in a build whose whole measured gate exists to stop repaints moving things. It is also the only way the pill physically fits: the verbs row has ~203px between the left inset and the rule, the three verbs already take 114px, and a "Save it" pill needs ~92px.

3. The count half is self-contradictory and introduces a checklist defect. It asks for a pill "spanning from the count to the dock's right inset" while also asking to "drop .dockCount entirely". And `3942 left` states in a second grammar the fact the desktop states as `113 / 4000` — "facts stated in two grammars" is on the standing defect list. A counter that materialises only within 200 of the limit also inserts a new object into the verbs row mid-burst and displaces the commit target at the worst possible instant. The current count is aria-hidden, 11px, always-on-when-live, and costs nothing.

4. What remains is taste stated as a defect. The finding concedes the accessible name is correct; it is gated at scripts/design/notes-interaction-check.mjs:590 ("it says what it does"), alongside four other assertions on this exact control, and notebook.js:781 carries the reasoning for why the commit is in the dock at all. A filled circular check at the end of a compose row is the settled mobile commit idiom (Things, Bear, iOS compose), and here it is the single filled object in an ink bar. There is no argument in the finding for why a word beats fill plus position, only the assertion that desktop has words.
